physics-1-1: Two asteroids attract each other with a gravitational force F. If the distance between their centres is doubled, the new force is:
F ∝ 1/r², so doubling r divides the force by 2² = 4.
The masses of two objects are both doubled and the distance between their centres is also doubled. The gravitational force between them:
F ∝ m₁m₂/r²: the numerator increases by 4 and the denominator by 4, so F is unchanged.
What is the gravitational force exerted by Earth on a 70 kg bushwalker standing at Earth's surface? (Use G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², M_{Earth} = 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg, R_{Earth} = 6.37 × 10⁶ m.)
Calculate the gravitational force exerted by Mars (mass 6.42 × 10²³ kg, radius 3.39 × 10⁶ m) on a 2.0 kg rock sample sitting on its surface. (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²)
Use the radius of Mars as the separation, and remember to square it.
Two 1000 kg cars are parked with their centres 5.0 m apart in a Melbourne car park. The gravitational force between them is closest to: (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²)
F = Gm₁m₂/r² = 6.67×10⁻¹¹ × 10⁶ / 25 ≈ 2.7×10⁻⁶ N. Dividing by r instead of r² gives 1.3×10⁻⁵ N.
An apple falls from a tree in a Yarra Valley orchard. Compared with the force Earth exerts on the apple, the force the apple exerts on Earth is:
equal in magnitude and opposite in direction
much smaller, because the apple's mass is smaller
much larger, because Earth's mass is larger
zero, because the apple is falling
Gravitational forces form a Newton's third law pair: equal magnitude, opposite direction, acting on different bodies.
The SI units of the universal gravitational constant G are:
Rearranging F = Gm₁m₂/r² gives G = Fr²/(m₁m₂), with units N m² kg⁻².
When a ball is dropped, Earth and the ball exert equal and opposite gravitational forces on each other. Explain why we observe the ball accelerating but not Earth.
The forces are equal in size, but a = F/m. Earth's mass is about 10²⁴ times larger than the ball's, so Earth's acceleration is far too small to notice, while the ball accelerates at about 9.8 m s⁻².
Full marks need both the equal forces (third law) and a = F/m with Earth's huge mass.

The Moon (mass 7.35 × 10²² kg) orbits Earth at a mean centre-to-centre distance of 3.84 × 10⁸ m. The gravitational force between Earth and the Moon is closest to: (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², M_{Earth} = 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg)
F = GMm/r² = 6.67×10⁻¹¹ × 5.97×10²⁴ × 7.35×10²² / (3.84×10⁸)² ≈ 1.98×10²⁰ N. Forgetting to square r gives 7.62×10²⁸ N.
If the distance between two spherical masses is tripled, the gravitational force between them becomes:
F ∝ 1/r², so tripling r reduces F by 3² = 9.
One of two masses is halved and the separation of their centres is also halved. The gravitational force:
Jupiter (mass 1.90 × 10²⁷ kg) and its moon Io (mass 8.93 × 10²² kg) are 4.22 × 10⁸ m apart, centre to centre. Calculate the gravitational force between them. (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²)
A common error is forgetting to square the separation.
The Sun (mass 1.99 × 10³⁰ kg) is 1.50 × 10¹¹ m from Earth. The gravitational force of the Sun on Earth is closest to: (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², M_{Earth} = 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg)
A spacecraft travels directly from Earth to the Moon (mass of Earth ≈ 81 × mass of the Moon). The point where the net gravitational force from Earth and the Moon is zero is located:
about 10% of the way from Earth to the Moon
about 90% of the way from Earth to the Moon
about 99% of the way from Earth to the Moon
Setting GM_{E}/x² = GM_{M}/(d − x)² gives x/(d − x) = √81 = 9, so x = 0.9d.
Which statement about the gravitational force between two masses is correct?
It can be attractive or repulsive depending on the masses
It acts perpendicular to the line joining their centres
It depends on the medium between the two masses
It is always attractive and acts along the line joining their centres
Gravity is always attractive, acts along the line joining the centres of mass, and is not affected by intervening material.
Gravity is described as the weakest of the fundamental forces, yet it holds us firmly on the ground. Explain this apparent contradiction.
G is very small (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹), so the gravitational force between everyday objects is tiny. We feel a large force from Earth only because its mass is enormous (about 6 × 10²⁴ kg).
Point to the small value of G and the very large mass of Earth.

A 1500 kg satellite orbits at an altitude equal to one Earth radius above the surface. The gravitational force on it is closest to: (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², M_{Earth} = 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg, R_{Earth} = 6.37 × 10⁶ m)
The orbital radius is 2R, so F = GMm/(2R)² is one quarter of the surface weight: ≈ 14 700/4 ≈ 3.68×10³ N. Using r = R gives 1.47×10⁴ N; halving instead of quartering gives 7.36×10³ N.
The gravitational force between two lead spheres in a Cavendish-type experiment is 8.0 × 10⁻⁹ N when their centres are 2.0 m apart. What is the force when their centres are 4.0 m apart?
Doubling the separation reduces the force by a factor of 4: 8.0×10⁻⁹/4 = 2.0×10⁻⁹ N.
In 1971 an Apollo astronaut dropped a hammer and a feather together on the Moon and they landed at the same time. The best explanation is that:
the Moon exerts the same gravitational force on both objects
there is no gravity on the Moon
the gravitational acceleration a = GM/r² does not depend on the mass of the falling object
the feather and hammer have the same mass on the Moon
F = GMm/r² and a = F/m, so m cancels; with no air resistance both accelerate equally. The forces themselves differ.
A student claims that Earth pulls on the Moon with a larger force than the Moon pulls on Earth because Earth is more massive. Evaluate this claim.

The claim is incorrect. The forces are a Newton's third law pair, and F = GMm/r² uses both masses symmetrically, so the forces are equal in size and opposite in direction. Earth's larger mass means it accelerates less, not that it pulls harder.
Mention the third law, or the symmetry of the formula, and separate force from acceleration.
Using g = 9.8 N kg⁻¹ at Earth's surface, R = 6.37 × 10⁶ m and G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², the mass of Earth is calculated to be closest to:
M = gR²/G = 9.8 × (6.37×10⁶)² / 6.67×10⁻¹¹ ≈ 5.96×10²⁴ kg. Forgetting to square R gives 9.36×10¹⁷ kg.
A student plots the gravitational force F between two fixed masses against 1/r², where r is their separation. The graph should be:
a straight line through the origin
a straight line with negative gradient
a curve that rises then flattens
F = (Gm₁m₂)(1/r²), so F is directly proportional to 1/r² with gradient Gm₁m₂.
Two 5.0 kg bowling balls sit with their centres 0.50 m apart. The gravitational force between them is: (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²)
F = Gm₁m₂/r² = 6.67×10⁻¹¹ × 25 / 0.25 = 6.67×10⁻⁹ N. Dividing by r instead of r² gives 3.3×10⁻⁹ N.
A spacecraft moves from an orbital radius of 7.0 × 10⁶ m out to 4.2 × 10⁷ m from Earth's centre. By what factor does the gravitational force on it decrease?
The radius increases by a factor of 4.2×10⁷/7.0×10⁶ = 6, so the force decreases by a factor of 6² = 36.
Inverse square law: the force factor is the square of the radius ratio.
Two 50 kg masses attract each other with a gravitational force of 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ N. Calculate the distance between their centres. (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²)
Rearrange F = Gm₁m₂/r² for r and remember the square root.
The distance between two masses is tripled and one of the masses is doubled. The gravitational force between them becomes:
F ∝ m₁m₂/r²: doubling a mass gives × 2, tripling r gives × 1/9, so F becomes 2/9 of its value.
physics-1-2: Using g = GM/R², the gravitational field strength at Earth's surface is closest to: (Use G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², M_{Earth} = 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg, R_{Earth} = 6.37 × 10⁶ m.)
g = 6.67×10⁻¹¹ × 5.97×10²⁴ / (6.37×10⁶)² ≈ 9.81 N kg⁻¹. Not squaring R gives 6.25×10⁷.
The unit N kg⁻¹ for gravitational field strength is equivalent to:
1 N = 1 kg m s⁻², so N kg⁻¹ = m s⁻², the unit of acceleration.

The International Space Station orbits about 400 km above Earth's surface. The gravitational field strength at its altitude is closest to: (Use G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², M_{Earth} = 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg, R_{Earth} = 6.37 × 10⁶ m.)
r = 6.37×10⁶ + 4.0×10⁵ = 6.77×10⁶ m, so g = GM/r² ≈ 8.69 N kg⁻¹, which is still about 89% of the surface value.
Calculate the gravitational field strength at the 'surface' of Jupiter (mass 1.90 × 10²⁷ kg, radius 6.99 × 10⁷ m). (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²)
At a height above Earth's surface equal to one Earth radius, the gravitational field strength is approximately:
The distance from the centre is 2R, so g = 9.8/2² ≈ 2.45 N kg⁻¹.
The Moon has mass 7.35 × 10²² kg and radius 1.74 × 10⁶ m. The gravitational field strength at its surface is closest to: (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²)
Planet P has twice the mass and twice the radius of Earth. The gravitational field strength at its surface, compared with Earth's, is:
Distinguish between mass and weight, using an astronaut travelling from Earth to the Moon as an example.

Mass is the amount of matter in an object (kg) and stays the same everywhere. Weight is the gravitational force on it, W = mg (N), so it depends on g. A 90 kg astronaut has a mass of 90 kg on both Earth and the Moon, but weighs about 882 N on Earth and about 146 N on the Moon (g ≈ 1.62 N kg⁻¹).
Both definitions plus the correct units earn full marks.
A planet has the same average density as Earth but twice Earth's radius. Its surface gravitational field strength is:
M = ρ(4/3)πR³, so g = GM/R² = (4/3)πGρR ∝ R. Doubling R doubles g.
The direction of the gravitational field at any point near a planet is:
away from the centre of the planet
towards the centre of mass of the planet
in the direction the planet rotates
Gravity attracts a test mass towards the centre of mass, so the field points radially inwards.
An 80 kg astronaut stands on Mars (mass 6.42 × 10²³ kg, radius 3.39 × 10⁶ m). Her weight on Mars is closest to: (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²)
g_{Mars} = GM/R² ≈ 3.73 N kg⁻¹, so W = mg = 80 × 3.73 ≈ 298 N. 784 N is her weight on Earth.
Planet X has 4 times the mass and 2 times the radius of Earth. Determine the gravitational field strength at its surface (g_{Earth} = 9.8 N kg⁻¹).
g ∝ M/R² = 4/2² = 1, so g_{X} = 9.8 N kg⁻¹, the same as Earth.
Use ratios rather than full values.
In a gravitational field diagram, regions where the field lines are closer together indicate:
The density of field lines shows field strength; closer lines mean a stronger field.
Gravitational field strength at a point is best defined as:
the gravitational force per unit mass on a small test mass placed at that point
the total gravitational force on any object at that point
the gravitational potential energy of a 1 kg mass at that point
the speed a falling object reaches at that point
g = F/m, the force per kilogram on a test mass, measured in N kg⁻¹.
At what altitude above Earth's surface is the gravitational field strength half its surface value? (R_{Earth} = 6.37 × 10⁶ m)
g ∝ 1/r², so r = √2 R = 9.01×10⁶ m and the altitude is r − R ≈ 2.64×10⁶ m. 9.01×10⁶ m is the radius, not the altitude.
Show how the expression g = GM/r² follows from Newton's law of universal gravitation.
The force on a test mass m at distance r is F = GMm/r². Field strength is force per unit mass, g = F/m = (GMm/r²)/m = GM/r².
State the definition g = F/m and show that m cancels.
Two identical stars are some distance apart. The net gravitational field strength at the midpoint between them is:
twice the field of one star at that point
the same as the field of one star at that point
directed towards one of the stars
At the midpoint, fields of equal size point in opposite directions and cancel.
Over a region the size of a sports oval near Earth's surface, the gravitational field is modelled as uniform. This means the field lines are drawn:
converging to a point above the oval
curved, closer together at the edges
parallel, equally spaced and pointing downwards
A uniform field has the same strength and direction everywhere, shown by parallel, equally spaced lines.
Astronauts on the International Space Station float freely inside the cabin. This is because:
they and the station are both in free fall, accelerating at the same rate towards Earth
the gravitational field at the station's altitude is zero
the station is beyond the reach of Earth's gravity
the station's mass cancels Earth's gravity
g at the ISS is about 8.7 N kg⁻¹; the astronauts feel weightless because everything falls together, so there is no normal force.
A planet has a surface gravitational field strength of 3.7 N kg⁻¹ and a radius of 3.39 × 10⁶ m. Calculate its mass. (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²)
This is approximately the mass of Mars.
A 10 kg box of equipment is taken from Earth to the Moon. On the Moon its mass is:
Mass is the amount of matter and does not change with location; only weight (mg) changes.
Geostationary satellites orbit 4.22 × 10⁷ m from Earth's centre. The gravitational field strength at this radius is closest to: (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², M_{Earth} = 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg)
A space probe is at a distance of 3R from Earth's centre, where R is Earth's radius. The field strength there, as a fraction of the surface value, is:
g ∝ 1/r², so at 3R it is (1/3)² = 1/9 of the surface value. Note that r is measured from the centre, not from the surface.
The measured value of g at Earth's poles (about 9.83 N kg⁻¹) is slightly greater than at the equator (about 9.78 N kg⁻¹). Give one reason for this.

Earth is slightly flattened (an oblate spheroid), so the poles are closer to Earth's centre than the equator. Because g ∝ 1/r², g is larger at the poles. (Earth's rotation also reduces the effective g at the equator.)
One clearly explained reason is enough.

A spacecraft lies on the line between Earth and the Moon, 3.0 × 10⁸ m from Earth's centre and 8.4 × 10⁷ m from the Moon's centre. Calculate the net gravitational field strength there and state its direction. (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², M_{Earth} = 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg, M_{Moon} = 7.35 × 10²² kg)

g_{Earth} = GM_{E}/r² = 3.98×10¹⁴ / (3.0×10⁸)² ≈ 4.42×10⁻³ N kg⁻¹ towards Earth. g_{Moon} = GM_{M}/r² = 4.90×10¹² / (8.4×10⁷)² ≈ 6.95×10⁻⁴ N kg⁻¹ towards the Moon. Net ≈ 3.7×10⁻³ N kg⁻¹ towards Earth.
The fields point in opposite directions, so subtract them.
A planet has twice the mass of Earth and twice its radius. The gravitational field strength at its surface is about:
g = GM/r²: 2M ÷ (2r)² = 2/4 = 1/2 of Earth's value, so 9.8 ÷ 2 = 4.9 N/kg.
physics-1-3: The ISS orbits at a radius of 6.77 × 10⁶ m from Earth's centre. Its orbital speed is closest to: (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², M_{Earth} = 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg)
v = √(GM/r) = √(3.98×10¹⁴ / 6.77×10⁶) ≈ 7.67×10³ m s⁻¹. Omitting the square root gives 5.88×10⁷.
The ISS (orbital radius 6.77 × 10⁶ m, speed 7.67 × 10³ m s⁻¹) has an orbital period closest to:
T = 2πr/v = 2π × 6.77×10⁶ / 7.67×10³ ≈ 5.55×10³ s ≈ 92 min. Leaving out the 2 gives about 46 min.
A geostationary satellite has a period of 24 hours. Its orbital radius from Earth's centre is closest to: (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², M_{Earth} = 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg)
r = ∛(GMT²/4π²) = ∛(3.98×10¹⁴ × 86400² / 4π²) ≈ 4.22×10⁷ m. 3.58×10⁷ m is the altitude above the surface, not the radius.
Starting from Newton's law of gravitation and the centripetal force, derive Kepler's third law, T² = 4π²r³/(GM), for a satellite in circular orbit.
GMm/r² = mv²/r and v = 2πr/T. Substituting: GM/r² = 4π²r/T², which rearranges to T² = 4π²r³/(GM).
Key steps: equate the forces, substitute v = 2πr/T, rearrange.
A satellite is moved to a circular orbit with four times the original radius. According to Kepler's third law, its period becomes:
Two satellites, one of 500 kg and one of 2000 kg, are in circular orbits of the same radius around Earth. Compared with the lighter satellite, the heavier one has:
v = √(GM/r) and T = 2π√(r³/GM) depend only on the central mass and the radius, not on the satellite's mass.
For a satellite in uniform circular orbit around Earth, the net force on the satellite is:
zero, because its speed is constant
the gravitational force, directed towards Earth's centre
Gravity provides the centripetal force; the velocity changes direction, so the net force is not zero. There is no outward 'centrifugal' force in the inertial frame.

A weather satellite is in a circular orbit with a period of 100 minutes. Calculate its altitude above Earth's surface. (Use G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², M_{Earth} = 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg, R_{Earth} = 6.37 × 10⁶ m.)
Convert minutes to seconds and subtract Earth's radius at the end.
A satellite is boosted from a low circular orbit to a higher circular orbit. In the higher orbit its orbital speed is:
v = √(GM/r), so a larger radius gives a smaller orbital speed.
Which set of conditions is required for a geostationary orbit?
Above the poles, period of 24 hours
Above the equator, period of 90 minutes, any direction
Above the equator, period of 24 hours, orbiting in the same direction as Earth's rotation
To stay above one point, the satellite must match Earth's rotation: equatorial, 24 h period, same direction.
The centripetal acceleration of a satellite in circular orbit is equal to:
the gravitational field strength at its orbital radius
its orbital speed divided by its period
The only force is gravity, so a = F/m = GM/r² = g at that radius.
Explain why geostationary satellites, such as the NBN Sky Muster satellites serving rural Australia, are well suited to communications.

A geostationary satellite stays above the same point on the equator because its 24-hour period matches Earth's rotation. Ground dishes can stay pointed at one fixed spot without tracking, giving continuous coverage of a large region.
Link the 24 h period and equatorial orbit to a fixed position in the sky.
The Moon orbits Earth at a radius of 3.84 × 10⁸ m. Using Kepler's third law, its period is closest to: (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², M_{Earth} = 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg)
Mars' moon Phobos orbits at a radius of 9.38 × 10⁶ m with a period of 2.76 × 10⁴ s. The mass of Mars is closest to: (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²)
If a satellite's orbital radius is doubled, its orbital speed changes by a factor of:
v ∝ 1/√r, so doubling r multiplies v by 1/√2 ≈ 0.71.
Mars orbits the Sun at a mean radius of 2.28 × 10¹¹ m and Earth at 1.50 × 10¹¹ m. Use Kepler's third law to find the orbital period of Mars in Earth years.
Using a ratio with Earth avoids needing the Sun's mass.
The work done by Earth's gravitational force on a satellite during one complete uniform circular orbit is:
zero, because the force is always perpendicular to the velocity
positive, because gravity keeps it moving
negative, because gravity slows it down
In a circular orbit gravity is always perpendicular to the displacement, so it does no work and the speed stays constant.
The kinetic energy of a satellite of mass m in a circular orbit of radius r around a planet of mass M is:
mv²/r = GMm/r² gives mv² = GMm/r, so KE = ½mv² = GMm/(2r).
Satellite A orbits Earth at radius r and satellite B at radius 4r. The ratio of their speeds v_{A} : v_{B} is:
The Moon orbits Earth at radius 3.84 × 10⁸ m with a period of 27.3 days. Calculate its orbital speed.
Two moons orbit the same planet. Moon Q's orbital radius is 9 times Moon P's. The ratio of their periods T_{Q} : T_{P} is:
GPS satellites have an orbital period of 12 hours. Given that the geostationary orbital radius (24-hour period) is 4.22 × 10⁷ m, the radius of a GPS orbit is closest to:
An astronaut on a bathroom scale inside an orbiting spacecraft reads zero. This is because:
gravity does not act in space
the astronaut and the scale are falling together, so there is no normal force between them
the astronaut's mass becomes zero in orbit
Apparent weight is the normal force. In free fall everything accelerates at g, so the normal force is zero.
Earth orbits the Sun at a radius of 1.50 × 10¹¹ m with a period of 3.16 × 10⁷ s. Calculate the mass of the Sun. (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²)
Rearranged Kepler's third law; the mass found is that of the central body.
A satellite in a low orbit experiences slight atmospheric drag. Explain what happens to its orbital radius and its speed over time.

Drag removes mechanical energy, so the satellite drops to a smaller orbital radius. Because v = √(GM/r), its speed actually increases as it spirals inwards: gravity does positive work as it falls, adding more kinetic energy than drag removes.
The surprising point is that the speed increases; a full answer links this to v = √(GM/r).
A satellite orbits Earth at a radius of 7.0 × 10⁶ m. Calculate its orbital speed and its period in minutes.
physics-1-4: physics-1-4-1
The area under a gravitational force versus distance graph between two radii represents:
the gravitational field strength
the momentum of the object
the change in gravitational potential energy of the object between those radii
the power required to move the object
Area = ∫F dr = work done against gravity = change in gravitational potential energy.
physics-1-4-2
The area under a gravitational field strength versus distance graph between two radii represents:
the total change in gravitational potential energy
the orbital speed at that radius
the gravitational force per metre
the change in gravitational potential energy per kilogram
Area = ∫g dr, measured in (N kg⁻¹)(m) = J kg⁻¹; multiply by mass to get the energy change.
physics-1-4-3
The units of the area under a gravitational field strength (N kg⁻¹) versus distance (m) graph are:
J kg⁻¹
N m⁻¹
J
N kg⁻¹ m⁻¹
N kg⁻¹ × m = N m kg⁻¹ = J kg⁻¹.
physics-1-4-4
Describe how a gravitational force–distance graph can be used to find the energy needed to move a satellite from one orbital radius to a higher one.

Find the area under the F–r graph between the two radii, for example by counting squares or using trapezia, and multiply by the scale of one square. This area is the work done against gravity, which equals the increase in the satellite's gravitational potential energy.
Name the area, the method for estimating it, and that it equals ΔU.
physics-1-4-5
A 2.0 kg bag is lifted 5.0 m onto a mezzanine floor. Taking g = 9.8 N kg⁻¹, its gravitational potential energy increases by:
physics-1-4-6

On a g–r graph, g is 9.8 N kg⁻¹ at r = 6.4 × 10⁶ m and 8.2 N kg⁻¹ at r = 7.0 × 10⁶ m. Treating the graph as a straight line between these points, the energy needed to raise a 1000 kg satellite between these radii is about:
Area per kg ≈ average g × Δr = 9.0 × 0.6×10⁶ = 5.4×10⁶ J kg⁻¹. Multiply by 1000 kg to get 5.4×10⁹ J. 5.4×10⁶ J leaves out the mass.
physics-1-4-7
Why is ΔU = mgΔh unsuitable for calculating the energy needed to lift a satellite to an altitude of 20 000 km?
mgh applies only to objects at rest
the satellite's mass changes with altitude
mgh ignores Newton's third law
g decreases significantly over that distance, so it cannot be treated as constant
mgh assumes a uniform field. Over large distances g varies with 1/r², so the area under the g–r graph must be used.
physics-1-4-8

The gravitational field strength is 8.13 N kg⁻¹ at r = 7.0 × 10⁶ m and 6.22 N kg⁻¹ at r = 8.0 × 10⁶ m from Earth's centre. Using a single trapezium, estimate the energy required to raise a 250 kg satellite between these radii.
Average g × Δr, then multiply by mass. This slightly overestimates because the curve sags below the chord.
physics-1-4-9
A probe moves from radius r₁ to a larger radius r₂ from Earth's centre. Ignoring changes in kinetic energy, the minimum energy needed equals:
the probe's mass multiplied by the area under the g–r graph from r₁ to r₂
the probe's mass multiplied by g at r₂ only
the area under the g–r graph from 0 to r₁
the gradient of the F–r graph at r₂
The energy needed is the gain in GPE, which equals m × ∫g dr from r₁ to r₂.
physics-1-4-10
A model rocket at Woomera rises vertically after its engine has stopped. As it rises, ignoring air resistance:
both its gravitational potential energy and its kinetic energy increase
its gravitational potential energy increases and its kinetic energy decreases
its gravitational potential energy decreases and its kinetic energy increases
its total mechanical energy decreases
Mechanical energy is conserved, so the kinetic energy turns into gravitational potential energy as height increases.
physics-1-4-11

On a g–r graph, each grid square represents 0.5 N kg⁻¹ by 1.0 × 10⁶ m. The region under the curve between two radii covers about 12 squares. The change in gravitational potential energy of a 200 kg satellite between those radii is:
Each square = 0.5 × 1.0×10⁶ = 5×10⁵ J kg⁻¹. 12 squares = 6.0×10⁶ J kg⁻¹, and × 200 kg = 1.2×10⁹ J.
physics-1-4-12
A student uses ΔU = mgΔh with g = 9.8 N kg⁻¹ to find the GPE gain of a payload lifted to 400 km altitude. Is the answer too high or too low? Explain.

Too high. g decreases with altitude (to about 8.7 N kg⁻¹ at 400 km), so the true average g over the climb is less than 9.8 N kg⁻¹. Using 9.8 N kg⁻¹ throughout overestimates the area under the g–r graph.
Must link the decrease in g to the overestimate.
physics-1-4-13

A meteoroid starts from rest far from Earth. The area under the g–r graph from its starting point to the top of the atmosphere is 3.2 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹. Ignoring other forces, its speed on reaching the atmosphere is about:
Energy gained per kg = ½v², so v = √(2 × 3.2×10⁶) ≈ 2.5×10³ m s⁻¹. Leaving out the factor 2 gives 1.8×10³.
physics-1-4-14
Above Earth's surface, a graph of gravitational field strength g against distance r from Earth's centre is best described as:
a curve decreasing in proportion to 1/r², approaching zero but never reaching it
a straight line decreasing to zero
a horizontal line at 9.8 N kg⁻¹
a straight line increasing with r
g = GM/r² is an inverse square relationship: it falls steeply at first, then flattens towards zero.
physics-1-4-15
For a 500 kg satellite, the area under its gravitational force–distance graph between two radii, compared with the area under the g–r graph between the same radii, is:
the same
500 times larger
500 times smaller
larger by a factor of 500²
F = mg at every r, so ∫F dr = m∫g dr: the area is 500 times larger.
physics-1-4-16

A 450 kg module is lifted from Earth's surface (g = 9.8 N kg⁻¹) to the ISS altitude of 400 km (g = 8.69 N kg⁻¹). Using the average field strength, estimate its increase in gravitational potential energy.
Convert 400 km to 4.0×10⁵ m.
physics-1-4-17
A meteorite falls towards Earth from rest at a great distance. Ignoring air resistance, the kinetic energy it gains equals:
the gradient of the force–distance graph
the gravitational force at the surface multiplied by its mass
the area under the force–distance graph over the distance it falls
zero, because gravity is a conservative force
The loss of GPE (the area under the F–r graph) turns into kinetic energy.
physics-1-4-18
A student estimates the area under a curved g–r graph (decreasing and concave up) by joining the end points with a straight line and finding the trapezium area. This estimate will be:
an underestimate, because the straight line lies below the curve
exact, because the area under any graph is a trapezium
an overestimate, because g increases with r
an overestimate, because the straight line lies above the curve
For a decreasing curve that is concave up, the chord between two points lies above the curve, so the trapezium includes extra area.
physics-1-4-19

The area under Earth's g–r graph from the surface (R = 6.37 × 10⁶ m) to infinity equals GM/R = 6.25 × 10⁷ J kg⁻¹. The minimum launch speed needed to escape Earth's gravity (ignoring air resistance) is closest to:
Set ½v² = 6.25×10⁷ J kg⁻¹, so v = √(1.25×10⁸) ≈ 1.12×10⁴ m s⁻¹. 7.91×10³ m s⁻¹ is the speed for a circular orbit at the surface.
physics-1-4-20

On a force–distance graph for a 1200 kg satellite, each grid square represents 100 N by 1.0 × 10⁵ m. The area under the curve between two orbital radii is 35 squares. Calculate the change in gravitational potential energy.
Because this is a force graph, the area is already energy; do not multiply by mass again.
physics-1-4-21
A cricket ball is thrown vertically upwards at 20 m s⁻¹. Using conservation of energy (g = 9.8 m s⁻²) and ignoring air resistance, its maximum height is closest to:
mgh = ½mv², so h = v²/(2g) = 400/19.6 ≈ 20.4 m. Leaving out the 2 gives about 41 m.
physics-1-4-22
A 60 kg hiker walks from Thredbo village (1365 m above sea level) to the summit of Mt Kosciuszko (2228 m). Taking g = 9.8 N kg⁻¹, her gain in gravitational potential energy is closest to:
ΔU = mgΔh = 60 × 9.8 × 863 ≈ 5.07×10⁵ J. Using the summit height alone gives 1.3×10⁶ J.
physics-1-4-23
A small mass moves from the surface of a planet out to 2R from its centre. Which graph's area gives the work done per kilogram against gravity?
The area under the gravitational force–distance graph from 0 to R
The gradient of the field strength–distance graph at R
The area under the field strength–distance graph from 0 to 2R
The area under the gravitational field strength–distance graph from R to 2R
Work per kg = ∫g dr over the actual path, from R to 2R.
physics-1-4-24

A coin is dropped from the Eureka Skydeck in Melbourne, 285 m above the ground. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 9.8 m s⁻², use energy conservation to find its speed just before hitting the ground.
Mass cancels; in reality air resistance would make the speed much lower.
physics-1-4-25
Explain why the gravitational potential energy of a satellite increases as it moves to a larger orbital radius, with reference to work done.

Gravity pulls the satellite towards Earth, so moving it outwards means work must be done against the gravitational force (the force and the displacement are opposite). This work is stored as an increase in gravitational potential energy, equal to the area under the F–r graph.
Say that work is done against gravity, and link it to the area.
physics-1-4-c1

On a graph of gravitational field strength against distance from a planet's centre, the area under the graph between r₁ and r₂ is 2.0 × 10⁶ J/kg. The minimum energy needed to move a 500 kg probe from r₁ to r₂ is:
The area under a g–r graph is the change in GPE per kilogram. Multiply by the mass: 2.0 × 10⁶ × 500 = 1.0 × 10⁹ J.
physics-2-1: Two small spheres carrying charges of +2.0 μC and +3.0 μC are 0.30 m apart. What is the magnitude and nature of the electrostatic force between them? (k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²)
F = kq₁q₂/r² = 8.99 × 10⁹ × (2.0 × 10⁻⁶)(3.0 × 10⁻⁶)/0.30² ≈ 0.60 N; like charges repel. 0.18 N results from forgetting to square r.
The distance between two point charges is tripled. The electrostatic force between them becomes:
Coulomb's law is an inverse square law, so F ∝ 1/r²; tripling r divides F by 3² = 9.
Both point charges are doubled in magnitude and the distance between them is also doubled. The force between them:
The product q₁q₂ increases by a factor of 4 and r² increases by a factor of 4, so F = kq₁q₂/r² is unchanged.
What is the electric field at a point 0.50 m from a point charge of +4.0 nC? (k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²)
1.4 × 10² N C⁻¹ directed towards the charge
72 N C⁻¹ directed away from the charge
2.9 × 10² N C⁻¹ directed away from the charge
1.4 × 10² N C⁻¹ directed away from the charge
E = kq/r² = 8.99 × 10⁹ × 4.0 × 10⁻⁹/0.25 ≈ 144 N C⁻¹. The field of a positive charge points away from it.
Two parallel plates 2.0 cm apart have a potential difference of 500 V across them. What is the electric field strength between the plates?
E = V/d = 500/0.020 = 2.5 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹. Remember to convert cm to m.
An electron is placed between two parallel plates where the uniform field strength is 2.5 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹. What is the magnitude of the force on the electron?
An electron is released from rest midway between two charged parallel plates. In which direction does it accelerate?
It does not accelerate because the field is uniform
The electric field points from the positive to the negative plate; an electron has negative charge, so the force on it is opposite to the field, towards the positive plate.
Which statement about electric field lines is correct?
They can cross at points where the field is very strong.
They are drawn further apart where the field is stronger.
They always show the actual path taken by a charged particle.
They begin on positive charges and end on negative charges.
Field lines point in the direction of force on a positive test charge, so they start on positive and end on negative charges; they never cross, and closer spacing means a stronger field.
Which statement best describes the electric field between two large, oppositely charged parallel plates, away from the edges?
It is uniform in both magnitude and direction.
It is strongest close to the positive plate.
It decreases with the inverse square of distance from each plate.
It is zero at the midpoint between the plates.
Between large parallel plates the field lines are parallel and evenly spaced, so E = V/d is the same at every point away from the edges.
How much work is done by the electric field on an electron accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 2000 V?
W = qV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 2000 = 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁶ J, which equals the kinetic energy gained.
Charges +Q and −Q of equal magnitude are fixed a distance apart. At the midpoint between them, the electric field is:
non-zero and perpendicular to the line joining the charges
The field from +Q points away from +Q (towards −Q) and the field from −Q points towards −Q, so both point the same way and add.
A charge of +4q and a charge of +q are separated by a distance d. At what point on the line between them is the electric field zero?
Set 4q/(d − x)² = q/x², giving d − x = 2x, so x = d/3 from the smaller charge.
At a distance r from a point charge the electric field strength is E. What is the field strength at a distance 2r?
The field of a point charge E = kq/r² follows an inverse square law, so doubling r reduces E by a factor of 4.
A proton is placed in a uniform electric field of 3.0 × 10³ N C⁻¹. What is the magnitude of its acceleration? (mₚ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg)
a = qE/m = (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 3.0 × 10³)/1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ ≈ 2.9 × 10¹¹ m s⁻². Using the electron mass gives 5.3 × 10¹⁴ m s⁻².
Which statement correctly compares electric and gravitational fields?
Gravitational fields of point masses follow an inverse square law but electric fields of point charges do not.
Electric fields only exert forces on moving charges.
Electric forces can be attractive or repulsive, whereas gravitational forces are only attractive.
The gravitational force between two protons is greater than the electric force between them.
Both fields of point sources are inverse square fields, but charge comes in two signs, so electric forces can repel; gravity only attracts and is far weaker between protons.
Two identical small conducting spheres carry charges of +6 μC and −2 μC. They are touched together and then returned to their original separation. Compared with the original force, the new force is:
one-third of the original magnitude, and attractive
two-thirds of the original magnitude, and repulsive
one-third of the original magnitude, and repulsive
Charge is shared: total +4 μC gives +2 μC each. Originally |q₁q₂| = 12 (μC)², now 4 (μC)², so the force is 1/3 as large and, with like charges, repulsive.
The unit N C⁻¹ for electric field strength is equivalent to:
1 V = 1 J C⁻¹ = 1 N m C⁻¹, so V m⁻¹ = N m C⁻¹ m⁻¹ = N C⁻¹.
An electron is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 500 V. What is its final speed? (mₑ = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg)
Calculate the magnitude of the electrostatic force between the electron and proton in a hydrogen atom, given their separation is 5.3 × 10⁻¹¹ m. State whether the force is attractive or repulsive.
Award marks for correct substitution, squaring r, and stating attractive (opposite charges).
Describe in words the electric field pattern around two equal positive point charges placed near each other.

Field lines radiate outwards from each charge and curve away from the region between them, so no lines connect the two charges. At the midpoint there is a neutral point where the field is zero. Lines never cross and are densest close to each charge.
Key points: lines outward, repel/bend away from each other, neutral point at the centre.
An electron enters the region between two horizontal charged parallel plates travelling horizontally. Explain why its path between the plates is parabolic.

The uniform field exerts a constant vertical force (qE), so the electron has constant vertical acceleration, while its horizontal velocity is unchanged because there is no horizontal force. Constant velocity in one direction combined with constant acceleration in the perpendicular direction produces a parabola, like a projectile.
Must mention constant force/acceleration perpendicular to the plates and constant horizontal velocity.
Two parallel plates are 5.0 mm apart. What potential difference must be applied to produce a uniform electric field of 4.0 × 10⁵ V m⁻¹ between them?
Common error: forgetting to convert 5.0 mm to 5.0 × 10⁻³ m.
A small charged sphere experiences a force of 2.4 × 10⁻³ N at a point where the electric field strength is 8.0 × 10³ N C⁻¹. Calculate the magnitude of the charge on the sphere.
Calculate the ratio of the electrostatic force to the gravitational force between two protons, and comment on the result. (k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², mₚ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg)
Fₑ/F_{g} = ke²/(Gm²) = (8.99 × 10⁹ × (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹)²)/(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × (1.67 × 10⁻²⁷)²) ≈ 1.2 × 10³⁶. The electric force is vastly larger, so gravity is negligible between subatomic particles.
The distance cancels because both forces are inverse square.
Point charges of +3.0 nC and −3.0 nC are 0.20 m apart. Calculate the magnitude and direction of the electric field at the midpoint between them.

Each charge is 0.10 m away: E = kq/r² = 8.99 × 10⁹ × 3.0 × 10⁻⁹/0.010 ≈ 2.7 × 10³ N C⁻¹. Both fields point towards the negative charge, so E_{total} ≈ 5.4 × 10³ N C⁻¹ directed towards the −3.0 nC charge.
Students often subtract the fields; here they add because both point towards −3.0 nC.
A +2 µC charge and a −8 µC charge are 0.30 m apart. Where is the electric field zero?
0.30 m from the +2 µC charge, on the side away from the −8 µC charge
0.10 m from the +2 µC charge, between the charges
0.30 m from the −8 µC charge, on the side away from the +2 µC charge
Between opposite charges the fields point the same way, so the zero point is outside, nearer the smaller charge: 2/x² = 8/(x + 0.30)² gives x + 0.30 = 2x, so x = 0.30 m.
physics-2-2: physics-2-2-1
A long straight wire lies horizontally on a bench and carries a current towards the north. What is the direction of the magnetic field at a point directly above the wire?
West
North
East
Vertically upwards
Using the right-hand grip rule with the thumb pointing north, the fingers curl so that the field above the wire points east (and below it points west).
physics-2-2-2
Which description best matches the magnetic field around a long straight current-carrying wire?
Straight lines radiating outward from the wire
Straight lines parallel to the wire
A uniform field directed along the wire
Concentric circles centred on the wire, in planes perpendicular to it
The field of a straight wire forms closed circular loops around it, perpendicular to the current, with direction given by the right-hand grip rule.
physics-2-2-3
The distance from a long straight current-carrying wire is doubled. The magnetic field strength:
halves
quarters
doubles
stays the same
The magnetic field of a long straight wire is proportional to I/r, so doubling the distance halves the field.
physics-2-2-4
Which statement best describes the magnetic field inside a long solenoid carrying a steady current?
It is zero because fields from opposite sides cancel.
It is approximately uniform and parallel to the solenoid's axis.
It forms circles around the axis of the solenoid.
It is strongest close to the windings and zero on the axis.
Contributions from all the loops add along the axis, giving a strong, nearly uniform field parallel to the axis inside a long solenoid.
physics-2-2-5
Looking at one end of a solenoid, the current is seen to flow anticlockwise. That end of the solenoid behaves as:
a south pole
neither pole, because poles only form with an iron core
a north pole
a north or south pole depending on the number of turns
Curl the fingers of your right hand anticlockwise in the direction of current; your thumb points towards you, so field lines emerge from that end, making it a north pole.
physics-2-2-6
Which change would NOT increase the magnetic field strength inside a solenoid?
Increasing the current
Winding more turns over the same length
Inserting a soft iron core
Stretching it to twice its length while keeping the same number of turns and current
The field depends on turns per unit length and current; stretching the coil reduces turns per metre and so weakens the field.
physics-2-2-7
Inside a bar magnet, the magnetic field lines are directed:
from the south pole to the north pole
from the north pole to the south pole
radially outwards from the centre
nowhere, because the field inside is zero
Magnetic field lines are closed loops: outside the magnet they run N to S, so inside they return from S to N.
physics-2-2-8
Which statement correctly distinguishes magnetic field lines from electric field lines?
Magnetic field lines begin on north monopoles and end on south monopoles.
Magnetic field lines always form closed loops, whereas electric field lines from static charges begin and end on charges.
Magnetic field lines can cross, but electric field lines cannot.
Electric field lines form closed loops around stationary charges.
No magnetic monopoles have been found, so magnetic field lines have no start or end point and form closed loops.
physics-2-2-9
Two long parallel wires carry currents in the same direction. The wires will:
repel each other
experience no force
attract each other
twist so that they become perpendicular
Each wire sits in the magnetic field of the other; applying the right-hand rules shows the forces point towards each other when currents are in the same direction.
physics-2-2-10
Two long parallel wires carry equal currents in the same direction. At the point midway between them, the magnetic field is:
twice the field due to one wire
equal to the field due to one wire
directed parallel to the wires
zero
At the midpoint the two fields are equal in size but, by the right-hand grip rule, opposite in direction, so they cancel.
physics-2-2-11
The tesla (T), the unit of magnetic field strength, is equivalent to:
N A⁻¹ m⁻¹
N C⁻¹
V m⁻¹
A m N⁻¹
From F = IlB, B = F/(Il), so 1 T = 1 N A⁻¹ m⁻¹.
physics-2-2-12
The north pole of a compass needle points towards Earth's geographic North Pole. This means that near Earth's geographic North Pole there is:
a magnetic north pole
a magnetic south pole
a region where Earth's magnetic field is zero
a magnetic pole that alternates between north and south daily
Opposite poles attract, so the north pole of a compass is attracted to a magnetic south pole, located near the geographic North Pole.
physics-2-2-13
In a magnetic field diagram, a region of stronger magnetic field is shown by:
field lines drawn further apart
field lines that cross each other
field lines drawn closer together
field lines that end at a point
The density of field lines represents field strength; lines never cross and magnetic lines never end.
physics-2-2-14
The current in a solenoid is doubled and the number of turns per metre is halved. The magnetic field inside the solenoid:
doubles
quadruples
halves
is unchanged
The field inside a long solenoid is proportional to nI (turns per metre × current); doubling I and halving n leaves nI unchanged.
physics-2-2-15
A long straight wire is vertical and carries current upwards. Viewed from above, the magnetic field lines around it circulate:
anticlockwise
clockwise
radially outward
vertically upwards, parallel to the wire
With the right thumb pointing up (towards a viewer looking down), the fingers curl anticlockwise.
physics-2-2-16
A long vertical wire carries current upwards. What is the direction of the magnetic field at a point 2.0 cm due east of the wire?
South
North
East
Vertically upwards
Viewed from above the field circulates anticlockwise; on the east side of the wire, anticlockwise circulation points north.
physics-2-2-17
What is the fundamental source of magnetic fields?
Stationary electric charges
Gravitational mass
Moving electric charges
Only permanent magnets
Magnetic fields are produced by moving charges, such as currents in wires and the motion and spin of electrons in magnetic materials.
physics-2-2-18
Iron filings are sprinkled around a current-carrying solenoid. The pattern outside the solenoid most closely resembles that of:
concentric circles centred on the middle of the solenoid
straight lines radiating outward in all directions
nothing, because the entire field is confined inside the solenoid
a bar magnet, with poles at each end
A solenoid's external field is like that of a bar magnet, emerging from the north end and re-entering at the south end.
physics-2-2-19
Describe the magnetic field around a long straight current-carrying wire and explain how its direction is found.

The field forms concentric circles around the wire in planes perpendicular to the current, getting weaker with distance from the wire. Its direction is found with the right-hand grip rule: point the right thumb in the direction of conventional current and the fingers curl in the direction of the field.
Marks for circular shape, perpendicular planes, and correct use of the right-hand grip rule.
physics-2-2-20
Explain why the magnetic field inside a long solenoid is strong and nearly uniform, while the field outside is relatively weak.

Inside, the fields from every loop point in the same direction along the axis and add together, giving a strong, nearly uniform field. Outside, the field lines spread out over a much larger region (and contributions from opposite sides of loops partly cancel), so the field is much weaker.
Key idea: superposition of fields from each turn.
physics-2-2-21
State two differences between magnetic field lines and electric field lines from static charges.

1. Magnetic field lines form closed loops, while electric field lines start on positive charges and end on negative charges. 2. The magnetic force on a moving charge is perpendicular to the field lines, whereas the electric force on a charge is along the field lines. (Also: magnetic fields exert no force on stationary charges.)
Any two valid differences.
physics-2-2-22
A wire perpendicular to this page carries current into the page. Describe the direction of the magnetic field around it as seen by someone looking at the page.
The field forms circles around the wire that run clockwise as seen by the viewer. With the right thumb pointing into the page, the fingers curl clockwise.
Into the page → clockwise; out of the page → anticlockwise.
physics-2-2-23
Two long parallel wires 10 cm apart carry equal currents in opposite directions. Explain what the magnetic field is like at the point midway between them.

The field from each wire at the midpoint has the same magnitude, and because the currents are opposite, the right-hand grip rule shows both fields point in the same direction. They add, so the field is twice that of one wire, directed perpendicular to the plane containing the wires.
Contrast with same-direction currents, where the midpoint field is zero.
physics-2-2-24
A solenoid produces a magnetic field of 4.0 mT inside it when the current is 2.0 A. What is the field when the current is increased to 5.0 A, with all else unchanged?
Direct proportion between solenoid field and current.
physics-2-2-25
Explain how the polarity of an electromagnet can be reversed and why a soft iron core is commonly used.

Reversing the direction of the current reverses the field, swapping the north and south poles. A soft iron core is easily magnetised, which greatly strengthens and concentrates the field, and it loses its magnetism quickly when the current is switched off.
Two parts: reverse current; soft iron strengthens field and demagnetises easily.
physics-2-2-c1
Two long parallel wires carry equal currents in the same direction. At the point midway between them, the magnetic field is:
Zero, and the wires attract each other
Double that of one wire, and the wires repel
Zero, and the wires repel each other
Double that of one wire, and the wires attract
By the right-hand grip rule the two fields point in opposite directions midway, so they cancel. Parallel currents attract.
physics-2-3: A straight wire 0.50 m long carries a current of 3.0 A at right angles to a uniform magnetic field of 0.20 T. What is the magnitude of the force on the wire?
A current-carrying wire is placed parallel to a uniform magnetic field. The magnetic force on the wire is:
equal to IlB, directed along the wire
equal to IlB, perpendicular to the wire
The force on a current depends on the component of the field perpendicular to the current; when parallel, F = 0.
A rectangular coil of 50 turns has a side of length 0.10 m perpendicular to a 0.40 T magnetic field. The coil carries 2.0 A. What is the force on that side?
F = nIlB = 50 × 2.0 × 0.10 × 0.40 = 4.0 N. 0.080 N is the force for a single turn.
A horizontal wire carries current towards the east in a magnetic field directed vertically downwards. What is the direction of the force on the wire?
Using the right-hand slap rule (fingers along B down, thumb along current east), the palm faces north; equivalently F ∝ I × B gives north.
An electron travels north through a uniform magnetic field directed vertically upwards. What is the direction of the magnetic force on the electron when it enters the field?
For a positive charge the force (v × B) would be east; the electron is negative, so the force is west.
A proton moves at 2.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ perpendicular to a 0.50 T magnetic field. What is the magnitude of the magnetic force on it?
An electron travelling at 3.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ enters a uniform magnetic field of 2.0 × 10⁻³ T at right angles. What is the radius of its circular path? (mₑ = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg)
A charged particle moves in a circle in a uniform magnetic field. How much work does the magnetic force do on the particle during one revolution?
qvB × 2πr, because the force acts all the way around the circle
A positive amount, because the particle is accelerating
A negative amount, because the force points towards the centre
Zero, because the force is always perpendicular to the velocity
Work requires a force component along the displacement; the magnetic force is always perpendicular to the motion, so it does no work and the speed stays constant.
A charged particle moving perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field has its speed doubled. The radius of its circular path:
r = mv/(qB), so r is directly proportional to v.
A proton and an electron enter the same uniform magnetic field with the same velocity, perpendicular to the field. Which statement is correct?
Both have the same radius but curve in opposite senses.
The proton's path has a much larger radius and curves in the opposite sense to the electron's.
The electron's path has the larger radius and both curve in the same sense.
The proton's path has the larger radius and both curve in the same sense.
They have equal and opposite charges, so they curve in opposite senses; r = mv/(qB) and the proton is about 1840 times more massive, so its radius is far larger.

A charged particle passes undeflected through a region where a uniform electric field of 2.0 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹ is perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.10 T (both perpendicular to its velocity). What is the particle's speed?
Undeflected means qE = qvB, so v = E/B = 2.0 × 10⁴/0.10 = 2.0 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹.
A charged particle moves in the same direction as a uniform magnetic field. Its subsequent motion is:
a circle in a plane perpendicular to the field
a parabola curving in the direction of the field
a straight line at constant speed
When v is parallel to B, F = qvB sinθ = 0, so the particle continues with constant velocity.
In a simple DC motor, what is the purpose of the split-ring commutator?
To reverse the current in the coil every half turn so the torque keeps acting in the same direction
To convert the DC supply into AC for the brushes
To increase the strength of the magnetic field
To keep the current in the coil flowing in the same direction at all times
Without the commutator the torque would reverse each half turn and the coil would just oscillate; the commutator reverses the coil current at the right moment.
In a DC motor, the coil sides that are parallel to the magnetic field at a given instant experience a force that is:
A current parallel to the field experiences no magnetic force (F = IlB sinθ with θ = 0).

An alpha particle (charge +2e, mass 4 u) and a proton (charge +e, mass 1 u) enter the same magnetic field with the same speed, perpendicular to the field. What is the ratio of the radius of the alpha particle's path to the proton's?
r = mv/(qB): the alpha has 4 times the mass and 2 times the charge, so its radius is 4/2 = 2 times larger.
For a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field, both the current direction and the magnetic field direction are reversed. The force on the wire:
stays in the same direction with the same magnitude
Reversing one of I or B reverses the force; reversing both reverses it twice, leaving the force unchanged.
A charged particle moves in a circle perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field. If its speed is increased, which statement is correct?
The radius increases but the period stays the same.
The radius and the period both increase.
The radius decreases and the period increases.
The radius stays the same but the period decreases.
r = mv/(qB) increases with v, while T = 2πr/v = 2πm/(qB) does not depend on speed.
A singly charged positive ion travelling at 1.0 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹ follows a circular path of radius 0.10 m in a 0.50 T magnetic field. What is the mass of the ion?
Show that a particle of mass m and charge q moving at speed v perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field B travels in a circle of radius r = mv/(qB).
The magnetic force qvB is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it provides the centripetal force: qvB = mv²/r. Rearranging gives r = mv/(qB).
Must identify the magnetic force as the centripetal force.
An electron travelling at 4.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ is to move in a circle of radius 0.050 m. What magnetic field strength is required? (mₑ = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg)
Explain why a magnetic field can change the direction of a moving charged particle but cannot change its speed.

The magnetic force is always perpendicular to the particle's velocity, so it has no component along the direction of motion and does no work. With no work done the kinetic energy, and therefore the speed, is constant; only the direction changes.
Key words: perpendicular, no work, kinetic energy constant.
A 20-turn rectangular coil has a side 5.0 cm long perpendicular to a 0.30 T magnetic field. If the coil carries 1.5 A, calculate the force on that side.
Remember to multiply by the number of turns and convert cm to m.
Explain the role of the split-ring commutator and brushes in a DC motor.

The brushes make a sliding electrical contact between the external DC supply and the rotating coil. The split-ring commutator reverses the direction of current in the coil every half rotation (when the coil plane is perpendicular to the field), so the forces on each side always produce torque in the same rotational direction and the motor keeps turning.
Mention reversing current each half turn and torque in a constant direction.

A horizontal wire of length 0.20 m and mass 6.0 g lies perpendicular to a horizontal magnetic field of 0.50 T. What current is needed in the wire for the magnetic force to support its weight? (g = 9.8 m s⁻²)
Convert 6.0 g to 6.0 × 10⁻³ kg; the current direction must give an upward force.
A positive ion travels horizontally towards the east and enters a region where the magnetic field points vertically upwards. In which direction is the ion initially deflected? Justify your answer.
South. Using F = qv × B (or the right-hand slap rule) with velocity east and field up, the force on a positive charge points south.
For a negative particle the deflection would be north.
An electron moves at 2.0 × 10⁶ m/s perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 5.0 mT. Find the radius of its path.
physics-2-4: physics-2-4-1
Where is the Australian Synchrotron located?
Lucas Heights, New South Wales
Parkes, New South Wales
Clayton, Victoria
Hobart, Tasmania
The Australian Synchrotron is in the Melbourne suburb of Clayton, next to Monash University; Lucas Heights hosts the OPAL research reactor.
physics-2-4-2
In the storage ring of a synchrotron, what is the main purpose of the bending magnets?
To increase the speed of the electrons
To produce the electrons by thermionic emission
To slow the electrons before they reach the beamlines
To change the direction of the electrons so they follow a closed path
Magnetic forces are perpendicular to velocity, so they steer the beam around the ring without changing its speed.
physics-2-4-3
What is the function of the radio-frequency (RF) cavities in a synchrotron storage ring?
To replace the energy the electrons lose as synchrotron radiation
To bend the electrons around the ring
To focus the X-rays onto samples
To remove unwanted electrons from the beam
RF cavities provide oscillating electric fields that give the electrons back the energy they radiate, keeping their energy constant.
physics-2-4-4
Synchrotron radiation is emitted when:
electrons collide with atoms in the vacuum tube
electrons are accelerated by changing direction in a magnetic field
electrons travel in a straight line at constant velocity
electrons are absorbed by the walls of the storage ring
Accelerating charges radiate electromagnetic energy; in a bending magnet the electrons are accelerated centripetally and emit intense light tangent to their path.
physics-2-4-5
In an electron gun, electrons released from a heated filament are accelerated by:
the magnetic field of the filament current
gravitational attraction towards the anode
the electric field between the cathode and the anode
collisions with gas molecules in the tube
The potential difference between cathode and anode creates an electric field that does work qV on each electron.
physics-2-4-6
An electron gun accelerates electrons from rest through 15 kV. What kinetic energy does each electron gain?
physics-2-4-7
Why are magnetic fields used to steer charged particles in accelerators, but not to increase their kinetic energy?
The magnetic force is perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work on the particles.
Magnetic fields only act on stationary charges.
Magnetic fields are too weak to affect electrons.
The magnetic force always acts opposite to the velocity, slowing the particles.
A force perpendicular to motion changes direction only; to change kinetic energy, a force component along the motion is needed.
physics-2-4-8
Why are electric fields used to accelerate charged particles in a linear accelerator?
Electric fields only exert forces perpendicular to the particle's motion.
The electric force acts along the field, so it can do work on the particles and increase their kinetic energy.
Electric fields keep the particles moving in a circle.
Electric fields reduce the mass of the particles.
A charge in an electric field experiences F = qE in the field direction; aligning the field with the motion transfers energy W = qV.
physics-2-4-9
As electrons gain speed in a synchrotron's booster ring, what must happen to the magnetic field in the bending magnets for the electrons to stay on the same circular path?
It must decrease.
It must stay constant.
It must increase.
It must reverse direction every lap.
The radius r = mv/(qB) increases with speed, so B must increase in step with the electrons' momentum to keep r constant.
physics-2-4-10
What is the role of the linear accelerator (linac) at the start of a synchrotron?
To store electrons for many hours
To bend the electrons into a circular orbit
To convert electrons into X-ray photons
To accelerate electrons from the electron gun to very high speed in a straight line using electric fields
The linac uses a series of electric fields to boost electrons to nearly the speed of light before injection into the booster ring.
physics-2-4-11
An electron is accelerated from rest through 100 V and then enters a 1.0 × 10⁻³ T magnetic field at right angles. What is the radius of its path? (mₑ = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg)
3.4 cm
2.4 cm
6.7 cm
1.7 cm
physics-2-4-12
In a mass spectrometer, ions with the same charge and speed enter a uniform magnetic field. Compared with lighter ions, heavier ions:
follow a path of smaller radius
follow a path of larger radius
follow the same path
travel in a straight line
r = mv/(qB), so for equal q, v and B, radius is directly proportional to mass.
physics-2-4-13
Which is a common use of synchrotron light at facilities such as the Australian Synchrotron?
Generating electricity for the power grid
Detecting gravitational waves
Determining the structure of proteins using X-ray diffraction
Powering nuclear fission reactions
The intense, highly collimated X-rays allow detailed diffraction studies of crystals, including proteins used in drug design.
physics-2-4-14
The accelerating voltage of an electron gun is increased by a factor of 4. Assuming non-relativistic speeds, the final speed of the electrons:
increases by a factor of 4
increases by a factor of 16
increases by a factor of √2
doubles
qV = ½mv², so v ∝ √V; four times the voltage gives √4 = 2 times the speed.
physics-2-4-15
Electrons in a synchrotron storage ring of circumference 216 m travel at very nearly the speed of light (3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹). Approximately how long does each lap take?
7.2 μs
1.4 μs
7.2 ms
t = distance/speed = 216/3.0 × 10⁸ ≈ 7.2 × 10⁻⁷ s = 0.72 μs.
physics-2-4-16
An alpha particle (charge +2e) is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 50 kV. How much kinetic energy does it gain?
W = qV = 2 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 5.0 × 10⁴ = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁴ J (100 keV). 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁵ J results from using charge e instead of 2e.
physics-2-4-17
An electron enters the region between two charged parallel plates moving parallel to the plates. While between the plates, its velocity component parallel to the plates:
increases steadily
decreases steadily
stays constant
becomes zero
The uniform electric field acts only perpendicular to the plates, so there is no force, and no acceleration, parallel to them.
physics-2-4-18
An electron moves in a circular path in a uniform magnetic field directed into the page. As seen by someone looking at the page, the electron circulates:
anticlockwise
in a straight line into the page
in an outward spiral at constant speed
clockwise
For an electron moving to the right with B into the page, the force qv × B (with negative q) points down the page, towards the centre below it, so the motion is clockwise.
physics-2-4-19
Outline the role of each of these parts of the Australian Synchrotron: electron gun, linac, booster ring, storage ring and beamlines.

Electron gun: produces electrons by thermionic emission and accelerates them with an electric field. Linac: uses electric fields to accelerate the electrons to near light speed in a straight line. Booster ring: further increases their energy as bending magnets' field increases to keep them on the circular path. Storage ring: bending magnets keep the electrons circulating for hours, producing synchrotron light, while RF cavities replace lost energy. Beamlines: channel the synchrotron light to experimental stations.
One correct role per part.
physics-2-4-20
Explain why electrons in a synchrotron storage ring emit synchrotron radiation and why energy must be continually supplied to them.

In the bending magnets the electrons change direction, so they are accelerating; accelerating charges emit electromagnetic radiation. This radiation carries energy away, so RF cavities must keep supplying energy, otherwise the electrons would lose energy and their orbit would not be maintained.
Link acceleration (change in direction) to radiation, and radiation to energy loss.
physics-2-4-21
An electron gun accelerates electrons from rest through 3.0 kV. Calculate the speed of the electrons leaving the gun. (mₑ = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg)
Non-relativistic treatment is acceptable at this speed (about 0.1c).
physics-2-4-22
Electrons travelling at 3.2 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹ enter a uniform magnetic field of 5.0 × 10⁻³ T at right angles. Calculate the radius of their circular path. (mₑ = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg)
Accept 3.6–3.7 cm depending on rounding of v.
physics-2-4-23
In a mass spectrometer, singly charged carbon-12 and carbon-14 ions enter the same magnetic field with the same speed. Find the ratio of the radius of the carbon-14 path to the carbon-12 path.
r = mv/(qB) with q, v and B equal, so r ∝ m. Ratio = 14/12 ≈ 1.17.
The heavier isotope follows the wider arc.
physics-2-4-24
Explain why the tubes in which electrons travel in a particle accelerator must be kept at a very high vacuum.

Any gas molecules in the tube would collide with the electrons, scattering them out of the beam and causing them to lose energy. A high vacuum lets the beam travel long distances (for hours in a storage ring) without these collisions.
Key idea: collisions with air molecules scatter and slow the beam.
physics-2-4-25
Two parallel plates 4.0 cm apart have a potential difference of 200 V. Calculate the acceleration of an electron between the plates. (mₑ = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg)
E = V/d = 200/0.040 = 5.0 × 10³ V m⁻¹; F = qE = 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁶ N; a = F/m = 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁶/9.1 × 10⁻³¹ ≈ 8.8 × 10¹⁴ m s⁻², towards the positive plate.
Show E, then F, then a.
physics-2-4-c1
In an electron gun, electrons are accelerated from rest through 5000 V. Find their kinetic energy in joules and their speed (non-relativistic).
KE = qV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 5000 = 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁶ J. v = √(2KE/m) = √(2 × 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁶ ÷ 9.11 × 10⁻³¹) ≈ 4.2 × 10⁷ m/s (about 0.14c, so the classical result is close enough).
physics-3-1: A 1200 kg car accelerates uniformly from rest to 20 m/s in 8.0 s. What is the magnitude of the net force on the car?
A book rests on a table. According to Newton's third law, the reaction force to the book's weight is:
the normal force exerted by the table on the book
the gravitational force exerted by the book on Earth
the force exerted by the book on the table
the friction force between the book and the table
Weight is Earth pulling the book by gravity, so its third-law partner is the book pulling Earth by gravity. The normal force is a different interaction.
A 70 kg student stands in a lift that is accelerating upwards at 1.5 m/s². What is the normal force from the floor on the student? Take g = 9.8 m/s².
A 50 kg person stands in a lift moving downwards at a constant 3.0 m/s. What is the normal force on the person? Take g = 9.8 m/s².
At constant velocity the acceleration is zero, so N = mg = 50 × 9.8 = 490 N.
A block slides down a frictionless ramp inclined at 30° to the horizontal. What is its acceleration? Take g = 9.8 m/s².
The component of gravity along the slope gives a = g sin θ = 9.8 × sin 30° = 4.9 m/s².
Two blocks of mass 3.0 kg and 2.0 kg sit side by side on a frictionless surface. A 20 N horizontal force pushes the 3.0 kg block, which pushes the 2.0 kg block. What is the force between the blocks?
The system accelerates at 20/5.0 = 4.0 m/s². The only horizontal force on the 2.0 kg block is the contact force, F = 2.0 × 4.0 = 8.0 N.
A 2.0 kg trolley on a frictionless bench is connected by a light string over a frictionless pulley to a 0.50 kg mass hanging freely. What is the acceleration of the system? Take g = 9.8 m/s².
The net force is the hanging weight, 0.50 × 9.8 = 4.9 N, acting on the total mass of 2.5 kg: a = 4.9/2.5 = 1.96 m/s².
For a 2.0 kg trolley on a frictionless bench pulled by a 0.50 kg hanging mass (system acceleration 1.96 m/s²), what is the tension in the string?
The tension is the only horizontal force on the trolley: T = 2.0 × 1.96 ≈ 3.9 N. It is less than the hanging weight (4.9 N) because the hanging mass accelerates downwards.
A passenger on a Melbourne tram lurches forward when the tram brakes suddenly. The best explanation is that:
the passenger tends to keep moving at the original velocity while the tram slows down
a forward force acts on the passenger when the brakes are applied
momentum is transferred from the tram to the passenger
the braking force on the tram is also applied to the passenger
By Newton's first law (inertia), the passenger keeps moving forward until a force (e.g. from the seat or a handrail) acts on them to slow them.
A ute tows a trailer along a straight highway and speeds up. How does the force of the ute on the trailer compare with the force of the trailer on the ute?
The ute's force on the trailer is larger, which is why they accelerate
They are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction
The trailer's force on the ute is larger because the trailer resists motion
They are equal only when the speed is constant
These are a Newton's third law pair and are always equal and opposite. The system accelerates because of the forward friction from the road on the ute's drive wheels.
A 5.0 kg box rests on a ramp inclined at 25° to the horizontal. What is the normal force on the box? Take g = 9.8 m/s².
Perpendicular to the slope the forces balance: N = mg cos θ = 5.0 × 9.8 × cos 25° ≈ 44 N.
A 10 kg box slides down a ramp inclined at 20° at constant velocity. What is the magnitude of the friction force on the box? Take g = 9.8 m/s².
Constant velocity means zero net force along the slope, so friction = mg sin θ = 98 × sin 20° ≈ 34 N.
A skydiver falls at terminal velocity. Which statement is correct?
The air resistance equals the skydiver's weight and the net force is zero
The air resistance is greater than the weight, so the skydiver slows
The acceleration of the skydiver is 9.8 m/s² downwards
The net force on the skydiver equals the skydiver's weight
At terminal velocity the velocity is constant, so by Newton's first law the forces are balanced: drag equals weight.
A 1500 kg car travelling at 25 m/s brakes with a constant net braking force of 6000 N. What is its stopping distance?
A child pulls a 40 kg toboggan across frictionless snow with a rope that makes 30° above the horizontal and has a tension of 150 N. What is the horizontal acceleration of the toboggan?
Only the horizontal component causes horizontal acceleration: a = 150 cos 30°/40 = 129.9/40 ≈ 3.2 m/s².
A locomotive pulls three identical 20 000 kg carriages along a frictionless level track with an acceleration of 0.50 m/s². What is the tension in the coupling between the first and second carriages?
The coupling behind the first carriage accelerates the last two carriages: T = (2 × 20 000) × 0.50 = 20 000 N.
An 80 kg astronaut stands on the Moon, where g = 1.6 m/s². Which describes the astronaut's mass and weight there?
Mass is unchanged by location. Weight = mg = 80 × 1.6 = 128 N.
A person whose true weight is 600 N stands on bathroom scales in a lift. The scales read 500 N. The lift could be:
A reading below the true weight means a downward acceleration. Moving up while slowing down is a downward acceleration; the other options involve zero or upward acceleration.
A child pulls a 40 kg toboggan across level snow with a rope at 30° above the horizontal and a tension of 150 N. Calculate the normal force from the snow on the toboggan. (g = 9.8 m/s²)
The upward component of the tension partly supports the toboggan, so the normal force is less than its weight. Deduct a mark for using 392 N.
A horse pulls a cart. A student argues that by Newton's third law the cart pulls back on the horse with an equal force, so they can never move. Explain the error in this argument.

The third-law pair forces act on different objects, so they do not cancel. The cart accelerates because the horse's forward pull on it is larger than the friction on the cart. The horse accelerates because the ground's forward friction on its hooves is larger than the cart's backward pull.
Key point: only forces acting on the same object can be added to find that object's net force.
A 65 kg passenger is in a lift moving downwards that slows down at 1.2 m/s². Calculate the normal force on the passenger. (g = 9.8 m/s²)
Slowing while moving down means the acceleration is upwards: N = m(g + a) = 65 × (9.8 + 1.2) = 715 N.
Students often wrongly subtract because the lift is moving down. What matters is the direction of the acceleration, not the direction of motion.
A 4.0 kg block slides down a ramp inclined at 35°, with a constant friction force of 10 N acting on it. Calculate its acceleration. (g = 9.8 m/s²)
Down-slope weight component = 4.0 × 9.8 × sin 35° ≈ 22.5 N. Net force = 22.5 − 10 = 12.5 N, so a = 12.5/4.0 ≈ 3.1 m/s² down the slope.
Resolve the weight along the slope first, then subtract friction, which opposes the motion.
Masses of 5.0 kg and 3.0 kg hang on either side of a light, frictionless pulley (an Atwood machine). Calculate the acceleration and the tension in the string. (g = 9.8 m/s²)
Check with the 5.0 kg mass: 5.0 × (9.8 − 2.45) = 36.75 N, which agrees.
A student claims that while a ball thrown upwards is rising, an upward force of the throw keeps acting on it. Evaluate this claim, ignoring air resistance.

The claim is wrong. After release, the only force on the ball is gravity, acting downwards. The ball keeps rising because of its inertia (its initial upward velocity), and the downward net force slows it at 9.8 m/s².
This is a common misconception: motion does not need a force in the direction of motion (Newton's first law).
A car tows a 500 kg trailer with a horizontal force of 1500 N. The trailer experiences 300 N of resistance. Calculate the trailer's acceleration.
Apply Newton's second law to the trailer alone, using only the forces acting on it.
A 20 N horizontal force pushes a 3.0 kg block, which pushes a 2.0 kg block in front of it across a frictionless floor. The force the 3.0 kg block exerts on the 2.0 kg block is:
a = 20 ÷ 5.0 = 4.0 m/s². The front block needs F = 2.0 × 4.0 = 8.0 N.
physics-3-2: A ball rolls horizontally off a wall 4.9 m high at 3.0 m/s. How far from the base of the wall does it land? Take g = 9.8 m/s². Ignore air resistance.
The fall time is t = √(2h/g) = √(9.8/9.8) = 1.0 s, so the horizontal distance = 3.0 × 1.0 = 3.0 m.
A stone is thrown horizontally from the top of a 20 m sea cliff. How long does it take to reach the water below? Take g = 9.8 m/s². Ignore air resistance.
The vertical motion starts from rest: t = √(2h/g) = √(40/9.8) ≈ 2.0 s. The horizontal speed does not affect this.
A football is kicked at 40° above the horizontal. At the highest point of its flight, ignoring air resistance:
its velocity is horizontal and its acceleration is 9.8 m/s² downwards
its velocity and acceleration are both zero
its velocity is zero and its acceleration is 9.8 m/s² downwards
its velocity is horizontal and its acceleration is zero
At the top only the vertical velocity is zero; the horizontal component remains. Gravity still acts, so the acceleration is g downwards throughout.
A football is kicked from level ground at 20 m/s at 30° above the horizontal. What is its maximum height? Take g = 9.8 m/s². Ignore air resistance.
The vertical component is 20 sin 30° = 10 m/s, so h = u²/(2g) = 100/19.6 ≈ 5.1 m.
A football is kicked from level ground at 20 m/s at 30° above the horizontal. What is its time of flight? Take g = 9.8 m/s². Ignore air resistance.
t = 2u sin θ/g = 2 × 10/9.8 ≈ 2.0 s (twice the time taken to reach maximum height).
A football is kicked from level ground at 20 m/s at 30° above the horizontal. What is its horizontal range? Take g = 9.8 m/s². Ignore air resistance.
Range = horizontal speed × time = 20 cos 30° × 2.04 ≈ 17.3 × 2.04 ≈ 35 m.
Ignoring air resistance, which launch angle gives the maximum range for a projectile launched from and landing on level ground?
Range = v² sin 2θ/g, which is greatest when sin 2θ = 1, i.e. θ = 45°.
On level ground with no air resistance, which pair of launch angles gives the same range for the same launch speed?
Complementary angles (adding to 90°) give the same sin 2θ, and so the same range.
Ignoring air resistance, how does the horizontal component of a projectile's velocity change during its flight?
It decreases to zero at the highest point
It increases as the projectile falls
It decreases uniformly throughout the flight
No horizontal force acts on the projectile, so by Newton's first law its horizontal velocity is constant.
From the same height and at the same instant, one ball is dropped and an identical ball is launched horizontally at 10 m/s. Ignoring air resistance, which reaches the level ground first?
It depends on the height of release
Both land at the same time
Both start with zero vertical velocity and have the same vertical acceleration, so their fall times are equal.
A ball is thrown vertically upwards at 14.7 m/s. How long does it take to reach its highest point? Take g = 9.8 m/s². Ignore air resistance.
At the top v = 0, so t = u/g = 14.7/9.8 = 1.5 s. (3.0 s is the total time to return to the hand.)
A netball is thrown horizontally at 8.0 m/s and is in the air for 0.60 s before it is caught at a lower height. What is its speed just before it is caught? Take g = 9.8 m/s². Ignore air resistance.
The vertical velocity is 9.8 × 0.60 = 5.88 m/s. Speed = √(8.0² + 5.88²) ≈ 9.9 m/s. Velocity components add as vectors, not by simple addition.
An archer fires an arrow horizontally at 50 m/s at a target 25 m away. How far does the arrow drop vertically before it hits the target? Take g = 9.8 m/s². Ignore air resistance.
A projectile is launched on level ground. If the launch speed is doubled with the angle unchanged, the range (ignoring air resistance) is:
Range = v² sin 2θ/g, so the range is proportional to v²; doubling v gives four times the range.
A ball is launched at 15 m/s at 60° above the horizontal. What is the horizontal component of its velocity?
vx = 15 cos 60° = 7.5 m/s. (13 m/s is the vertical component, 15 sin 60°.)
A projectile is launched with a horizontal velocity component of 15 m/s and a vertical component of 20 m/s upwards. What is its speed 1.0 s after launch? Take g = 9.8 m/s². Ignore air resistance.
After 1.0 s, vy = 20 − 9.8 = 10.2 m/s and vx = 15 m/s, so speed = √(15² + 10.2²) ≈ 18 m/s.
Compared with the ideal (no air resistance) path, a real cricket ball hit at the same speed and angle has:
the same range but a lower maximum height
a longer range because the air supports the ball
a lower maximum height, a shorter range and a steeper descent than ascent
a symmetrical path with a shorter range
Drag removes energy and reduces both velocity components. This lowers the peak and shortens the range, and the horizontal speed is lower on the way down, so the descent is steeper.
A marble rolls horizontally off a bench 1.8 m high and lands 1.2 m from the base of the bench. What was its launch speed? Take g = 9.8 m/s². Ignore air resistance.
A golf ball is hit from level ground at 30 m/s at 40° above the horizontal. Ignoring air resistance, calculate its horizontal range. (g = 9.8 m/s²)
Either the range formula or the component method earns full marks if the working is shown.
A golf ball is hit from level ground at 30 m/s at 40° above the horizontal. Ignoring air resistance, calculate its maximum height. (g = 9.8 m/s²)
Only the vertical component matters for the maximum height.
