A stone is thrown horizontally at 12 m/s from a bridge 45 m above a river. Calculate the time of flight and how far horizontally it travels. (g = 9.8 m/s², ignore air resistance)
The vertical motion (from rest) sets the time; the horizontal motion is at constant velocity.
Explain why the horizontal and vertical components of a projectile's motion can be analysed independently.

Ignoring air resistance, the only force is gravity, which acts vertically. So there is no horizontal acceleration (constant horizontal velocity), while the vertical motion has constant acceleration g. Perpendicular vectors do not affect each other, and the two components are linked only by time.
Mention that gravity is vertical and that time is the common variable.

A footballer kicks a ball at 18 m/s at 35° above the horizontal towards goalposts 20 m away. The crossbar is 2.4 m high. Determine whether the ball passes over the crossbar. (g = 9.8 m/s², ignore air resistance)
Find the time to reach the posts from the horizontal motion first, then substitute it into the vertical equation.
A stone is thrown horizontally at 12 m/s from a bridge 45 m above a river. Calculate its speed just before it hits the water. (g = 9.8 m/s², ignore air resistance)
Conservation of energy gives the same result: v² = u² + 2gh.

A supply package is released from a plane flying horizontally at 60 m/s at an altitude of 500 m. Ignoring air resistance, how far horizontally from the release point does it land, and where is the plane when it lands?
t = √(2 × 500/9.8) ≈ 10.1 s, so the horizontal distance = 60 × 10.1 ≈ 606 m (about 610 m). The plane is directly above the package when it lands, because both have the same horizontal velocity.
The package keeps the plane's horizontal velocity, so it stays directly beneath the plane throughout its fall.
A ball is thrown horizontally at 15 m/s from the top of a 20 m cliff. How long is it in the air and how far from the base of the cliff does it land? (Ignore air resistance.)
Vertical: 20 = ½ × 9.8 × t², so t = 2.02 s. Horizontal: x = 15 × 2.02 ≈ 30 m. The horizontal velocity is constant.
physics-3-3: A 1000 kg car travels around a flat curve of radius 50 m at a constant 15 m/s. What friction force is needed to keep it on the curve?
F = mv²/r = 1000 × 15²/50 = 4500 N, supplied by sideways friction on the tyres.
For an object in uniform circular motion, the net force on it is directed:
tangent to the circle in the direction of motion
towards the centre of the circle
away from the centre of the circle
in the direction of the velocity
The velocity's direction changes continually towards the centre, so the acceleration, and therefore the net force, points towards the centre.
A ball on a string moves in a horizontal circle of radius 0.80 m, completing 2.0 revolutions per second. What is its speed?
A curve of radius 80 m is to be banked so that cars at 20 m/s need no sideways friction. What is the required banking angle? Take g = 9.8 m/s².
A car travels around a banked track at exactly its design speed. Ignoring friction and air resistance, which statement is correct?
Only gravity and the normal force act, and their resultant is horizontal towards the centre
Gravity, the normal force and a centripetal force act on the car
The resultant force points down the slope of the bank
The normal force equals the car's weight
Centripetal force is not an extra force; it is the horizontal resultant of the weight and the normal force, which points towards the centre of the circle.
A car rounds a flat curve. If its speed doubles while the radius stays the same, the required centripetal force:
F = mv²/r is proportional to v², so doubling v quadruples F.
A roller-coaster car goes over the top of a vertical loop of radius 10 m on the inside of the track. What is the minimum speed at the top for it to stay in contact with the track? Take g = 9.8 m/s².
At minimum speed the normal force is zero and gravity alone provides the centripetal force: mg = mv²/r, so v = √(gr) = √98 ≈ 9.9 m/s.
A 0.50 kg ball on a string moves in a vertical circle of radius 1.0 m. At the lowest point its speed is 6.0 m/s. What is the tension in the string there? Take g = 9.8 m/s².
At the bottom T − mg = mv²/r, so T = 4.9 + 0.50 × 36/1.0 = 4.9 + 18 = 22.9 N.
A 1200 kg car drives over the top of a hump-back bridge (radius 40 m) at 12 m/s. What is the normal force on the car at the top? Take g = 9.8 m/s².
What is the maximum speed at which a car can drive over the top of a hump of radius 25 m without losing contact with the road? Take g = 9.8 m/s².
Contact is lost when N = 0, which happens when mg = mv²/r. So v = √(gr) = √245 ≈ 15.7 m/s.
A car travels around a banked curve faster than its design speed. Sideways friction on the tyres acts:
up the slope of the bank
down the slope of the bank
nowhere, because friction is not needed
Above the design speed more centripetal force is needed, and the car tends to slide up the bank. Friction opposes this by acting down the slope, adding an inward component.
A cyclist rounds a flat corner at Albert Park. What provides the centripetal force?
The normal force from the road
Friction between the tyres and the road
On a flat road the normal force and weight are vertical, so only sideways friction can provide the horizontal inward force.
Which statement about an object in uniform circular motion is correct?
Its speed is constant but its velocity is changing
Its velocity is constant but its speed is changing
Both its speed and its velocity are constant
Its acceleration is zero because its speed is constant
The magnitude (speed) is constant, but the direction keeps changing, so the velocity changes and there is a centripetal acceleration.
A curve of radius 120 m is banked at 15°. What is its design speed? Take g = 9.8 m/s².
A child rides a merry-go-round at a radius of 2.0 m and completes one revolution every 4.0 s. What is the child's centripetal acceleration?
A car rounds a frictionless banked curve at its design speed. Compared with the car's weight, the normal force on the car is:
The vertical component N cos θ must balance mg, so N = mg/cos θ, which is greater than mg.
A hammer thrower releases the hammer while it moves in a horizontal circle. Immediately after release, viewed from above, the hammer moves:
along the tangent to the circle at the point of release
along a curved path continuing the circle
Once the inward tension is removed there is no centripetal force, so the hammer continues in the direction of its instantaneous velocity, which is tangential.
A 0.20 kg puck on a frictionless air table moves in a circle of radius 0.50 m on a string, with a period of 0.50 s. What is the tension in the string?
Show that the design speed v of a curve of radius r banked at angle θ satisfies tan θ = v²/(rg).
Vertically: N cos θ = mg. Horizontally (towards the centre): N sin θ = mv²/r. Dividing the second equation by the first gives tan θ = v²/(rg).
Award marks for resolving N into vertical and horizontal components correctly, then eliminating N.
A racetrack curve of radius 200 m is to be designed for cars travelling at 108 km/h. Calculate the banking angle needed so that no friction is required. (g = 9.8 m/s²)
A common error is forgetting to convert km/h to m/s (divide by 3.6).
A student swings a bucket of water in a vertical circle of radius 0.90 m. Calculate the minimum speed at the top so the water stays in the bucket, and explain why. (g = 9.8 m/s²)

v = √(gr) = √(9.8 × 0.90) ≈ 3.0 m/s. At this speed gravity alone provides exactly the centripetal force needed, so the water needs no push from the bucket base; any slower and gravity would pull it out of the circular path.
The key idea is that the normal force from the bucket becomes zero at the minimum speed.
A 60 kg passenger passes through the bottom of a roller-coaster loop of radius 12 m at 20 m/s. Calculate the normal force on the passenger. (g = 9.8 m/s²)
N − mg = mv²/r, so N = 60 × (9.8 + 400/12) = 60 × 43.1 ≈ 2.6 × 10³ N (about 4.4 times their weight).
At the bottom the normal force must both support the weight and provide the centripetal force.
A 1400 kg car rounds a flat curve of radius 40 m. The maximum sideways friction available is 7000 N. Calculate the maximum speed for the curve.
Friction is the sole centripetal force on a flat curve.
Passengers in a car going around a sharp corner feel 'thrown outwards'. Explain why this is not caused by a real outward force.

The passengers' inertia tends to keep them moving in a straight line (Newton's first law). The car turns inwards beneath them until the door or seat pushes them inwards, providing the centripetal force. No outward force acts; the sensation comes from the inward push of the car.
'Centrifugal force' is not a real force in an inertial frame; credit references to inertia and to an inward net force.
A 1500 kg car travels around a banked curve of radius 100 m at its design speed of 25 m/s. State the magnitude and direction of the net force on the car.
F = mv²/r = 1500 × 625/100 = 9375 N (about 9.4 × 10³ N), directed horizontally towards the centre of the curve.
The net force is horizontal, not parallel to the banked surface.
At what angle should a curve of radius 50 m be banked so that a car travelling at 20 m/s needs no sideways friction?
The horizontal component of the normal force provides the centripetal force: tan θ = v²/(rg) = 400 ÷ (50 × 9.8) = 0.816, so θ ≈ 39°.
physics-3-4: A 0.16 kg cricket ball travelling at 30 m/s is hit straight back at 40 m/s. What is the magnitude of the impulse on the ball?
Taking the return direction as positive, Δp = 0.16 × (40 − (−30)) = 0.16 × 70 = 11.2 N s. The reversal of direction must be included.
A 58 g tennis ball hits a racquet at 20 m/s and leaves in the opposite direction at 30 m/s. The contact time is 5.0 ms. What is the average force on the ball?
A 1200 kg car travelling at 15 m/s collides with a stationary 800 kg car, and they lock together. What is their speed just after the collision?
Momentum is conserved: 1200 × 15 = 2000v, so v = 18 000/2000 = 9.0 m/s.
A 1200 kg car at 15 m/s collides with a stationary 800 kg car and they move off together at 9.0 m/s. How much kinetic energy is transformed in the collision?
Initial KE = ½ × 1200 × 15² = 135 000 J; final KE = ½ × 2000 × 9.0² = 81 000 J. The loss is 54 000 J, mostly to heat, sound and deformation.
Which statement best describes an elastic collision?
Momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not
Kinetic energy is conserved but momentum is not
Both momentum and total kinetic energy are conserved
The objects stick together after colliding
Momentum is conserved in all collisions of an isolated system; a collision is elastic only if total kinetic energy is also conserved.
Car airbags reduce injuries in a crash mainly because they:
reduce the occupant's change in momentum
increase the occupant's change in momentum
reduce the occupant's kinetic energy before the crash
increase the time over which the occupant's momentum changes, reducing the average force
The change in momentum is fixed by the crash; spreading it over a longer time gives a smaller average force, since F = Δp/Δt.
A shopper pushes a 30 kg trolley 15 m across a level car park with a constant 80 N force directed 20° below the horizontal. How much work does this force do on the trolley?
W = Fs cos θ = 80 × 15 × cos 20° ≈ 1128 J ≈ 1.1 kJ. Only the component of the force in the direction of motion does work.
A spring with spring constant 200 N/m is compressed by 0.15 m. How much elastic potential energy does it store?
A ball is dropped from rest from a height of 5.0 m. What is its speed just before it hits the ground? Take g = 9.8 m/s². Ignore air resistance.
A 4.0 kg rifle fires a 10 g bullet horizontally at 400 m/s. What is the rifle's recoil speed?
The total momentum is zero before and after: 0.010 × 400 = 4.0 × v, so v = 1.0 m/s.
The impulse acting on an object is equal to:
the force divided by the time
its final momentum multiplied by the time
A lift raises an 800 kg load 20 m at constant speed in 16 s. What is the minimum average power output of the lift motor? Take g = 9.8 m/s².
A 0.50 kg mass hung from a spring stretches it by 4.9 cm. What is the spring constant? Take g = 9.8 m/s².
A 50 kg skateboarder rolls at 3.0 m/s at the bottom of a frictionless ramp. What maximum height can they reach up the ramp? Take g = 9.8 m/s².
½mv² = mgh, so h = v²/(2g) = 9.0/19.6 ≈ 0.46 m. The mass cancels.
Two ice skaters of mass 60 kg and 40 kg stand at rest and push off each other. The 40 kg skater moves off at 3.0 m/s. What is the speed of the 60 kg skater?
The total momentum stays zero: 60v = 40 × 3.0, so v = 2.0 m/s in the opposite direction.
The total momentum of a system of colliding objects is conserved when:
the net external force on the system is zero
Momentum is conserved for any isolated system, whatever the type of collision, provided no net external force acts.
A car's braking force is constant. If the car's initial speed is doubled, its braking distance:
Work done by brakes = Fd = ½mv², so d is proportional to v²; doubling v gives four times the distance.
An object of mass 3.0 kg has a momentum of 12 kg m/s. What is its kinetic energy?
v = 12/3.0 = 4.0 m/s, so KE = ½ × 3.0 × 4.0² = 24 J (equivalently p²/2m = 144/6).

A 3000 kg truck travelling at 10 m/s collides with a stationary 1000 kg car. Immediately after, the car moves forward at 12 m/s. Calculate the truck's velocity after the collision and determine whether the collision is elastic.

30 000 = 3000v + 1000 × 12, so v = 6.0 m/s forward. KE before = ½ × 3000 × 10² = 150 000 J; KE after = ½ × 3000 × 6² + ½ × 1000 × 12² = 54 000 + 72 000 = 126 000 J. KE is not conserved, so the collision is inelastic.
Both a momentum calculation and a kinetic energy comparison are needed for full marks.
Explain how the crumple zones of a car reduce the force on occupants in a collision.

Crumple zones deform progressively, increasing the time over which the car (and its occupants) come to rest. The change in momentum is the same, so by F = Δp/Δt a longer stopping time means a smaller average force. They also absorb kinetic energy through deformation.
Reference to the same Δp with a longer Δt is essential.
A toy launcher uses a spring with k = 400 N/m compressed by 0.10 m to fire a 50 g ball horizontally. Assuming all the elastic energy becomes kinetic energy, calculate the launch speed.
Remember to convert grams to kilograms.
A 1500 kg car travelling at 20 m/s brakes to a stop in 40 m. Calculate the average braking force using energy methods.
KE = ½ × 1500 × 20² = 300 000 J. The work done by the brakes, F × 40, equals this KE, so F = 300 000/40 = 7500 N.
The work-energy theorem gives the answer without first finding the acceleration.
A 0.45 kg football is kicked from rest to 25 m/s, with a foot contact time of 0.010 s. Calculate the impulse on the ball and the average force from the foot.
Impulse units can be written as N s or kg m/s.
A 2.0 kg ball is dropped from 1.25 m onto a floor and rebounds to 0.80 m. Calculate the impulse the floor exerts on the ball. (g = 9.8 m/s², ignore air resistance)
Impact speed = √(2 × 9.8 × 1.25) ≈ 4.95 m/s downwards; rebound speed = √(2 × 9.8 × 0.80) ≈ 3.96 m/s upwards. Impulse = 2.0 × (3.96 + 4.95) ≈ 17.8 N s upwards.
The velocities are in opposite directions, so their magnitudes add.
A 500 kg roller-coaster car starts from rest at a height of 30 m. Ignoring friction, calculate its speed at a point 12 m above the ground. (g = 9.8 m/s²)
Drop in height = 18 m. ½v² = gΔh, so v = √(2 × 9.8 × 18) = √352.8 ≈ 18.8 m/s.
The mass cancels; use the change in height, not the final height.
A 2.0 kg trolley at 6.0 m/s collides with and sticks to a 1.0 kg trolley at rest. The kinetic energy lost is:
Momentum: 2.0 × 6.0 = 3.0v, so v = 4.0 m/s. KE before 36 J, after ½ × 3.0 × 4.0² = 24 J; 12 J is lost. Sticking means it is inelastic.
physics-4-1: physics-4-1-1
Which statement is Einstein's first postulate of special relativity?
The laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames of reference.
The speed of light depends on the motion of its source.
Time passes at the same rate for all observers.
All motion is measured relative to a stationary aether.
The first postulate (principle of relativity) says no inertial frame is special: all physical laws take the same form in every one.
physics-4-1-2
Which statement is Einstein's second postulate of special relativity?
The speed of light is greatest when the source moves towards the observer.
The speed of light in a vacuum is the same for all observers, regardless of the motion of the source or observer.
Light requires a medium, the aether, to travel through.
Nothing can travel at the speed of light, including light pulses in a vacuum.
The second postulate states that c is invariant: every inertial observer measures light in a vacuum travelling at 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.
physics-4-1-3
An inertial frame of reference is best described as a frame that is:
moving at the speed of light
accelerating at a constant rate
not accelerating, so it is at rest or moving at constant velocity
attached to the surface of the Sun
Newton's first law holds in an inertial frame, which requires zero acceleration (constant velocity, including at rest).
physics-4-1-4
Which of the following is NOT an inertial frame of reference?
A V/Line train travelling at a constant 120 km/h on a straight, level track
A spacecraft drifting with its engines off, far from any planets or stars
A laboratory bench at rest on Earth's surface (to a good approximation)
A car travelling around a roundabout at a constant 40 km/h
Moving in a circle involves centripetal acceleration even at constant speed, so the car's frame is non-inertial.
physics-4-1-5
A spacecraft travelling at 0.50c relative to Earth switches on a forward-pointing headlight. What speed does an observer on Earth measure for the light from the headlight?
c
By the second postulate, all inertial observers measure light in a vacuum at c regardless of the source's motion.
physics-4-1-6
A spacecraft moves away from Earth at 0.60c. A laser pulse is sent from Earth towards the spacecraft. What speed does the astronaut on the spacecraft measure for the pulse?
c
The speed of light is invariant: the astronaut measures c, not c minus the spacecraft's speed.
physics-4-1-7
What was the main result of the Michelson–Morley experiment?
A clear fringe shift showed Earth's speed through the aether.
Light was found to travel faster in the direction of Earth's motion.
No significant change in the interference pattern was detected, giving no evidence for the aether.
Light was shown to need a medium to travel through space.
The null result showed no detectable aether wind, consistent with light having the same speed in all directions and frames.
physics-4-1-8

A passenger in a windowless carriage of a smoothly moving train at constant velocity drops a ball and does several pendulum experiments. Which idea explains why she cannot work out the train's speed from these experiments?
Light travels at the same speed for all observers.
Objects with mass cannot reach the speed of light.
Time dilation makes moving clocks run slow.
The laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames.
Because physical laws are identical in every inertial frame, no experiment done inside the carriage can reveal its uniform motion.
physics-4-1-9
Proper time is the time interval between two events measured by an observer:
for whom the two events occur at the same location
who is at rest on Earth
who is moving fastest relative to the events
who measures the longest time interval
Proper time Δt₀ is measured in the frame where both events happen at the same place; it is the shortest measured interval.
physics-4-1-10
The proper length of an object is the length measured by an observer who is:
moving at the speed of light relative to the object
at rest relative to the object
moving at the greatest possible speed relative to the object
on Earth, regardless of the object's motion
Proper length L₀ is measured in the object's rest frame and is the longest length any observer measures.
physics-4-1-11

Two lightning strikes hit opposite ends of a long platform at the same time according to an observer standing on the platform. According to a passenger on a train moving rapidly along the platform, the strikes:
must occur at the same time, because simultaneity is absolute
occur at the same time only if the train is accelerating
generally do not occur at the same time
occur at the same location
Simultaneity is relative: spatially separated events that are simultaneous in one frame are generally not simultaneous in a frame moving relative to it.
physics-4-1-12
Einstein was motivated to develop special relativity mainly by a conflict between:
Newton's law of gravitation and Kepler's laws
the wave and particle models of electrons
Ohm's law and Faraday's law
Maxwell's electromagnetism, which predicts a fixed speed of light, and Galilean (classical) velocity addition
Maxwell's equations give c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀) with no reference frame, contradicting the classical idea that the speed of light should change with the observer's motion.
physics-4-1-13
Which quantity is measured to have the same value by all inertial observers, whatever their relative motion?
The speed of light in a vacuum
The time interval between two events
The length of a moving rod
The kinetic energy of a moving particle
Only c is invariant in this list; time intervals, lengths and kinetic energies depend on the observer's frame.
physics-4-1-14
A train moves at speed v relative to the track and turns on its headlight. Using classical Galilean velocity addition, what speed would a trackside observer be predicted to measure for the light?
c
c + v
c − v
v
Galilean addition simply adds velocities, predicting c + v; experiments show the actual measured value is c, as special relativity requires.
physics-4-1-15
Which statement about the scope of special relativity is correct?
It applies only to objects travelling at the speed of light.
It applies only to accelerating frames of reference.
It applies to observers in inertial (non-accelerating) frames of reference.
It applies only to light and not to objects with mass.
Special relativity deals with inertial frames; accelerated frames and gravity are treated by general relativity.
physics-4-1-16
Why can a spacecraft with mass never reach the speed of light?
Air resistance in space becomes too large near c.
The spacecraft's length would become negative.
The second postulate forbids objects from moving faster than 0.5c.
As v approaches c, the Lorentz factor approaches infinity, so infinite energy would be needed.
Kinetic energy is (γ − 1)mc², and γ → ∞ as v → c, so the energy required becomes unbounded.
physics-4-1-17

Lightning strikes the front and back of a fast-moving train simultaneously in the ground frame. A passenger sits exactly in the middle of the train. According to the passenger, which strike happened first?
The strike at the front of the train
The strike at the back of the train
Both strikes happened at the same time
It depends on the colour of the light
The passenger moves towards the light from the front, so it reaches her first; since light travels at c in her frame from equal distances, she concludes the front strike occurred first.
physics-4-1-18
Astronauts Ana and Ben pass each other in spacecraft moving at constant relative velocity. Each finds that the other's clock is running slow. Which statement is correct?
Only Ana is correct, because she noticed it first.
Both are correct, because each is in an inertial frame and the situation is symmetric.
Only the faster astronaut is correct.
Neither is correct, because clocks always run at the same rate.
By the first postulate neither inertial frame is preferred, so each observer correctly measures the other's clock as running slow.
physics-4-1-19
State Einstein's two postulates of special relativity.
1. The laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames of reference. 2. The speed of light in a vacuum is the same (c) for all observers, regardless of the motion of the source or observer.
Both postulates need to be stated; the words 'inertial frames' and 'in a vacuum' are key marking points.
physics-4-1-20
Galileo argued that a person below deck on a smoothly sailing ship could not tell whether the ship was moving. Explain this using Einstein's first postulate.

The ship moving at constant velocity is an inertial frame. Since the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames, any experiment below deck gives exactly the same result as on land, so there is no way to detect the ship's uniform motion.
Link 'constant velocity' to 'inertial frame' and state that experiments give identical results.
physics-4-1-21
Explain the significance of the null result of the Michelson–Morley experiment for the development of special relativity.

The experiment detected no change in the speed of light with Earth's motion, so there was no evidence for an aether. This supported the idea that light travels at the same speed c in all directions and for all observers, which became Einstein's second postulate.
Mention both the absence of an aether and the constancy of the speed of light.
physics-4-1-22
Use the second postulate to explain why two events that are simultaneous for one observer may not be simultaneous for another observer moving relative to the first.

Light from each event travels at c in every frame. An observer moving towards one event meets its light sooner, and because they must also measure both light signals at speed c over equal distances in their own frame, they conclude that the events occurred at different times. So simultaneity depends on the frame.
Credit the key idea that c is fixed in every frame, so a moving observer cannot attribute the different arrival times to different light speeds.
physics-4-1-23
Distinguish between an inertial and a non-inertial frame of reference, giving one example of each.

An inertial frame is not accelerating (at rest or moving at constant velocity), e.g. a tram travelling at constant speed along a straight track. A non-inertial frame is accelerating, e.g. a car braking or a car turning a corner.
Any valid examples are acceptable; turning at constant speed counts as accelerating.
physics-4-1-24
A rocket travelling at 0.90c relative to Earth fires a laser pulse backwards, towards Earth. What speed does an observer on Earth measure for the pulse? Justify your answer.
c (3.0 × 10⁸ m/s). By Einstein's second postulate, the speed of light in a vacuum is the same for all observers, regardless of the motion of the source.
A common error is 0.10c (c − 0.90c), which uses classical velocity addition.
physics-4-1-25
Two observers in relative motion measure different time intervals between the same pair of events. Explain why this is not a contradiction.

Time intervals are not absolute in special relativity; they depend on the observer's frame of reference. Each observer's measurement is correct in their own inertial frame, and no frame is preferred, so both measurements are valid.
Key point: measurements of time are frame-dependent and both are valid; only c is the same for all.
physics-4-1-c1
A spaceship moving at 0.5c relative to Earth switches on its headlight. An observer on Earth measures the speed of the light as:
It depends on the direction the Earth observer faces
c
Einstein's second postulate: the speed of light in a vacuum is the same for all observers in inertial frames.
physics-4-2: What is the Lorentz factor γ for a spacecraft travelling at 0.60c?
What is the Lorentz factor γ for a particle travelling at 0.80c?
γ = 1/√(1 − 0.64) = 1/√0.36 = 1/0.60 = 1.67; 2.78 comes from forgetting the square root.
A proton in the Australian Synchrotron's booster ring is travelling at 0.99c. What is its Lorentz factor, to three significant figures?
γ = 1/√(1 − 0.9801) = 1/√0.0199 = 1/0.141 = 7.09; 50.3 results from omitting the square root.
At what speed is the Lorentz factor equal to 2.0?
Which equation correctly relates the dilated time Δt to the proper time Δt₀?
The moving clock's proper interval is stretched by γ when measured by an observer in relative motion, so Δt = γΔt₀.
An astronaut on a spacecraft travelling at 0.60c relative to Earth measures the time between her heartbeats as 1.00 s. What time between heartbeats would an observer on Earth measure?
The astronaut measures proper time, so Δt = γΔt₀ = 1.25 × 1.00 = 1.25 s.
A spacecraft travels at 0.80c. The journey takes 6.0 years according to clocks on the spacecraft. How long does the journey take according to clocks on Earth?
Ship clocks record proper time, so Δt = γΔt₀ = (5/3) × 6.0 = 10 years.
Observers on Earth measure a spacecraft's journey at 0.80c to take 20 years. How much does the astronaut age during the journey?
The astronaut's proper time is Δt₀ = Δt/γ = 20/1.67 = 12 years.
A Qantas aircraft cruises at 300 m/s. Which best describes the Lorentz factor for the aircraft relative to the ground?
v²/c² = (300/3.0 × 10⁸)² = 1 × 10⁻¹², so γ ≈ 1 + ½(v²/c²) = 1 + 5 × 10⁻¹³: always above 1 but negligible at everyday speeds.
A clock on a spacecraft ticks once per second. Which observer measures the proper time between two ticks?
An observer on Earth watching the spacecraft pass
An astronaut travelling with the clock on the spacecraft
An observer on a second spacecraft moving relative to the first
Any observer, because all observers measure the same interval
Both ticks happen at the same place for the astronaut moving with the clock, so that observer measures proper time.
Which statement about the Lorentz factor γ is always true?
γ can be negative for objects moving away
γ = 1 only at the speed of light
Since 0 ≤ v²/c² < 1, the denominator √(1 − v²/c²) is at most 1, so γ is at least 1 (equal to 1 only at rest).
What is the Lorentz factor for an object moving at 0.50c?
γ = 1/√(1 − 0.25) = 1/√0.75 = 1/0.866 = 1.15; 1.33 comes from forgetting the square root.
A particle in an accelerator has a Lorentz factor of 5.0. What is its speed?
1 − v²/c² = 1/25 = 0.04, so v/c = √0.96 = 0.980; 0.960c forgets to take the square root.
A pion has a mean lifetime of 26 ns when at rest. Pions in a beam travel at 0.95c. What mean lifetime is measured in the laboratory?
GPS satellites orbit at about 3.9 km/s. Considering special relativity alone, how do the satellite clocks behave compared with clocks on the ground?
They run fast, as seen from the ground.
They run at exactly the same rate.
They run slow, as seen from the ground.
Moving clocks are measured to run slow (time dilation); this small effect must be corrected for GPS to stay accurate.
A spacecraft's speed increases from 0.40c to 0.80c. Which describes the change in its Lorentz factor?
It doubles from about 1.09 to about 2.18.
It stays the same, because γ only depends on acceleration.
It increases from about 1.09 to about 1.67.
γ(0.40c) = 1/√0.84 = 1.09 and γ(0.80c) = 1/√0.36 = 1.67; γ is not proportional to speed.
A spacecraft passes Earth at 0.60c. While 50 minutes pass on Earth clocks, how much time do Earth observers measure passing on the spacecraft's clock?
The ship clock measures proper time, so Earth observers find Δt₀ = Δt/γ = 50/1.25 = 40 minutes.
In the 'twin paradox', a twin travels to a distant star at high speed and returns, while her brother stays on Earth. Why is it the travelling twin who is younger when they reunite?
Her heart beats more slowly because of the cold of space.
She changes inertial frames (accelerates) to turn around, so the situation is not symmetric.
Light travels faster on the return journey.
Her spacecraft gains mass, which slows down biological processes.
Only the stay-at-home twin remains in a single inertial frame; the travelling twin's turnaround breaks the symmetry, so she ages less.
Calculate the Lorentz factor for a spacecraft travelling at 0.90c.
A spacecraft travels at 0.70c to a distant star. The journey takes 20.0 years according to Earth observers. How much does the astronaut age during the journey?
The astronaut experiences proper time, which is shorter than the Earth-measured time.
An unstable particle has a lifetime of 1.8 μs in its own rest frame. In the laboratory its lifetime is measured as 9.0 μs. Calculate the Lorentz factor and the particle's speed.
Award marks separately for γ and for the speed; 0.96c is a common error.
Using the idea of a light clock (a light pulse bouncing between two mirrors), explain why a moving clock is measured to run slow.

To an outside observer the light in the moving clock follows a longer, diagonal path between the mirrors. Because the speed of light is the same (c) for all observers, the longer path takes more time, so each tick of the moving clock takes longer: it runs slow.
Key points: longer diagonal path, constant c, therefore longer time per tick.
At what speed, in m/s, would a moving clock be measured to run at half the rate of an identical stationary clock?
Running at half rate means each tick takes twice as long, so γ = 2.
Explain why time dilation is not noticed in everyday life, using a car travelling at 30 m/s on the Monash Freeway as an example.
For v = 30 m/s, v/c = 1 × 10⁻⁷, so v²/c² = 1 × 10⁻¹⁴ and γ ≈ 1 + 5 × 10⁻¹⁵. The difference from 1 is far too small to notice; time dilation only becomes significant at speeds close to c.
Students should show that γ is extremely close to 1 at everyday speeds.
An astronaut on a spacecraft travelling at 0.80c relative to Earth takes 30 minutes to eat a meal, measured on her own clock. How long does the meal take according to observers on Earth?
The astronaut's measurement is proper time because the meal takes place at one location in her frame.
A spaceship travels at 0.80c. Clocks on board record a 6.0-year journey. How long does the journey take according to Earth observers?
γ = 1 ÷ √(1 − 0.64) = 1.67. The ship's clocks measure proper time, so Earth time = 1.67 × 6.0 = 10 years.
physics-4-3: Which equation gives the length L of a moving object measured by an observer, where L₀ is its proper length?
Moving objects are contracted along their direction of motion, so L = L₀/γ is shorter than L₀.
Length contraction of a moving object occurs:
only perpendicular to the direction of motion
only in the direction of motion
only when the object is accelerating
Only the dimension parallel to the relative velocity is contracted; perpendicular dimensions are unchanged.
A spacecraft has a proper length of 100 m. What length does an observer on Earth measure as it flies past at 0.60c?
A rod has a proper length of 2.0 m and moves lengthwise at 0.80c past an observer. What length does the observer measure?
A spacecraft with a proper length of 50 m and a proper width of 10 m flies lengthwise past Earth at 0.80c. What width do Earth observers measure?
The width is perpendicular to the motion, so it is not contracted.
A star is 4.0 light-years from Earth, measured in Earth's frame. An astronaut travels to it at 0.60c. What distance to the star does the astronaut measure?
In the astronaut's frame the Earth–star distance is moving and contracted: L = 4.0/1.25 = 3.2 light-years.
A star is 4.0 light-years from Earth in Earth's frame. An astronaut travels there at 0.60c. How long does the trip take according to the astronaut's clock?
In the astronaut's frame the distance is 3.2 ly, so t = 3.2/0.60 = 5.3 years (Earth time is 6.7 years, and 6.7/1.25 = 5.3).
Which observer measures the proper length of a spacecraft?
An observer on Earth as the spacecraft flies past
An observer moving at 0.99c relative to the spacecraft
Any observer, because all measure the same length
An observer at rest relative to the spacecraft
Proper length is measured in the object's own rest frame.
Where are most of the muons detected at Earth's surface produced?
High in the atmosphere, when cosmic rays collide with nuclei of atmospheric gases
In the Sun's core, by nuclear fusion
Inside Earth's crust, by radioactive decay
Cosmic-ray protons strike atmospheric nuclei about 10–15 km up, producing pions that decay into muons.
A muon has a mean lifetime of 2.2 μs at rest and travels at 0.99c. Ignoring relativity, what mean distance would it travel before decaying?
d = vt = 0.99 × 3.0 × 10⁸ × 2.2 × 10⁻⁶ = 653 m, far less than the height of the atmosphere.
A muon with a rest-frame mean lifetime of 2.2 μs travels at 0.99c (γ = 7.09). Taking time dilation into account, what mean distance does it travel in Earth's frame before decaying?
In the muon's own frame of reference, the muon lives for only about 2.2 μs. How does an observer in the muon's frame explain the muon reaching Earth's surface?
The muon's clock runs fast in its own frame.
The muon travels faster than light in its own frame.
The muon's lifetime is time dilated in its own frame.
The atmosphere is moving relative to the muon, so its thickness is length contracted.
In the muon's frame its lifetime is the proper time; instead the distance to the ground is contracted by γ.
Muons travel at 0.995c (γ = 10.0). In the muon's frame, how thick is a 10 km layer of atmosphere?
Why does the detection of muons at sea level provide evidence for special relativity?
Muons travel faster than light in the atmosphere.
Far more muons reach sea level than classical physics predicts from their short lifetime.
Muons are detected at the same rate at all altitudes.
Muons have no mass, so they do not decay.
Classically almost all muons should decay within about 650 m; their high detection rate at sea level matches time dilation and length contraction.
An observer on Earth and an observer travelling with a muon analyse its journey through the atmosphere. On which quantity do they agree?
The speed of the muon relative to Earth
The time taken for the muon to reach the ground
Both measure the same relative speed; they disagree on lifetime (time dilation) and atmosphere thickness (length contraction).
At what speed would a metre ruler moving lengthwise be measured to be 60 cm long?
A train with a proper length of 200 m travels at 0.60c through a tunnel with a proper length of 160 m. What is the train's length in the tunnel's frame?
160 m, the same as the tunnel's length
L = 200/1.25 = 160 m, so in the tunnel's frame the train just fits.
A train with a proper length of 200 m travels at 0.60c through a tunnel with a proper length of 160 m. What is the tunnel's length in the train's frame?
In the train's frame the tunnel moves and is contracted: L = 160/1.25 = 128 m, so the train does not fit.
A spacecraft has a proper length of 120 m. Calculate its length as measured by an observer it passes at 0.90c.
Check that the contracted length is shorter than the proper length.
An astronaut travelling at 0.95c measures the length of her own spacecraft. Explain whether she observes it to be contracted.
No. She is at rest relative to her spacecraft, so she measures its proper length. Length contraction is only observed for objects moving relative to the observer.
Key point: in her own frame the ship is at rest.
Muons produced 12 km above the ground travel at 0.98c and have a mean lifetime of 2.2 μs in their rest frame. Calculate the mean distance they travel in Earth's frame before decaying.
Students must apply time dilation in Earth's frame; without it the distance is only 650 m.
A muon travels at 0.98c (γ = 5.03) relative to Earth. In the muon's frame, how thick is a 12 km layer of atmosphere?
The 12 km is the proper length because it is measured in Earth's frame, where the atmosphere is at rest.
Explain how the detection of large numbers of muons at sea level is evidence for both time dilation and length contraction.

In Earth's frame, the muons' lifetimes are time dilated, so they live long enough to travel through the atmosphere. In the muons' frame, their lifetime is normal but the atmosphere is length contracted, so the distance is short enough to cover. Both frames predict the same observed result: many muons reach the ground.
Both frames must be described, and the agreement on the outcome noted.
A star is 8.0 light-years from Earth in Earth's frame. At what speed must an astronaut travel for her to measure the distance as 4.8 light-years?
The Earth-frame distance is the proper length.
A spacecraft flies from Earth to the Moon. Identify which observer measures the proper length of the spacecraft and which measures the proper length of the Earth–Moon distance, explaining why.

The astronaut on the spacecraft measures the spacecraft's proper length, because the spacecraft is at rest in her frame. An observer on Earth measures the proper Earth–Moon distance, because Earth and the Moon are (approximately) at rest in that frame.
Proper length is always measured in the rest frame of the object or distance.
A muon has a mean lifetime of 2.2 µs in its own frame and travels at 0.995c. How far does it travel in one mean lifetime, as measured from Earth?
γ = 1 ÷ √(1 − 0.995²) ≈ 10.0. Earth-frame time = 10.0 × 2.2 µs = 22 µs. Distance = 0.995 × 3.0 × 10⁸ × 22 × 10⁻⁶ ≈ 6.6 km (without relativity only about 660 m).
physics-4-4: In the equation E = mc², where m is the rest mass of a body, the equation states that:
a body at rest has energy in proportion to its mass
mass can only be converted to light
a body's energy depends only on its speed
energy can be created from nothing
E = mc² gives the rest energy: mass is a form of energy, with c² as the conversion factor.
What is the rest energy of an electron (mass 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg)?
An electron (rest energy 8.19 × 10⁻¹⁴ J) travels at 0.60c. What is its kinetic energy?
Ek = (γ − 1)mc² = 0.25 × 8.19 × 10⁻¹⁴ = 2.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ J; 1.5 × 10⁻¹⁴ J is the classical ½mv² value and 1.0 × 10⁻¹³ J is the total energy.
Which expression gives the total energy of a particle of rest mass m moving with Lorentz factor γ?
Total energy is γmc², the sum of rest energy mc² and kinetic energy (γ − 1)mc².
Which expression gives the relativistic kinetic energy of a particle of rest mass m?
Kinetic energy is total energy minus rest energy: γmc² − mc² = (γ − 1)mc².
The Sun radiates energy at a rate of about 3.8 × 10²⁶ W. At what rate does the Sun's mass decrease as a result?
In a nuclear fission reaction, the total mass of the products compared with the total mass of the reactants is:
exactly the same, because mass is always conserved
smaller, with the mass difference released as energy
smaller, with the lost mass converted into extra neutrons
The mass defect Δm is released as energy according to E = Δmc².
How much work must be done to accelerate a proton (mass 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg) from rest to 0.80c?
mc² = 1.50 × 10⁻¹⁰ J and γ = 5/3, so Ek = (2/3) × 1.50 × 10⁻¹⁰ = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ J; 4.8 × 10⁻¹¹ J is the classical value.
Why does the classical formula Ek = ½mv² fail for particles moving close to the speed of light?
It underestimates the energy, because the true energy required approaches infinity as v approaches c.
It overestimates the energy, because mass decreases at high speeds.
It gives the correct energy but the wrong direction.
It only fails for particles with no charge.
Relativistic Ek = (γ − 1)mc² grows without limit as v → c, whereas ½mv² stays finite, so the classical formula is far too small.
A proton has a rest energy of 938 MeV. What is its total energy when it travels at 0.60c?
E = γmc² = 1.25 × 938 MeV = 1173 MeV ≈ 1.17 GeV; 235 MeV is the kinetic energy only.
An electron and a positron, each with mass 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg, annihilate while at rest. How much energy is released?
Total mass 1.82 × 10⁻³⁰ kg is converted: E = 1.82 × 10⁻³⁰ × 9.0 × 10¹⁶ = 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ J.
A cup of hot coffee cools down on a bench. According to mass–energy equivalence, which statement is correct?
Its mass stays exactly the same, because only nuclear reactions change mass.
Its mass increases as it cools.
Its mass decreases very slightly, by an amount too small to measure.
Any loss of energy ΔE reduces mass by ΔE/c²; for thermal energy this is around 10⁻¹² kg or less, which is undetectable.
In the Sun, about 0.7% of the mass of hydrogen is converted to energy when it fuses to form helium. How much energy is released when 1.0 kg of hydrogen fuses?
An electron gains kinetic energy equal to its rest energy. What is its Lorentz factor?
Ek = (γ − 1)mc² = mc² gives γ − 1 = 1, so γ = 2.
An electron (rest energy 0.511 MeV) is accelerated until γ = 3.0. What is its kinetic energy?
Ek = (γ − 1)mc² = 2.0 × 0.511 = 1.02 MeV; 1.53 MeV is the total energy.
If 1.0 g of mass were converted completely into energy, how much energy would be released?
E = mc² = 1.0 × 10⁻³ kg × 9.0 × 10¹⁶ = 9.0 × 10¹³ J; remember to convert grams to kilograms.
Protons in a particle accelerator are already travelling at 0.999c. More energy is supplied to them. Which statement is correct?
Their total energy increases greatly while their speed increases only slightly.
Their speed increases in proportion to the energy supplied, exceeding c.
Their energy stays the same, because they cannot go faster.
Their rest mass increases while their kinetic energy stays the same.
Near c, γ rises steeply with tiny increases in speed, so the added energy appears as large increases in γmc² while v approaches but never reaches c.
The fission of one uranium-235 nucleus releases about 3.2 × 10⁻¹¹ J (200 MeV). What mass is converted into energy in one fission?
The Loy Yang power stations in the Latrobe Valley produce about 2.2 GW of electrical power. If this energy came entirely from converting mass, how much mass would be converted each day?
Check the conversion of one day to 86 400 s.
An electron (mass 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg) travels at 0.80c. Calculate its total energy and its kinetic energy.
mc² = 8.19 × 10⁻¹⁴ J and γ = 1.67. Total energy E = γmc² = 1.67 × 8.19 × 10⁻¹⁴ = 1.37 × 10⁻¹³ J. Ek = E − mc² = 5.5 × 10⁻¹⁴ J.
Using the relativistic kinetic energy equation, explain why an object with mass can never reach the speed of light.
Ek = (γ − 1)mc², and γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²) approaches infinity as v approaches c. So an infinite amount of energy would be needed to reach c, which is impossible.
Key link: γ → ∞ as v → c, so Ek → ∞.
Explain why, at everyday speeds, the classical kinetic energy ½mv² gives practically the same result as the relativistic kinetic energy (γ − 1)mc².
When v is much less than c, γ ≈ 1 + ½v²/c². Then (γ − 1)mc² ≈ ½(v²/c²)mc² = ½mv². So the two formulas agree at low speeds, and differ only near c.
Full credit for showing γ − 1 ≈ ½v²/c², or for a numerical example showing the two agree.
A proton (rest energy 938 MeV) is given 938 MeV of kinetic energy. Find its Lorentz factor and its speed.
Total energy is then 1876 MeV, twice the rest energy.
Explain, using mass–energy equivalence, where the energy released by nuclear fusion in the Sun comes from.

The total mass of the helium nucleus (and other products) is less than the total mass of the hydrogen nuclei that fused. This mass difference Δm is converted into energy according to E = Δmc², released mainly as kinetic energy of particles and as radiation.
Key point: the products have less mass than the reactants.
An electron's total energy is three times its rest energy. Calculate its speed.
Note that it is the total energy, γmc², that equals 3mc².
The Sun radiates about 3.8 × 10²⁶ J every second. How much mass does it lose each second?
Δm = E/c² = 3.8 × 10²⁶ ÷ (3.0 × 10⁸)² ≈ 4.2 × 10⁹ kg. Dividing by c instead of c² gives the 10¹⁸ answer.
physics-5-1: What is the SI unit of magnetic flux?
Magnetic flux Φ = B⊥A has units T m², which is defined as the weber.
A flat loop of area 0.020 m² sits perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.50 T. What is the magnetic flux through the loop?
A loop is oriented so that its plane is parallel to a uniform magnetic field of strength B. If the loop has area A, the flux through it is
With the plane parallel to the field, no field lines pass through the loop, so the perpendicular component of B through the area is zero.
Define magnetic flux and state the equation used to calculate it for a flat loop in a uniform field.
Magnetic flux is a measure of the total magnetic field passing through an area. Φ = B⊥A, where B⊥ is the component of the magnetic field perpendicular to the area A; it is measured in webers (Wb).
Award marks for the idea of field 'through' an area and for using only the perpendicular component.
A square coil of side 10 cm is placed perpendicular to a 0.40 T magnetic field. What is the flux through one turn of the coil?
The flux through each turn of a 200-turn coil increases uniformly from 0 to 3.0 × 10⁻³ Wb in 0.050 s. What is the magnitude of the average induced emf?
A 50-turn coil of area 0.010 m² is perpendicular to a magnetic field that falls uniformly from 0.80 T to zero in 0.20 s. What is the magnitude of the average induced emf?
A circular loop of radius 5.0 cm is perpendicular to a uniform 0.60 T magnetic field. Calculate the flux through the loop.
Common error: using the radius in cm or using the diameter instead of the radius.
Which of the following will NOT induce an emf in a flat coil?
Rotating the coil about an axis perpendicular to the field
Moving the coil at constant velocity entirely within a region of uniform, constant magnetic field
Increasing the strength of the field through the stationary coil
Pulling the coil out of the field region
An emf requires a change in flux; translating the coil within a uniform field leaves the flux through it unchanged.
According to Faraday's law, the magnitude of the induced emf in a coil is proportional to
the rate of change of magnetic flux through the coil
the magnetic flux through the coil
the magnetic field strength at the coil
ε = −NΔΦ/Δt, so it depends on how quickly the flux changes, not on the flux itself.
A coil experiences a given flux change. If the number of turns is doubled and the time taken for the same flux change is halved, the average induced emf becomes
ε = NΔΦ/Δt; doubling N doubles ε and halving Δt doubles it again, giving a factor of 4.
A 150-turn coil of area 4.0 × 10⁻³ m² is perpendicular to a 0.50 T field. It is pulled completely out of the field in 0.080 s. Calculate the average emf induced.
Check that the number of turns is included and that the final flux is zero.
A 100-turn coil of area 0.050 m² in a 0.20 T field is rotated from having its plane perpendicular to the field to having its plane parallel to the field in 0.10 s. What is the average induced emf?
A single loop of area 0.040 m² is perpendicular to a 0.25 T field. It is flipped through 180° in 0.020 s. What is the average induced emf?
The flux reverses from +BA to −BA, so ΔΦ = 2BA = 2 × 0.25 × 0.040 = 0.020 Wb and ε = 0.020 / 0.020 = 1.0 V.
A loop of area 0.30 m² is in a uniform 0.20 T field. The normal to the loop makes an angle of 60° with the field. What is the flux through the loop?
Only the component of B along the normal counts: Φ = BA cos 60° = 0.20 × 0.30 × 0.5 = 0.030 Wb.
A rectangular loop moves at constant speed through a large region of uniform magnetic field, staying entirely inside the field. Explain why no current is induced in the loop.

The flux through the loop is BA and both B and A stay constant while the loop is fully inside the field, so the flux does not change. With ΔΦ/Δt = 0, Faraday's law gives zero emf and therefore no current.
The key idea is that emf depends on a change in flux, not on motion itself.
A student pushes a bar magnet into a coil, first slowly and then quickly, starting and finishing in the same positions. Compared with the slow push, the quick push produces
the same emf and the same total change in flux
a larger emf and a larger total change in flux
a smaller emf, because there is less time for current to build up
a larger emf, but the same total change in flux
The flux change depends only on start and end positions, but the emf depends on the rate of change, which is greater for the quick push.
The flux through each turn of a 25-turn coil increases uniformly from 2.0 mWb to 6.0 mWb over 40 ms. What is the average induced emf?
While the flux through a coil is held constant at a large non-zero value, the induced emf in the coil is
An emf is only induced when the flux changes; constant flux means ΔΦ/Δt = 0.
State three ways to increase the emf induced in a coil by a moving bar magnet.

Any three of: move the magnet faster (increase the rate of change of flux); use a stronger magnet; increase the number of turns on the coil; increase the cross-sectional area of the coil (or use an iron core to increase the flux).
Each method must link to increasing N or the rate of change of flux.
Which combination of units is equivalent to the volt?
From ε = NΔΦ/Δt, an emf has units of webers per second.
A 400-turn coil has a steady emf of 6.0 V induced in it for 0.30 s while the flux changes at a constant rate. What is the change in flux through each turn?
A coil of fixed area is placed in a magnetic field at Monash's physics lab. Which change would increase the flux through the coil the most?
Doubling the field strength while rotating the coil from 60° to 0° between its normal and the field
Rotating the coil from 0° to 60° between its normal and the field
Halving the field strength while rotating the coil from 60° to 0°
Φ = BA cos θ; doubling B and increasing cos θ from 0.5 to 1 multiplies the flux by 4, more than any other option.
An 80-turn coil of area 0.025 m² is perpendicular to a magnetic field that increases uniformly from 0.10 T to 0.50 T in 0.20 s. The coil has a resistance of 4.0 Ω. Calculate the induced current.
Use the change in field (0.40 T), not the final field.
Distinguish between magnetic flux density (B) and magnetic flux (Φ).
Magnetic flux density B is the strength of the magnetic field at a point, measured in tesla. Magnetic flux Φ is the amount of field passing through a given area, Φ = B⊥A, measured in webers.
Students should give both the meaning and the units of each quantity.
A 200-turn coil of area 0.010 m² is perpendicular to a 0.50 T field. The field falls uniformly to zero in 0.20 s. Find the average induced emf.
physics-5-2: physics-5-2-1
Lenz's law is a direct consequence of the law of conservation of
charge
momentum
energy
mass
If the induced current aided the change, energy would be created from nothing; opposing the change means work must be done to produce electrical energy.
physics-5-2-2
The north pole of a bar magnet is pushed towards one end of a coil connected in a closed circuit. The induced current makes the end of the coil nearest the magnet
a north pole, repelling the magnet
a south pole, attracting the magnet
a south pole, repelling the magnet
neither pole, as only an emf is produced
The induced current opposes the approach of the magnet, so the near end becomes a north pole that repels the incoming north pole.
physics-5-2-3
The north pole of a bar magnet is pulled away from one end of a closed coil. The induced current makes the end of the coil nearest the magnet
a north pole, repelling the magnet
a north pole, attracting the magnet
a south pole, attracting the magnet
a south pole, repelling the magnet
The induced current opposes the magnet moving away, so the near end becomes a south pole which attracts the retreating north pole.
physics-5-2-4
State Lenz's law.
The direction of an induced current (or emf) is such that the magnetic field it produces opposes the change in magnetic flux that caused it.
The word 'change' is essential: the induced field opposes the change in flux, not the field itself.
physics-5-2-5
A strong magnet dropped down a vertical copper pipe falls much more slowly than one dropped beside the pipe. The best explanation is that
copper is ferromagnetic and attracts the magnet
air trapped in the pipe creates extra drag
the pipe shields the magnet from gravity
eddy currents induced in the pipe produce magnetic fields that oppose the magnet's motion
The moving magnet changes the flux through rings of the pipe, inducing currents whose fields oppose the relative motion (Lenz's law). Copper is not ferromagnetic.
physics-5-2-6
A flat loop lies in the plane of the page in a magnetic field directed into the page. The field strength is increasing. Viewed from the front, the induced current in the loop is
clockwise
zero
alternating between clockwise and anticlockwise
anticlockwise
The induced current must produce a field out of the page to oppose the increasing inward flux, which requires an anticlockwise current.
physics-5-2-7
A flat loop lies in the plane of the page in a magnetic field directed into the page. The field strength is decreasing. Viewed from the front, the induced current in the loop is
anticlockwise
zero
alternating between clockwise and anticlockwise
clockwise
The induced current tries to maintain the inward flux, so it produces a field into the page, which requires a clockwise current.
physics-5-2-8
Use the principle of conservation of energy to explain why the induced current in a coil must oppose the motion of a magnet pushed into it.

If the induced current attracted the magnet, the magnet would speed up and more current would be produced with no work input, creating energy from nothing. Because the induced current opposes the motion, work must be done to push the magnet in, and this work is converted into electrical energy.
Look for the link between opposing force, work done and electrical energy produced.
physics-5-2-9
A flat loop lies in the plane of the page in a magnetic field directed out of the page. The field strength is increasing. Viewed from the front, the induced current is
anticlockwise
clockwise
zero
alternating between clockwise and anticlockwise
To oppose increasing outward flux the induced field must point into the page, which a clockwise current produces.
physics-5-2-10
A square loop is pulled at constant speed out of a region where a uniform field points into the page. While the loop is partly out of the field, the induced current, viewed from the front, is
anticlockwise
clockwise
zero
clockwise then anticlockwise
The inward flux through the loop is decreasing, so the induced current produces an inward field to oppose the decrease, which is clockwise.
physics-5-2-11
A bar magnet is pushed into a coil. Compared with when the coil is open-circuited, when the coil is connected to a resistor the force needed to push the magnet in at the same speed is
smaller, because the induced current attracts the magnet
greater, because the induced current produces a field that opposes the magnet's motion
the same, because the flux change is the same
zero, because the coil does work on the magnet
A current flows only in the closed circuit, and its field opposes the motion, so extra work must be done, which becomes electrical energy.
physics-5-2-12
A strong magnet is dropped into a long vertical copper pipe. Explain why it reaches a terminal velocity.

As the magnet falls, the changing flux induces eddy currents in the pipe whose fields oppose its motion (Lenz's law), producing an upward force. This force increases with speed, so the magnet speeds up until the upward magnetic force equals its weight; the net force is then zero and it falls at constant (terminal) velocity.
Must mention the force growing with speed until it balances the weight.
physics-5-2-13
An aluminium ring rests over the top of a vertical solenoid with an iron core. When the switch to the solenoid is closed, the ring jumps upwards because
aluminium is strongly attracted to iron
the increasing flux induces a current in the ring whose field repels the solenoid's field
the solenoid's field pushes on the ring's own permanent magnetism
the ring is heated and expands upwards
The sudden rise in flux induces a current in the ring that opposes the increase, making the ring and solenoid repel.
physics-5-2-14
The aluminium ring in a 'jumping ring' demonstration is replaced with an identical ring that has a narrow cut through it. When the switch is closed, the cut ring
jumps higher because its resistance is lower
jumps to the same height as the complete ring
has a current induced but no emf, so it does not jump
has an emf induced but no current, so it does not jump
The changing flux still induces an emf, but without a complete circuit no current flows, so there is no opposing magnetic force.
physics-5-2-15
Some trains use eddy-current brakes, where electromagnets near the steel rails induce currents in the rails. The main energy transformation in this braking is
thermal energy to kinetic energy
kinetic energy to chemical energy
gravitational potential energy to kinetic energy
kinetic energy to thermal energy in the rails
The eddy currents dissipate energy as heat in the rail's resistance, and that energy comes from the train's kinetic energy.
physics-5-2-16
A wire loop lies flat on a bench in a vertical magnetic field that points upwards. The field is switched off. Viewed from above, what is the direction of the induced current? Explain.

Anticlockwise viewed from above. The upward flux decreases, so the induced current produces an upward field inside the loop to oppose the decrease; by the right-hand grip rule this needs an anticlockwise current viewed from above.
Students should state the direction of the induced field before deducing the current direction.
physics-5-2-17
In Faraday's law, ε = −NΔΦ/Δt, the negative sign indicates that
the emf is always negative
flux always decreases when an emf is induced
the induced emf opposes the change in flux that produces it
the induced current flows from negative to positive terminal outside the source
The negative sign represents Lenz's law: the direction of the induced emf is such that it opposes the change in flux.
physics-5-2-18

A coil is connected to a centre-zero galvanometer. Pushing the north pole of a magnet into the coil makes the needle deflect to the right. Which action would also make the needle deflect to the right?
Pushing the south pole of the magnet into the same end of the coil
Pulling the south pole of the magnet out of the same end of the coil
Pulling the north pole of the magnet out of the same end of the coil
Holding the north pole of the magnet stationary inside the coil
Removing a south pole reduces flux pointing towards the magnet, which is the same change in flux as adding flux pointing away from the magnet, as happens when a north pole is inserted.
physics-5-2-19
A magnet is dropped through a vertical coil whose ends are not connected to anything. Ignoring air resistance, as it falls through the coil the magnet
falls with acceleration less than g, because an emf is induced
accelerates at g, because no current flows to produce an opposing force
falls at constant speed
slows down while inside the coil
An emf is induced, but with an open circuit there is no current, so there is no magnetic force opposing the fall.
physics-5-2-20
In a jumping-ring demonstration, explain why the ring jumps when the switch is closed but does not jump while a steady DC current flows.

When the switch is closed the current, and therefore the flux through the ring, increases rapidly, inducing a current in the ring whose field opposes the solenoid's field, so the ring is repelled. Once the current is steady the flux is constant, so no emf or current is induced and there is no repulsion.
Key idea: only a changing flux induces a current.
physics-5-2-21

A long straight wire carries a constant current upwards in the plane of the page. A rectangular loop to the right of the wire, in the same plane, moves directly away from the wire. Viewed from the front, the induced current in the loop is
anticlockwise
clockwise
zero
clockwise then anticlockwise
To the right of the wire the field points into the page and gets weaker with distance, so the inward flux decreases; the induced current produces an inward field, which is clockwise.
physics-5-2-22
A copper plate swinging as a pendulum between the poles of a magnet stops quickly. If many deep slots are cut into the plate, it swings for much longer because
the slots reduce the mass of the plate
the slots reduce the size of eddy currents, so there is less magnetic braking
the slots make the plate magnetic
the slots increase air resistance
Slots break up the closed current paths, reducing the eddy currents and therefore the opposing magnetic force.
physics-5-2-23
A conducting loop is held stationary near a stationary bar magnet. Which statement is correct?
A steady current is induced because flux passes through the loop
A current is induced that opposes the magnet's field
No current is induced because the flux through the loop is not changing
An alternating current is induced
Induction requires a changing flux; a constant flux through a stationary loop produces no emf.
physics-5-2-24
Electric vehicles use regenerative braking, where the drive motor acts as a generator. Explain how this slows the car.

When braking, the wheels turn the motor's coil in its magnetic field, inducing a current that charges the battery. By Lenz's law, the induced current produces a force (torque) that opposes the rotation, slowing the car while converting kinetic energy into electrical energy.
Award marks for identifying the opposing torque and the energy transformation.
physics-5-2-25
The north pole of a magnet is moved towards the end of a coil. Viewed from the magnet's side, in which direction does the induced current flow around the coil? Explain.

Anticlockwise as viewed from the magnet. The near end of the coil must become a north pole to oppose the approaching north pole, and a current that appears anticlockwise when viewed from an end makes that end a north pole.
Use the right-hand grip rule: fingers curl with the current, thumb points to the north pole.
physics-5-2-c1
The north pole of a bar magnet is pushed towards one end of a coil. The induced current makes that end of the coil:
A south pole, so it attracts the magnet
A north pole, so it repels the approaching magnet
Neither pole, because no current flows until the magnet stops
A north pole, so it attracts the magnet
Lenz's law: the induced current opposes the change in flux. If it attracted the magnet, energy would be created from nothing.
physics-5-3: physics-5-3-1
An alternator (AC generator) connects its rotating coil to the external circuit using
a split-ring commutator
a rectifier diode
a permanent magnet
slip rings
Slip rings keep each end of the coil connected to the same external terminal, so the output alternates.
physics-5-3-2
The function of a split-ring commutator in a DC generator is to
keep the coil's connections fixed so the output alternates
increase the peak emf of the generator
reverse the coil's connection to the external circuit every half turn, so the output has one polarity
reduce friction between the brushes and the coil
By swapping the connections each half rotation, the commutator ensures the current in the external circuit always flows in the same direction.
physics-5-3-3
A coil rotates at constant speed in a uniform magnetic field. The induced emf is at its maximum when
the plane of the coil is perpendicular to the field
the plane of the coil is parallel to the field
the flux through the coil is at its maximum
the coil has rotated 45° from the perpendicular position
When the plane is parallel to the field the flux is zero but changing most rapidly, giving maximum emf.
physics-5-3-4
A coil rotates in a uniform magnetic field. Explain why the induced emf is a maximum when the plane of the coil is parallel to the field, even though the flux through it is zero.

The emf depends on the rate of change of flux, not the flux itself. When the plane is parallel to the field, the flux is passing through zero and changing at its fastest rate (the steepest part of the flux–time graph), so the emf is maximum.
Common error: thinking maximum flux gives maximum emf.
physics-5-3-5
A coil rotates at constant speed in a uniform magnetic field. At the instant the flux through the coil is a maximum, the induced emf is
zero
a maximum
half its maximum
equal to the RMS value
At maximum flux the flux is momentarily not changing (the turning point of the flux–time graph), so the emf is zero.
physics-5-3-6
The rotation rate of a simple AC generator is doubled. What happens to the peak emf and the frequency of the output?
Both double
Peak emf doubles; frequency stays the same
Peak emf stays the same; frequency doubles
Peak emf quadruples; frequency doubles
Rotating faster halves the time for each flux change, doubling the emf, and also doubles the number of cycles per second.
physics-5-3-7
Australian household mains supply is 230 V RMS. What is the approximate peak voltage?
physics-5-3-8
Australian mains electricity is 230 V RMS at 50 Hz. Calculate the peak voltage and the period of the supply.
Both values are needed for full marks.
physics-5-3-9
A generator coil rotates at 50 revolutions per second. What is the period of the AC output?
50 ms
2.0 ms
20 ms
10 ms
physics-5-3-10
What is the peak-to-peak voltage of the 230 V RMS mains supply?
V_{peak} = 230√2 ≈ 325 V, and peak-to-peak is twice the peak, about 650 V.
physics-5-3-11
A 1000 W heater operates from the 230 V RMS mains. What is the peak current through it?
physics-5-3-12
The rotation speed of a simple AC generator is halved. Describe the effect on the peak emf and on the frequency of the output.
Both are halved. The flux changes half as quickly, so the peak emf halves, and the coil completes half as many rotations per second, so the frequency halves.
Students often forget that the peak emf, not just the frequency, changes.
physics-5-3-13
The RMS value of an alternating voltage is best described as
the average value of the voltage over one cycle
the maximum value of the voltage
half the peak-to-peak voltage
the steady DC voltage that would deliver the same average power to a resistor
RMS is defined by equivalent heating effect: it gives the same average power in a resistor as a DC voltage of that value.
physics-5-3-14
A sinusoidal AC voltage with a peak of 20 V is applied across a 10 Ω resistor. What is the average power dissipated?
V_{RMS} = 20/√2 = 14.1 V, so P = V_{RMS}²/R = 200/10 = 20 W. Using the peak voltage gives the wrong answer of 40 W.
physics-5-3-15

A generator has a 100-turn coil of area 0.020 m² in a 0.50 T field, rotating at 25 revolutions per second. What is the average emf during a quarter turn starting from the position where the plane is perpendicular to the field?
ΔΦ = BA = 0.010 Wb per turn and a quarter turn takes 1/(4 × 25) = 0.010 s, so ε = 100 × 0.010 / 0.010 = 100 V.
physics-5-3-16
A 2400 W electric kettle is connected to the 230 V RMS mains. Calculate the RMS current and the resistance of the heating element.
Use RMS values for power calculations with AC.
physics-5-3-17
A coil rotates at constant speed in a uniform magnetic field. The average emf over one complete revolution is
zero
equal to the peak emf
equal to the RMS emf
equal to half the peak emf
After a full revolution the flux returns to its starting value, so ΔΦ = 0 and the average emf over the revolution is zero.
physics-5-3-18
In a generator, the brushes
reverse the current direction every half turn
produce the magnetic field
increase the speed of rotation
provide a sliding electrical contact between the rotating coil and the external circuit
Brushes (usually carbon) press against the slip rings or commutator to connect the rotating coil to the stationary circuit.
physics-5-3-19
The output of a simple single-coil DC generator with a split-ring commutator is best described as
a constant, steady voltage
a series of half-sine pulses, all of the same polarity
a sinusoidal voltage that alternates in polarity
a square wave alternating in polarity
The commutator flips the negative half-cycles, so the output varies in size but never changes polarity.
physics-5-3-20
Explain the difference between the output of a generator fitted with slip rings and one fitted with a split-ring commutator.

Slip rings keep each end of the coil connected to the same external terminal, so the output current reverses every half turn (AC). A split-ring commutator swaps the connections every half turn, so the output always has the same polarity (varying DC).
Award marks for linking each device to its output type.
physics-5-3-21
A wind turbine's generator becomes harder to turn when a load is connected to it. This is because
the current in the coil experiences a magnetic force that opposes its rotation
the coil's resistance increases when current flows
the magnetic field disappears when current flows
friction in the brushes increases with current
With a closed circuit, current flows in the coil and, by Lenz's law, the resulting force opposes the motion, so more mechanical work is needed.
physics-5-3-22
Large alternators in Victorian power stations rotate an electromagnet inside stationary output coils. A key advantage of this design is that
it produces DC without a commutator
it does not need a magnetic field
the large output current does not need to pass through sliding contacts
it eliminates the need for a turbine
With stationary output coils, the high output current is taken directly from fixed terminals; only the small field current passes through slip rings.
physics-5-3-23
An AC supply has a peak voltage of 340 V. What is its RMS voltage?
physics-5-3-24
A 50-turn coil of area 0.030 m² is in a uniform 0.20 T field, with its plane perpendicular to the field. It rotates through half a turn in 0.010 s. Calculate the average emf.
After half a turn the flux reverses, so ΔΦ = 2BA = 2 × 0.20 × 0.030 = 0.012 Wb per turn. ε = NΔΦ/Δt = 50 × 0.012 / 0.010 = 60 V.
Common error: using ΔΦ = BA and getting 30 V.
physics-5-3-25
Explain why RMS values, rather than peak values, are used to rate AC appliances and supplies.

The RMS value gives the equivalent DC value that delivers the same average power to a resistor, so power can be calculated directly with P = V_{RMS} I_{RMS}. Peak values would overstate the average power, since the voltage is only at its peak for an instant.
Key idea: RMS links AC to the same heating effect as DC.
physics-5-3-c1
An alternator produces a peak voltage of 340 V. Its rotation speed is then doubled. Which statement is correct?
The RMS voltage stays 240 V and the frequency doubles
The peak voltage stays 340 V and the frequency doubles
The peak voltage becomes 680 V and the frequency doubles
The peak voltage becomes 680 V and the frequency is unchanged
Faster rotation changes the flux faster, doubling the emf (RMS goes from 240 V to 480 V), and doubles the number of cycles per second.
physics-5-4: physics-5-4-1
An ideal transformer has 1150 turns on its primary and 60 turns on its secondary. It is connected to the 230 V RMS mains. What is the secondary voltage?
physics-5-4-2
A transformer will not work if its primary is connected to a steady DC supply because
a steady current produces a constant flux, so no emf is induced in the secondary
DC cannot flow through copper coils
the iron core is demagnetised by DC
DC flows only in the secondary coil
Transformers rely on a changing flux in the core; once a DC current is steady, the flux is constant and no emf is induced.
physics-5-4-3
An ideal step-up transformer has a turns ratio of 1 : 20 (primary : secondary). The primary current is 50 A. What is the secondary current?
For an ideal transformer, I_{s} = I_{p} × N_{p}/N_{s} = 50 × 1/20 = 2.5 A, so power in equals power out.
physics-5-4-4
Explain how a transformer produces an alternating voltage in its secondary coil.

An alternating current in the primary coil produces a changing magnetic flux in the iron core. The core carries this changing flux through the secondary coil, and by Faraday's law the changing flux induces an alternating emf in the secondary.
Must include changing flux and Faraday's law.
physics-5-4-5
Transformer cores are made from thin laminated sheets of soft iron, insulated from each other, in order to
increase the turns ratio
prevent the core from becoming magnetised
reduce energy losses due to eddy currents
allow the transformer to work with DC
Insulated laminations break up current paths in the core, reducing eddy currents and the heat they produce.
physics-5-4-6
The power lost as heat in a transmission line carrying current I with total resistance R is
V²/R using the transmission voltage
VI using the transmission voltage
I²R
IR
The heat loss in the line depends on the current through it and its resistance, P_{loss} = I²R.
physics-5-4-7
A power station transmits 10 MW. If the transmission voltage is increased from 20 kV to 200 kV, the power lost in the lines is
reduced to 1/10 of its original value
unchanged
increased 100 times
reduced to 1/100 of its original value
I = P/V falls by a factor of 10, and P_{loss} = I²R falls by a factor of 10² = 100.
physics-5-4-8
A substation transformer steps 66 kV down to 11 kV. The primary has 1800 turns. Calculate the number of secondary turns, assuming an ideal transformer.
Check that the ratio is inverted correctly for a step-down transformer.
physics-5-4-9
500 kW of power is transmitted at 10 kV along lines with a total resistance of 4.0 Ω. What is the power lost in the lines?
2.5 kW
25 MW
10 kW
physics-5-4-10
500 kW of power is sent at 10 kV along lines with a total resistance of 4.0 Ω. What is the voltage at the load end of the lines?
10 kV
9.6 kV
9.8 kV
I = 50 A, so the voltage drop is IR = 50 × 4.0 = 200 V, leaving 10 000 − 200 = 9800 V at the load.
physics-5-4-11
A student calculates the power loss in a transmission line using P = V²/R with V equal to the 10 kV transmission voltage. This is incorrect because
V²/R only applies to DC circuits
the formula should be V/R²
the 10 kV is not the voltage across the line resistance; only the much smaller voltage drop across the lines should be used
the power loss does not depend on resistance
P = V²/R requires the voltage across the resistance itself, which is the voltage drop along the lines, not the supply voltage.
physics-5-4-12
Explain why electricity is transmitted at very high voltages over long distances.

For a given power, P = VI, so a higher voltage means a smaller current. The power lost as heat in the lines is P_{loss} = I²R, so reducing the current greatly reduces losses (halving the current reduces losses by a factor of 4).
Must link high voltage to low current and to I²R.
physics-5-4-13
An ideal transformer has 4800 turns on its primary. It converts 240 V RMS to 12 V RMS. How many turns are on the secondary?
physics-5-4-14
An ideal transformer supplies 60 W to a 12 V lamp. The primary is connected to 240 V RMS. What is the primary current?
Power in equals power out, so I_{p} = P/V_{p} = 60/240 = 0.25 A.
physics-5-4-15
Transformer cores are made of soft iron mainly because soft iron
is easily magnetised and concentrates the changing flux so it links both coils
is a good electrical conductor that carries current between the coils
stays permanently magnetised
has a high resistance that reduces heat in the coils
The core channels the changing flux produced by the primary through the secondary, improving flux linkage.
physics-5-4-16
100 kW is to be transmitted through lines with a total resistance of 0.50 Ω. Calculate the power loss if it is transmitted at (a) 415 V and (b) 11 kV.
The comparison shows how much higher voltage reduces losses.
physics-5-4-17
Which statement about an ideal step-down transformer is correct?
The secondary has more turns and carries a larger current than the primary
The secondary has fewer turns and carries a smaller current than the primary
The secondary delivers more power than the primary receives
The secondary has fewer turns and carries a larger current than the primary
Fewer secondary turns lowers voltage; since power is conserved, the secondary current must be larger.
physics-5-4-18
