A 1 : 10 step-up transformer is connected to a 50 Hz supply. What is the frequency of the secondary output?
500 Hz
5 Hz
50 Hz
0 Hz
The secondary emf is induced by the same changing flux, so it has the same frequency as the primary.
physics-5-4-19
For the same power delivered, the transmission voltage is doubled. The power lost in the lines becomes
half its original value
double its original value
one quarter of its original value
unchanged
Doubling V halves I, and P_{loss} = I²R becomes (1/2)² = 1/4 of the original.
physics-5-4-20
Explain why transformer cores are laminated.

The changing flux induces eddy currents in the iron core, which waste energy as heat. Laminations (thin sheets insulated from each other) break up the paths for these currents, reducing eddy currents and so reducing energy loss.
Key idea: insulation between layers increases the resistance of eddy current paths.
physics-5-4-21
2.0 MW is transmitted at 40 kV through lines with a total resistance of 5.0 Ω. Approximately what percentage of the transmitted power is lost in the lines?
physics-5-4-22
The main reason AC rather than DC has traditionally been used for electricity distribution in Australia is that
AC loses no energy in transmission lines
AC voltages can be easily stepped up and down using transformers
AC travels faster along wires than DC
AC is easier to store in batteries
Transformers require a changing current, so AC allows efficient high-voltage transmission and safe low-voltage use.
physics-5-4-23
A zone substation transformer steps 22 kV down to 415 V. What is the approximate primary : secondary turns ratio?
N_{p}/N_{s} = V_{p}/V_{s} = 22 000/415 ≈ 53, so the ratio is about 53 : 1.
physics-5-4-24
An ideal transformer's secondary supplies 4.0 A at 24 V to a load. The primary is connected to 240 V RMS. Calculate the primary current and the turns ratio.
Power in equals power out for an ideal transformer.
physics-5-4-25
A farm shed needs 20 kW at 240 V and is supplied by a line of total resistance 0.20 Ω. Calculate the voltage drop along the line and the power lost in it.
Students should see that low-voltage supply over a line causes significant loss.
physics-5-4-c1
10 MW is transmitted through lines of total resistance 5.0 Ω. Compare the power lost at 22 kV with the power lost at 220 kV.
About 1.0 MW at 22 kV and 10 kW at 220 kV: 100 times less
I = P/V: 455 A or 45.5 A. P(loss) = I²R: 1.03 × 10⁶ W or 1.03 × 10⁴ W. Ten times the voltage gives one-tenth the current and one-hundredth the loss.
physics-6-1: A red laser emits light of wavelength 600 nm in a vacuum. What is the frequency of this light? (c = 3.0 × 10^8 m s⁻¹)
Light passes from air into a glass block. Which property of the light remains unchanged?
Frequency is set by the source and does not change at a boundary; speed and wavelength both decrease in glass.
According to Maxwell's theory, electromagnetic waves are produced by:
a steady direct current in a straight wire
Only accelerating charges produce changing electric and magnetic fields that propagate as an electromagnetic wave.
In an electromagnetic wave travelling through space, the electric and magnetic fields are:
parallel to each other and perpendicular to the direction of travel
perpendicular to each other, with the electric field along the direction of travel
parallel to each other and to the direction of travel
perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel
EM waves are transverse: E and B oscillate at right angles to each other and to the propagation direction.
Triple J broadcasts on an FM frequency of about 100 MHz. What is the wavelength of these radio waves?
Which scientist showed theoretically that electromagnetic waves should travel at about 3 × 10^8 m s⁻¹, suggesting that light is an electromagnetic wave?
Maxwell's equations predict a wave speed of 1/√(μ₀ε₀) ≈ 3.0 × 10^8 m s⁻¹, matching the measured speed of light.
Which colour of visible light has the highest frequency?
Violet has the shortest visible wavelength, so by f = c/λ it has the highest frequency.
What is the period of a light wave with frequency 5.0 × 10^14 Hz?
A green laser pointer emits light of wavelength 532 nm. What is its frequency?
Light of frequency 5.0 × 10^14 Hz travels through a plastic in which its speed is 2.0 × 10^8 m s⁻¹. What is its wavelength in the plastic?
Which statement correctly describes a key difference between light and sound?
Sound travels faster than light in air.
Light is a longitudinal wave, but sound is transverse.
Light can travel through a vacuum, but sound requires a medium.
Sound can be polarised, but light cannot.
Light is a self-propagating electromagnetic wave needing no medium; sound is a mechanical longitudinal wave.
In the wave model of light, increasing the amplitude of a light wave of fixed frequency increases its:
Wave intensity is proportional to the square of amplitude; frequency, speed and wavelength are unaffected.
In the 1850s, Foucault showed that light travels more slowly in water than in air. This result supported:
the idea that light needs no medium
the idea that light is a longitudinal wave
The wave model predicts light slows in a denser medium when refracting towards the normal, whereas Newton's model predicted it speeds up.
Which observation could NOT be explained by the classical wave model of light?
The photoelectric effect requires light to be treated as photons; the other three are explained well by waves.
Electromagnetic radiation with a wavelength of 1.0 × 10^-10 m is best classified as:
Wavelengths around 10^-10 m (0.1 nm) lie in the X-ray region; UV is roughly 10–400 nm.
Two points along the direction of travel of a 600 nm light wave are 900 nm apart. The oscillations at these two points are:
a quarter of a cycle apart
in phase, because all points on a light wave move together
exactly out of phase (half a cycle apart)
900 nm = 1.5λ, so the points are separated by one and a half wavelengths, which is half a cycle out of phase.
In Huygens' description of light, a wavefront is:
a surface joining points of the wave that are in the same phase
the path followed by a single light particle
the leading edge of a light pulse only
the direction in which the wave's energy travels
Wavefronts join points in phase; rays are drawn perpendicular to them to show the direction of travel.
A radio wave, a visible light wave and an X-ray all travel through a vacuum. Which statement is correct?
The X-ray travels fastest because it has the highest frequency.
They all travel at the same speed but have different frequencies.
The radio wave travels fastest because it has the longest wavelength.
They have the same frequency but different speeds.
All EM waves travel at c in a vacuum; they differ in frequency and wavelength.
Explain why electromagnetic waves, unlike sound, do not need a medium in which to travel.

An EM wave consists of oscillating electric and magnetic fields. A changing electric field produces a changing magnetic field, and a changing magnetic field produces a changing electric field, so the wave regenerates itself and propagates through empty space without any particles needing to vibrate.
Award marks for: oscillating E and B fields; each change induces the other (Maxwell/Faraday); no material medium required.
Red light with frequency 4.6 × 10^14 Hz travels through water at 2.25 × 10^8 m s⁻¹. Calculate its wavelength in water.
Use the speed in the medium, not c. The frequency is unchanged, so the wavelength in water is shorter than in air.
A 4G mobile phone tower transmits at 2.6 GHz. Calculate the wavelength of the signal.
Distinguish between transverse and longitudinal waves, giving one example of each.

In a transverse wave the oscillation is perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer (e.g. light or any EM wave, waves on a string). In a longitudinal wave the oscillation is parallel to the direction of energy transfer (e.g. sound in air).
Both the definition and a correct example are needed for each type.
Outline Maxwell's contribution to the understanding of light.

Maxwell unified electricity and magnetism in a set of equations that predicted self-sustaining electromagnetic waves. The predicted speed, 1/√(μ₀ε₀) ≈ 3.0 × 10^8 m s⁻¹, matched the measured speed of light, so he concluded that light is an electromagnetic wave.
Key points: unification of E and M, prediction of EM waves, calculated speed equals c.
Describe what happens to the speed, frequency and wavelength of light as it passes from air into glass.
The speed decreases, the frequency stays the same, and the wavelength decreases (since λ = v/f).
Common error: saying frequency changes. Frequency is fixed by the source.
How many wavelengths of 500 nm light fit into a distance of 1.0 mm?
Convert both quantities to metres before dividing.
Light of wavelength 600 nm in air enters glass, where it slows down. Its frequency in air, and what happens to its frequency in glass, are:
f = c/λ = 3.0 × 10⁸ ÷ 600 × 10⁻⁹ = 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Frequency is set by the source; the wavelength shortens instead.
physics-6-2: In a Young's double-slit experiment, a bright fringe occurs at a point where the path difference from the two slits is:
an odd number of half wavelengths
a whole number of wavelengths, nλ
Waves arriving with path difference nλ are in phase and interfere constructively.
In a Young's double-slit pattern, a dark fringe occurs where the path difference is:
A path difference of an odd number of half wavelengths means the waves arrive half a cycle out of phase, producing destructive interference.
Light of wavelength 600 nm passes through two slits 0.30 mm apart and falls on a screen 2.0 m away. What is the spacing between adjacent bright fringes?
In a Young's double-slit experiment, the slit separation is increased while everything else is unchanged. The fringe spacing will:
Δx = λL/d, so a larger d gives a smaller fringe spacing.
A Young's double-slit experiment is repeated with blue light instead of red light. Compared with the red pattern, the blue fringes will be:
replaced by a single bright band
Blue light has a shorter wavelength, and Δx is proportional to λ.
The screen in a Young's double-slit experiment is moved further from the slits. The fringe spacing will:
Δx = λL/d, so fringe spacing is proportional to the slit-to-screen distance L.
Light of wavelength 500 nm is used in a double-slit experiment. What is the path difference to the third bright fringe either side of the central maximum?
For bright fringes, path difference = nλ with the central fringe n = 0, so the third is 3 × 500 nm = 1500 nm = 1.5 µm.
Light of wavelength 600 nm is used in a Young's experiment. What is the path difference at the second dark fringe from the centre?
Dark fringes occur at (n − ½)λ; for n = 2, path difference = 1.5 × 600 nm = 900 nm.
In a double-slit experiment using 500 nm light, point P on the screen has a path difference of 1.25 µm. What is observed at P?
A dark fringe (the third dark fringe from the centre)
A bright fringe, because 1.25 µm is greater than λ
1.25 µm / 500 nm = 2.5, an odd number of half wavelengths (0.5, 1.5, 2.5), so P is the third dark fringe.
In Young's original experiment, light from a single source was passed through a single slit before the double slits. The main purpose was to make the two slits act as:
coherent sources with a constant phase relationship
Interference fringes are only stable if the two sources are coherent: same frequency and a constant phase difference.
Two identical car headlights shining on a wall do not produce a visible interference pattern because the light from them is:
Independent sources emit with randomly changing phases, so any fringe pattern shifts too rapidly to be seen.
A double-slit pattern has a fringe spacing of 2.4 mm when the slits are 0.50 mm apart and the screen is 2.0 m away. What is the wavelength of the light?
Young's double-slit experiment provided strong evidence that light:
travels faster in glass than in air
Interference (alternating bright and dark fringes) is a wave property that a simple particle model could not explain.
A Young's double-slit apparatus is completely immersed in water, where light travels more slowly than in air. The fringe spacing will:
The frequency is unchanged but the speed falls, so λ decreases in water and Δx = λL/d decreases.
In a double-slit pattern the fringe spacing is 2.0 mm. What is the distance from the centre of the central bright fringe to the centre of the third dark fringe?
The third dark fringe has path difference 2.5λ, so it lies 2.5Δx = 2.5 × 2.0 mm = 5.0 mm from the centre.
Destructive interference between two light waves of equal amplitude occurs when the waves arrive:
half a cycle out of phase
a whole cycle out of phase
with a path difference of zero
Crests meet troughs, so the displacements cancel.
In a double-slit interference pattern, what happens to the light energy that does not reach the dark fringes?
It is destroyed by destructive interference.
It is reflected back towards the source.
It is redistributed to the bright fringes.
It is converted into heat in the slits.
Energy is conserved: interference redistributes energy, so bright fringes are brighter than they would be without interference.
Light of wavelength 650 nm passes through slits 0.25 mm apart onto a screen 1.5 m away. How far from the centre of the central maximum is the fourth bright fringe?
Δx = (650 × 10^-9 × 1.5)/(0.25 × 10^-3) = 3.9 mm, so the fourth bright fringe is at 4 × 3.9 = 15.6 mm.
Explain, using the idea of path difference, how bright and dark fringes form in Young's double-slit experiment.

Light from the two coherent slits travels different distances to each point on the screen. Where the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths (nλ) the waves arrive in phase and interfere constructively, giving a bright fringe. Where the path difference is (n − ½)λ the waves arrive half a cycle out of phase and interfere destructively, giving a dark fringe.
Marks for: coherent sources, path difference, nλ → constructive/bright, (n − ½)λ → destructive/dark.
A 532 nm green laser produces fringes 4.0 mm apart on a screen 3.0 m from a double slit. Calculate the slit separation.
Rearrange Δx = λL/d and keep all values in metres.
Light of wavelength 640 nm is used in a double-slit experiment. What is the path difference to the first dark fringe?
The first dark fringe is where the waves are half a wavelength out of step: (n − ½)λ with n = 1.
During a Young's double-slit experiment, one slit is covered. Describe how the pattern on the screen changes.
The two-source interference fringes disappear. Only the single-slit diffraction pattern remains: a broad central bright band with much fainter side bands, and the overall intensity is lower.
Interference requires two coherent sources; with one slit only diffraction occurs.
A student measures that 10 fringe spacings cover 25 mm on a screen 1.0 m from a double slit with separation 0.20 mm. Calculate the wavelength of the light.
Measuring across many fringes reduces the uncertainty in Δx.
Describe the pattern seen when white light is used in a Young's double-slit experiment, and explain it.

The central fringe is white because all wavelengths have zero path difference there. Either side are coloured fringes, with violet/blue on the inner edge and red on the outer edge, because Δx = λL/d is larger for longer wavelengths. Further out the colours overlap and the pattern washes out.
Key idea: fringe spacing is proportional to wavelength, so colours separate.
Explain why Young's double-slit result was a problem for Newton's particle model of light.

Newton's particle model predicted just two bright bands behind the two slits. Young observed many alternating bright and dark fringes, including darkness where light from both slits overlapped. Adding light to light to produce darkness can only be explained by wave interference.
Highlight that particles cannot cancel each other to give dark regions.
In a Young's double-slit experiment, λ = 600 nm, the slit separation is 0.30 mm and the screen is 2.0 m away. Find the fringe spacing, and state what happens to it if blue light is used.
Δx = λL/d = 600 × 10⁻⁹ × 2.0 ÷ 0.30 × 10⁻³ = 4.0 × 10⁻³ m. Blue light has a shorter wavelength, so the fringes move closer together.
physics-6-3: physics-6-3-1
Diffraction of a wave through a gap is most noticeable when:
the wavelength is similar to or larger than the gap width
the gap width is much larger than the wavelength
the wave has a very high frequency
the wave has a very large amplitude
The extent of diffraction depends on λ/w; significant spreading occurs when λ/w is about 1 or greater.
physics-6-3-2
Light of wavelength 500 nm passes through each of the following slits. Which produces the greatest diffraction?
A 5 µm slit
A 0.5 µm slit
A 50 µm slit
A 5 mm slit
λ/w = 500 nm / 0.5 µm = 1, the largest ratio of the options.
physics-6-3-3
A single slit is made narrower while the wavelength of light is unchanged. The central bright band of the diffraction pattern will:
become narrower
stay the same width
become wider
split into two bands
Decreasing w increases λ/w, so the light spreads more.
physics-6-3-4
You can hear people talking in a corridor around a corner, but cannot see them. The best explanation is that:
sound travels faster than light
light cannot be diffracted
sound is a transverse wave
sound wavelengths are comparable to the doorway width, but light wavelengths are far smaller
Sound (λ ≈ 1 m) diffracts significantly through a doorway; light (λ ≈ 500 nm) has a tiny λ/w and barely diffracts.
physics-6-3-5
Red light and blue light pass in turn through the same narrow slit. Compared with the blue pattern, the red diffraction pattern is:
wider
narrower
the same width
not formed at all
Red has the longer wavelength, so λ/w is larger and diffraction is greater.
physics-6-3-6
When light diffracts through a narrow slit in air, which statement is correct?
Its wavelength increases.
Its wavelength, frequency and speed are all unchanged.
Its speed decreases.
Its frequency decreases.
Diffraction changes the direction of travel (spreading) but not the wave's speed, frequency or wavelength in the same medium.
physics-6-3-7
In hilly regions of country Victoria, AM radio (wavelength about 300 m) is often received better than FM radio (wavelength about 3 m). This is mainly because:
AM waves travel faster than FM waves
FM waves cannot be diffracted
longer-wavelength AM waves diffract more around hills
AM waves have a higher frequency
Hills are hundreds of metres across, comparable to AM wavelengths, so AM signals bend around them much more.
physics-6-3-8
Microwaves of wavelength 3.0 cm pass through a gap of 6.0 cm. What is the value of λ/w?
λ/w = 3.0 cm / 6.0 cm = 0.50, which gives noticeable diffraction.
physics-6-3-9
Light of wavelength 500 nm passes through a 2.0 mm wide gap. Which best describes the diffraction?
Negligible, because λ/w is about 2.5 × 10^-4
Very significant, because λ/w is about 4 × 10^3
Very significant, because λ/w is about 1
None at all, because light cannot diffract
physics-6-3-10
Large telescopes such as those at Siding Spring Observatory have wide apertures partly because a larger aperture:
increases the wavelength of the incoming light
reduces diffraction, allowing finer detail to be resolved
increases diffraction, making images brighter
polarises the incoming light
A larger aperture gives a smaller λ/w, so less diffraction blurs the image and closer objects can be distinguished.
physics-6-3-11
Ocean waves of wavelength 20 m approach a harbour entrance 20 m wide. Inside the harbour the waves will:
continue in a narrow straight beam
stop completely at the entrance
spread out significantly into the harbour
double in wavelength
λ/w = 1, so diffraction is significant and the waves spread widely behind the entrance.
physics-6-3-12
The wavelength of light and the width of a slit are both doubled. Compared with the original, the amount of diffraction will be:
doubled
halved
four times greater
the same
Diffraction depends on the ratio λ/w, which is unchanged (2λ/2w = λ/w).
physics-6-3-13
Which change will increase the diffraction of light passing through a single slit?
Using light of a longer wavelength
Using light of a higher frequency
Making the slit wider
Increasing the brightness of the light
Increasing λ increases λ/w. Higher frequency means shorter λ, and a wider slit reduces λ/w.
physics-6-3-14
The intensity of a laser beam passing through a single slit is increased. The diffraction pattern will be:
wider and brighter
brighter, but the same width
narrower and brighter
unchanged in brightness but wider
Intensity does not affect λ or w, so the angular spread is unchanged; only brightness increases.
physics-6-3-15
For monochromatic light passing through a single slit, the pattern on the screen consists of:
equally spaced bright fringes of equal brightness
a single sharp bright line the same width as the slit
a broad, bright central band with much fainter, narrower side bands
a continuous spectrum of colours
A single-slit pattern has a dominant central maximum about twice the width of the weaker side maxima.
physics-6-3-16
Laser light passing the sharp edge of a razor blade produces faint bright and dark bands at the edge of the shadow. This is mainly due to:
refraction
polarisation
dispersion
diffraction
Light bends around the edge into the geometric shadow, producing diffraction bands.
physics-6-3-17
Which wave would diffract MOST when passing through a 1.0 m wide doorway?
Sound of frequency 340 Hz (λ = 1.0 m)
Sound of frequency 3400 Hz (λ = 0.10 m)
Infrared radiation (λ = 10 µm)
Visible light (λ = 500 nm)
The 340 Hz sound has λ/w = 1, the largest ratio of the options.
physics-6-3-18
Which observation is the strongest evidence from diffraction that light behaves as a wave?
Light travels in straight lines through a wide window.
Light spreads into the region of geometric shadow after passing through a narrow gap.
Light reflects from a mirror at equal angles.
Light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth.
A simple particle model predicts sharp shadows; spreading into the shadow is a characteristic wave behaviour.
physics-6-3-19
State how the amount of diffraction depends on wavelength and gap width.
Diffraction depends on the ratio λ/w. It is significant when λ/w is about 1 or greater, and becomes negligible when λ/w is much less than 1. Increasing λ or decreasing w increases diffraction.
Students should refer to the ratio, not just one variable.
physics-6-3-20
A Wi-Fi router transmits at 2.4 GHz. The signal passes through a 0.125 m gap between two steel shelves. Calculate λ/w and comment on the diffraction.
λ = c/f = (3.0 × 10^8)/(2.4 × 10^9) = 0.125 m. λ/w = 0.125/0.125 = 1.0, so the signal diffracts significantly and spreads widely beyond the gap.
Show the wavelength calculation first, then the ratio.
physics-6-3-21
Explain why you can hear a radio playing in the next room through an open door, even though you cannot see it.

Sound waves have wavelengths around 0.1–3 m, comparable to the doorway width, so λ/w is close to 1 and they diffract strongly around the edges. Light has wavelengths around 400–700 nm, so λ/w is tiny and it hardly diffracts, travelling almost in straight lines.
Must compare both wavelengths to the gap size.
physics-6-3-22
Describe the single-slit diffraction pattern produced by a red laser, and how it changes as the slit is made narrower.

The pattern is a wide, bright central band with fainter, narrower bands on either side. As the slit narrows, λ/w increases, so the whole pattern spreads out: the central band becomes wider (and dimmer, because less light passes through).
Marks for describing the pattern and the widening with narrower slits.
physics-6-3-23
A red laser (650 nm) passing through a 0.10 mm slit produces a certain amount of diffraction. What slit width would give the same diffraction for blue light of 450 nm?
Keep λ/w constant: w = 0.10 mm × (450/650) ≈ 0.069 mm (about 69 µm).
Same diffraction means the same λ/w ratio.
physics-6-3-24
Microchip manufacturers use ultraviolet light rather than visible light to make extremely small circuit features. Explain why, in terms of diffraction.

UV light has a shorter wavelength than visible light. For tiny features of a given width, λ/w is smaller, so there is less diffraction and spreading of the light, allowing sharper, smaller features to be produced.
Link shorter λ to smaller λ/w and less blurring.
physics-6-3-25
Explain how the diffraction of light supports the wave model rather than Newton's particle model.

Newton's particle model predicts that light travels in straight lines and casts sharp-edged shadows. When light passes through a narrow gap it spreads into the geometric shadow and forms bright and dark bands, which is characteristic of waves and is explained by Huygens' wavelets interfering.
Mention spreading into the shadow and the banded pattern.
physics-6-3-c1
Which combination gives the most noticeable diffraction through a gap?
Wavelength 500 nm, gap 1.0 µm
Wavelength 500 nm, gap 1.0 mm
Wavelength 400 nm, gap 0.10 mm
Wavelength 700 nm, gap 10 mm
Diffraction is significant when λ/w is close to or above 1. Here λ/w = 0.5, much larger than the others.
physics-6-4: physics-6-4-1
The fact that light can be polarised shows that light is:
a longitudinal wave
a stream of particles
a transverse wave
a mechanical wave
Only transverse waves have an oscillation direction that can be restricted to a single plane.
physics-6-4-2
Unpolarised light passes through an ideal polarising filter. The intensity of the transmitted light is:
the same as the original intensity
a quarter of the original intensity
zero
half the original intensity
On average only the component of the electric field along the transmission axis passes, so half the intensity is transmitted.
physics-6-4-3
Two ideal polarising filters are placed with their transmission axes at 90° to each other. Unpolarised light is shone through both. The light emerging is:
zero
half the original intensity
a quarter of the original intensity
the same as the original intensity
The first filter polarises the light; the second, crossed filter blocks all of that polarised light.
physics-6-4-4
Sound waves in air cannot be polarised because they are:
too slow
longitudinal
mechanical waves with long wavelengths
unable to diffract
In a longitudinal wave the oscillation is along the direction of travel, so there is no perpendicular direction to select.
physics-6-4-5
Polarised sunglasses reduce glare from the surface of Port Phillip Bay because:
the lenses absorb all wavelengths equally
the lenses diffract the reflected light away from the eyes
reflected light is partly horizontally polarised and the lenses only transmit vertically polarised light
reflected light is vertically polarised and the lenses block vertical light
Light reflected from horizontal surfaces is largely horizontally polarised; vertical transmission axes block it.
physics-6-4-6
Plane-polarised light is light in which:
all wavelengths are the same
the waves are all in phase
the magnetic field is zero
the electric field oscillates in only one plane
Polarisation describes the direction of the electric field oscillation; in plane-polarised light it is confined to one plane.
physics-6-4-7
A polarising filter is rotated slowly through 360° in front of a beam of plane-polarised light. The transmitted intensity:
goes from maximum to zero twice
stays constant
goes from maximum to zero once
goes from maximum to zero four times
Maximum transmission occurs at 0° and 180°, and zero at 90° and 270°.
physics-6-4-8
A polarising filter is rotated in front of an unpolarised light source such as an incandescent globe. The transmitted intensity:
varies between maximum and zero
stays constant at half the original
stays constant at the original intensity
drops to zero
Unpolarised light has electric field components in all directions equally, so every orientation transmits half.
physics-6-4-9
A third polarising filter with its axis at 45° is placed between two crossed polarisers. Unpolarised light is shone through all three. What is observed?
No light emerges, as before.
The full original intensity emerges.
Some light now emerges from the final filter.
The light emerges unpolarised.
The middle filter transmits a component at 45°, which then has a component along the final filter's axis, so some light passes.
physics-6-4-10
Which of these waves can be polarised?
Sound waves in air
Ultrasound in body tissue
Seismic P-waves
Microwaves
Microwaves are transverse EM waves; the others are longitudinal mechanical waves.
physics-6-4-11
By convention, the direction of polarisation of an electromagnetic wave is the direction of oscillation of its:
electric field
magnetic field
wave velocity
energy transfer
Polarisation is defined by the electric field, which is perpendicular to the magnetic field.
physics-6-4-12
A TV station broadcasts horizontally polarised signals. For best reception, the rods of a rooftop antenna should be:
vertical
horizontal
at 45°
pointing directly at the transmitter along the line of travel
The electric field is horizontal, so it drives charges most effectively along horizontal rods.
physics-6-4-13
A student wearing polarised sunglasses looks at a laptop screen and tilts her head 90°. The screen becomes much darker. This shows that light from the screen is:
unpolarised
longitudinal
polarised
coherent and monochromatic
LCD screens emit polarised light, so rotating the polarising lenses relative to it reduces transmission.
physics-6-4-14
Unpolarised light of intensity 80 W m⁻² passes through two ideal polarisers with parallel transmission axes. The final intensity is:
80 W m⁻²
20 W m⁻²
0 W m⁻²
40 W m⁻²
The first filter halves the intensity to 40 W m⁻²; the second, parallel filter transmits all of this already polarised light.
physics-6-4-15
Huygens believed light was a longitudinal wave. Which observation is inconsistent with this belief?
Light can be polarised.
Light can be diffracted.
Light can be refracted.
Light shows interference.
Diffraction, refraction and interference occur for longitudinal waves too, but polarisation only occurs for transverse waves.
physics-6-4-16
A photographer uses a polarising filter to darken the blue sky in landscape photos. This works because:
the filter changes the wavelength of blue light
scattered skylight is partly polarised
the filter refracts blue light away from the lens
sunlight is fully polarised before entering the atmosphere
Light scattered by the atmosphere is partly polarised, so a suitably oriented filter blocks much of it.
physics-6-4-17
An electromagnetic wave travels in the +x direction with its electric field oscillating along the y-axis. Its magnetic field oscillates along the:
y-axis
x-axis
z-axis
y-axis and z-axis equally
In an EM wave E, B and the direction of travel are mutually perpendicular, so B is along z.
physics-6-4-18
Light from the Sun is described as unpolarised. This means that:
its electric field oscillates parallel to its direction of travel
it contains no electric field
it contains only one wavelength
its electric field oscillates in all directions perpendicular to its direction of travel
Unpolarised light is a random mixture of all transverse oscillation directions.
physics-6-4-19
Explain why polarisation provides evidence that light is a transverse wave.

Polarisation means restricting the oscillation to a single plane. This is only possible for transverse waves, where oscillations can occur in many directions perpendicular to the direction of travel. In a longitudinal wave the oscillation is always along the direction of travel, so there is nothing to filter. Because light can be polarised, it must be transverse.
Contrast transverse with longitudinal waves.
physics-6-4-20
Explain how polarised sunglasses reduce glare from a wet road.

Light reflecting off a horizontal surface such as a wet road is largely horizontally polarised. The lenses have vertical transmission axes, so they block most of this horizontally polarised reflected light while still transmitting about half of the unpolarised light from other objects.
Must mention the polarisation of the reflected light and the orientation of the lenses.
physics-6-4-21
Unpolarised light of intensity 120 W m⁻² passes through a polariser, then through a second polariser whose axis is at 90° to the first. State the intensity after each filter.
After the first filter: 60 W m⁻² (half). After the second, crossed filter: 0 W m⁻².
The first filter always halves unpolarised light; crossed filters transmit nothing.
physics-6-4-22
Describe a simple test to determine whether a light source is polarised.

Look at the light through a single polarising filter and rotate the filter through 180°. If the brightness stays constant, the light is unpolarised. If the brightness varies, dropping to (near) zero at one orientation, the light is plane-polarised.
The rotating filter is the key step.
physics-6-4-23
Distinguish between polarised and unpolarised light.
In unpolarised light the electric field oscillates in all directions perpendicular to the direction of travel. In plane-polarised light the electric field oscillates in only one plane.
Refer to the electric field direction relative to the direction of travel.
physics-6-4-24
Explain why sound waves cannot be polarised.

Sound in air is a longitudinal wave: the air particles oscillate parallel to the direction of travel. There is only one possible oscillation direction, so it cannot be restricted to a particular plane perpendicular to the motion.
Link the inability to polarise directly to the longitudinal nature.
physics-6-4-25
Maxwell's theory predicted that light is a transverse electromagnetic wave. Explain how the polarisation of light supports this prediction.

Maxwell's theory describes light as oscillating electric and magnetic fields perpendicular to the direction of travel, which is a transverse wave. Polarisation filters can select one direction of the electric field oscillation, which is only possible for a transverse wave, so polarisation is consistent with Maxwell's model.
Link the perpendicular E field in Maxwell's model to the ability to polarise.
physics-6-4-c1
Unpolarised light passes through two polarisers at 90° to each other, and no light emerges. A third polariser at 45° is placed between them. Now:
Some light emerges, because the middle filter passes a component the last filter can transmit
Still no light emerges, because the first and last filters remain crossed at 90°
All the original light emerges, because the middle filter cancels out the crossing
Light emerges only around the middle filter's edges, because light diffracts around it
Each polariser transmits the component parallel to its axis. The 45° filter creates light with a component along the final axis. Polarisation shows light is a transverse wave.
physics-7-1: Using hc = 1.24 × 10^-6 eV m, what is the energy of a photon of wavelength 500 nm?
E = hc/λ = (1.24 × 10^-6)/(500 × 10^-9) = 2.48 eV. The value 3.98 × 10^-19 is the energy in joules, not eV.
Sodium has a work function of 2.30 eV. Taking h = 4.14 × 10^-15 eV s, what is its threshold frequency?
f₀ = W/h = 2.30/(4.14 × 10^-15) = 5.56 × 10^14 Hz. Using h in J s with W in eV gives the nonsensical 3.47 × 10^33 Hz.
Light of wavelength 400 nm falls on a metal with work function 2.30 eV. What is the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons? (hc = 1.24 × 10^-6 eV m)
Explain why increasing the intensity of red light that is below the threshold frequency of a metal does not cause photoelectrons to be emitted.

Each red photon has energy hf less than the work function. Electrons absorb one photon at a time, so increasing intensity only increases the number of photons, not the energy of each, and no electron gains enough energy to escape.
Key marks: photon energy hf < W; one photon–one electron interaction; intensity = number of photons.
Photons of energy 4.0 eV eject electrons from a metal with work function 2.5 eV. What is the stopping voltage?
Ek max = hf − W = 1.5 eV, and the stopping voltage satisfies eV₀ = Ek max, so V₀ = 1.5 V.
A metal surface is illuminated with light above its threshold frequency. The intensity is doubled while the frequency is kept constant. Which statement is correct?
The photocurrent increases but the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons is unchanged.
The maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons doubles.
Both the photocurrent and the maximum kinetic energy double.
More intense light delivers more photons per second, ejecting more electrons, but each photon still has the same energy hf.
Red light below the threshold frequency of a metal shines on it. The intensity is increased greatly. What happens?
Photoelectrons are emitted after a time delay.
No photoelectrons are emitted at any intensity.
Photoelectrons are emitted with very low kinetic energy.
The work function of the metal decreases.
Each photon has energy hf less than the work function, and an electron absorbs one photon at a time, so no electron can escape regardless of intensity.
Ultraviolet light of wavelength 250 nm shines on zinc (work function 4.3 eV). Calculate the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons in eV. (hc = 1.24 × 10^-6 eV m)
Use Ek max = hc/λ − W. Accept 0.66–0.67 eV.
A graph of maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons (y-axis) against frequency of incident light (x-axis) is a straight line. Its gradient equals:
Ek max = hf − W has the form y = mx + c with gradient h.
On a graph of maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons against frequency, the intercept on the energy axis (extrapolated) equals:
the negative of the work function
From Ek max = hf − W, setting f = 0 gives Ek max = −W.
Ek max versus frequency graphs are drawn for potassium and for zinc. Compared with each other, the two lines:
are parallel but have different frequency-axis intercepts
have different gradients but the same intercepts
have gradients proportional to the work functions
Both have gradient h, which is a universal constant; the different work functions give different threshold frequencies (x-intercepts).
In a photocell, the photocurrent reaches a maximum (saturation) value as the anode is made more positive. Explain why.

Once the anode is positive enough, every photoelectron emitted from the cathode is collected. Further increasing the voltage cannot increase the current because the rate of emission is fixed by the number of photons arriving per second.
Link the saturation current to the photon arrival rate (intensity), not to the voltage.
Which observation of the photoelectric effect could NOT be explained by the wave model of light?
The photocurrent increases with light intensity.
No electrons are emitted below a certain frequency, however intense the light.
Some light is reflected from the metal surface.
More intense light delivers more energy per second to the surface.
The wave model predicts any frequency would eventually emit electrons if intense enough; the existence of a threshold frequency requires light to be quantised into photons.
What is the momentum of a photon of wavelength 600 nm? (h = 6.63 × 10^-34 J s)
A 5.0 mW laser pointer emits light of wavelength 650 nm. Approximately how many photons does it emit per second? (h = 6.63 × 10^-34 J s, c = 3.00 × 10^8 m s^-1)
A student measures stopping voltages of 0.50 V at 6.0 × 10^14 Hz and 1.33 V at 8.0 × 10^14 Hz. Determine Planck's constant in eV s and the work function of the metal.
Gradient of Ek max versus f gives h; the work function follows from either data point.
Which change would increase the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons emitted from a given metal?
Using brighter light of the same wavelength
Moving the light source closer to the metal
Increasing the area of the metal plate
Shorter wavelength means higher frequency and therefore higher photon energy hf; the other changes only alter the number of photons.
A photon has an energy of 3.0 eV. What is its wavelength? (hc = 1.24 × 10^-6 eV m)
In a photoelectric experiment, the stopping voltage depends on:
the intensity of the light only
the area of the illuminated metal
the frequency of the light and the work function of the metal
the distance between the light source and the cell
eV₀ = hf − W, so only the photon frequency and the work function determine the stopping voltage.
Explain how the absence of a time delay in photoelectron emission supports the particle model of light.

The wave model predicts that with dim light, energy would spread over the surface and an electron would need time to accumulate enough to escape. In fact electrons are emitted instantly, consistent with each electron absorbing a whole photon's energy in one interaction.
Contrast the wave prediction (gradual accumulation) with the observation (instant emission).
Photoelectrons are emitted with a range of kinetic energies up to a maximum value. The best explanation is that:
photons have a range of energies even in monochromatic light
the work function varies randomly with time
electrons further below the surface or more tightly bound lose extra energy escaping
The work function is the minimum energy to free the least-bound surface electrons; others need more energy, so they emerge with less kinetic energy.
A metal has a threshold wavelength of 540 nm. What is its work function? (hc = 1.24 × 10^-6 eV m)
If the wavelength of monochromatic light is halved, the energy of each photon:
E = hc/λ, so energy is inversely proportional to wavelength.
Describe how the stopping voltage is measured in a photoelectric experiment.

A reverse voltage is applied so the anode is negative relative to the photoemissive cathode. The voltage is increased until the photocurrent just falls to zero; this voltage is the stopping voltage, where eV₀ equals the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons.
Mention reverse potential, current reaching zero, and eV₀ = Ek max.
A 1.0 W green light source emits only light of wavelength 530 nm. Calculate the number of photons emitted per second. (h = 6.63 × 10^-34 J s, c = 3.00 × 10^8 m s^-1)
Number per second = power ÷ energy per photon.
Light of wavelength 400 nm falls on a metal with a work function of 2.3 eV. Find the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons and the stopping voltage.
E(photon) = hc/λ = 1240 eV nm ÷ 400 nm = 3.1 eV. KE(max) = 3.1 − 2.3 = 0.80 eV, so a stopping voltage of 0.80 V is needed.
physics-7-2: What is the de Broglie wavelength of an electron travelling at 2.0 × 10^6 m s^-1? (h = 6.63 × 10^-34 J s, mₑ = 9.11 × 10^-31 kg)
An electron is accelerated from rest through 100 V. What is its de Broglie wavelength? (h = 6.63 × 10^-34 J s, mₑ = 9.11 × 10^-31 kg, e = 1.60 × 10^-19 C)
An electron and a proton travel at the same speed. Compared with the electron, the proton's de Broglie wavelength is:
longer by a factor of about 43
λ = h/(mv); at the same speed the proton, being about 1836 times more massive, has a wavelength about 1836 times shorter.
In the Davisson–Germer experiment, electrons were accelerated through 54 V. Calculate their de Broglie wavelength. (h = 6.63 × 10^-34 J s, mₑ = 9.11 × 10^-31 kg, e = 1.60 × 10^-19 C)
Steps: Ek = qV, p = √(2mEk), λ = h/p.
An electron and a proton have the same kinetic energy. Which statement is correct?
The proton's wavelength is about 43 times longer than the electron's.
The electron's wavelength is about 43 times longer than the proton's.
The electron's wavelength is about 1836 times longer than the proton's.
p = √(2mEk), so λ ∝ 1/√m; √1836 ≈ 43, so the lighter electron has the longer wavelength.
The speed of an electron doubles (non-relativistic). Its de Broglie wavelength:
λ = h/(mv), so λ is inversely proportional to v.
The accelerating voltage on an electron gun is increased by a factor of four. The de Broglie wavelength of the electrons:
Ek ∝ V, p ∝ √Ek ∝ √V, so λ ∝ 1/√V; four times the voltage halves the wavelength.
Explain how an electron diffraction pattern provides evidence for the wave nature of matter.

A diffraction pattern of bright and dark rings forms because electron waves scattered by regularly spaced atoms interfere constructively and destructively. Interference and diffraction are wave properties, and the ring spacing matches the de Broglie wavelength λ = h/p.
Refer to interference and to agreement with λ = h/p.
An electron beam and an X-ray beam produce identical diffraction patterns when passed through the same crystal. The electrons and X-ray photons must have the same:
Diffraction pattern spacing depends only on wavelength relative to the atomic spacing.
Electron microscopes can resolve much finer detail than optical microscopes mainly because:
the electrons' de Broglie wavelength is much shorter than visible light wavelengths
Diffraction limits resolution; a shorter wavelength produces less diffraction blurring, so smaller features can be distinguished.
The observation that a beam of electrons produces a diffraction pattern when passed through a thin crystal provides evidence that:
Diffraction is a wave phenomenon, so electron diffraction confirms de Broglie's hypothesis of matter waves.

An X-ray beam of photon energy 8.0 keV and an electron beam produce the same diffraction pattern from a crystal. Calculate the kinetic energy of the electrons in eV. (mₑ = 9.11 × 10^-31 kg, c = 3.00 × 10^8 m s^-1, e = 1.60 × 10^-19 C)
Same pattern means same wavelength and hence the same momentum. p = E/c = (8000 × 1.60 × 10^-19)/3.00 × 10^8 = 4.27 × 10^-24 kg m s^-1. Electron Ek = p²/(2m) = 1.0 × 10^-17 J ≈ 62 eV.
Common error: assuming the electron has the same energy (8.0 keV) as the photon.
A 0.16 kg cricket ball is bowled at 40 m s^-1. Its de Broglie wavelength is approximately: (h = 6.63 × 10^-34 J s)
What is the momentum of an electron with a de Broglie wavelength of 0.20 nm? (h = 6.63 × 10^-34 J s)
What speed must an electron have for its de Broglie wavelength to be 0.50 nm? (h = 6.63 × 10^-34 J s, mₑ = 9.11 × 10^-31 kg)
Explain why an electron microscope can produce images with greater detail than a light microscope.

Electrons accelerated through thousands of volts have de Broglie wavelengths far shorter than visible light (around 400–700 nm). Less diffraction occurs for a given aperture or feature size, so finer detail can be resolved.
Link shorter wavelength to less diffraction and better resolution.
An electron has a de Broglie wavelength of 0.20 nm. What is its kinetic energy in eV? (h = 6.63 × 10^-34 J s, mₑ = 9.11 × 10^-31 kg)
p = h/λ = 3.3 × 10^-24; Ek = p²/(2m) = 6.0 × 10^-18 J ≈ 38 eV. 6200 eV is the energy of a photon of this wavelength.
For a beam of electrons to show noticeable diffraction from a crystal, their de Broglie wavelength should be:
exactly equal to the wavelength of visible light
similar to the spacing between atoms, around 10^-10 m
Significant diffraction occurs when λ is comparable to the gap or spacing, and atomic spacings are around 0.1 nm.
In an electron diffraction tube, the accelerating voltage is increased. The diffraction rings:
become brighter but do not change size
Higher voltage gives higher momentum and a shorter wavelength, so electrons diffract through smaller angles.
A neutron (mass 1.67 × 10^-27 kg) has a de Broglie wavelength of 0.10 nm. Calculate its speed. (h = 6.63 × 10^-34 J s)
A photon and an electron each have a wavelength of 0.25 nm. Which statement is correct?
They have the same energy and the same momentum.
They have the same momentum, but the photon has more energy.
The electron has more momentum and more energy.
They have the same energy, but the electron has more momentum.
p = h/λ for both. The photon's energy is pc while the electron's kinetic energy is p²/(2m) = pv/2, which is far smaller since v ≪ c.
An X-ray photon has an energy of 5.0 keV. What is its wavelength? (hc = 1.24 × 10^-6 eV m)
Approximately what accelerating voltage gives electrons a de Broglie wavelength of 0.10 nm? (h = 6.63 × 10^-34 J s, mₑ = 9.11 × 10^-31 kg, e = 1.60 × 10^-19 C)
p = h/λ = 6.63 × 10^-24; Ek = p²/(2m) = 2.4 × 10^-17 J ≈ 151 eV, so about 150 V. 12 400 V is the photon energy in eV for this wavelength.
Explain why the wave nature of a moving car is never observed.

A car's momentum is very large, so its de Broglie wavelength λ = h/(mv) is extremely small (around 10^-38 m), far smaller than any gap or obstacle. Diffraction is therefore negligible and no wave effects can be detected.
Must compare wavelength with the size of gaps or obstacles.
The speed of electrons in a diffraction tube is doubled. Describe and explain the change in the diffraction pattern.
The de Broglie wavelength halves because λ = h/(mv). Electrons diffract through smaller angles, so the rings become smaller and closer together (roughly half the radius for small angles).
Accept 'rings closer together/smaller' with the reason λ ∝ 1/v.
An electron and a proton have the same kinetic energy. Compared with the proton, the electron's de Broglie wavelength is:
p = √(2mK), so λ = h/√(2mK) ∝ 1/√m. √(1840) ≈ 43, and the lighter electron has the longer wavelength.
physics-7-3: Hydrogen has energy levels E₁ = −13.6 eV, E₂ = −3.40 eV and E₃ = −1.51 eV. What is the energy of the photon emitted when an electron moves from n = 3 to n = 2?
In hydrogen, E₂ = −3.40 eV and E₄ = −0.85 eV. What is the wavelength of the photon emitted in the n = 4 to n = 2 transition? (hc = 1.24 × 10^-6 eV m)
What is the minimum energy needed to ionise a hydrogen atom in its ground state (E₁ = −13.6 eV)?
Ionisation moves the electron from −13.6 eV to 0 eV, requiring 13.6 eV.
Calculate the frequency of the photon emitted when an electron in hydrogen moves from n = 3 (−1.51 eV) to n = 1 (−13.6 eV). (h = 4.14 × 10^-15 eV s)
Hydrogen atoms are excited to the n = 4 level. How many different photon energies can be emitted as they return to the ground state?
A photon of energy 11.0 eV passes through hydrogen gas in the ground state (E₁ = −13.6 eV, E₂ = −3.40 eV, E₃ = −1.51 eV). What is most likely to happen?
The photon excites an atom to n = 2 and a 0.8 eV photon continues.
The photon excites an atom to n = 3.
A photon must be absorbed whole and its energy must exactly match a transition (10.2 or 12.09 eV); 11.0 eV matches none.
When white light passes through a cool gas and is then viewed with a spectroscope, the result is:
a series of bright lines on a dark background
a continuous spectrum with dark lines at specific wavelengths
a continuous spectrum with no gaps
Atoms absorb photons only at energies matching their level differences, removing those wavelengths and leaving dark absorption lines.
Explain why the emission spectrum of a heated gas consists of discrete bright lines rather than a continuous spectrum.

Electrons in the atoms can only occupy specific, quantised energy levels. When an electron drops from a higher level to a lower level it emits a photon with energy equal to the difference, E = hf, so only specific frequencies and wavelengths appear.
Key ideas: quantised levels, photon energy equals level difference.
The emission spectrum of a gas consists of discrete lines because:
the gas absorbs all other colours
the atoms' electron energy levels are quantised
electrons emit continuously as they orbit
Transitions occur between fixed levels, so only specific photon energies, and hence wavelengths, are emitted.
Transitions in hydrogen ending on the n = 1 level (E₁ = −13.6 eV, E₂ = −3.40 eV) produce photons in which part of the electromagnetic spectrum?
The smallest such transition (2→1) is 10.2 eV, about 122 nm, which is ultraviolet; the others are even higher in energy.
Which hydrogen transition emits the photon of highest frequency? (E₁ = −13.6 eV, E₂ = −3.40 eV, E₃ = −1.51 eV, E₄ = −0.85 eV)
The 4→1 transition has the largest energy difference (12.75 eV), and f = E/h.
Explain how an absorption spectrum forms when white light passes through a cool gas.

Atoms in the gas absorb only photons whose energies exactly match differences between their energy levels. Those wavelengths are removed from the beam, and the re-emitted light goes in all directions, so dark lines appear on the continuous spectrum at those wavelengths.
Mention exact energy match and re-emission in random directions.
An atom has energy levels of −10.0 eV, −6.0 eV, −4.0 eV and −1.0 eV. Which photon energy could NOT be emitted by this atom?
Possible differences are 4.0, 6.0, 9.0, 2.0, 5.0 and 3.0 eV; 7.0 eV is not one of them.
An atom has energy levels of −10.0 eV, −6.0 eV, −4.0 eV and −1.0 eV, and zero energy corresponds to a free electron. What is its ionisation energy from the ground state?
Ionisation takes the electron from −10.0 eV to 0 eV.
In de Broglie's explanation of the stable electron orbits in the Bohr model, the circumference of an allowed orbit equals:
the wavelength of the emitted photon
a whole number of electron wavelengths
An allowed orbit supports a standing wave, nλ = 2πr, so the electron does not radiate energy.
An atom has energy levels E₁ = −8.0 eV, E₂ = −4.5 eV and E₃ = −2.0 eV. Atoms excited to E₃ return to the ground state. List all the photon energies that can be emitted.
E₃ → E₂: 2.5 eV; E₂ → E₁: 3.5 eV; E₃ → E₁: 6.0 eV.
Three transitions give three distinct photon energies.
A fluorescent mineral absorbs ultraviolet light and emits visible light. This is best explained by:
electrons dropping back to the ground state through intermediate energy levels
electrons gaining energy from the visible light
the ultraviolet photons slowing down inside the mineral
the mineral reflecting the ultraviolet light
Each smaller downward step releases a lower-energy photon, which can be in the visible range.
A photon of energy 2.0 eV is absorbed by an atom. What is its wavelength? (hc = 1.24 × 10^-6 eV m)
Sodium street lights emit yellow light of wavelength 589 nm. What energy gap in the sodium atom produces this light? (hc = 1.24 × 10^-6 eV m)
ΔE = hc/λ = 1.24 × 10^-6/589 × 10^-9 = 2.11 eV. The value 3.37 × 10^-19 is the energy in joules.
A ground-state hydrogen atom (E₁ = −13.6 eV, E₂ = −3.40 eV) can be excited by an electron with 11.0 eV of kinetic energy, but not by a photon of 11.0 eV. Explain why.

A photon must be absorbed completely, so its energy must exactly equal a transition energy, and 11.0 eV matches none. A colliding electron can transfer only part of its kinetic energy, so it can give 10.2 eV to raise the atom to n = 2 and keep 0.8 eV.
Contrast all-or-nothing photon absorption with partial energy transfer in collisions.
Atomic energy levels are usually given negative values. This indicates that:
the electron has negative kinetic energy
the electron is moving towards the nucleus
energy is released when an electron is ionised
the electron is bound to the atom and energy must be supplied to free it
Zero is defined as a free electron at rest; bound states have less energy, so they are negative.
Dark lines in the spectrum of the Sun can be used to identify elements in its outer atmosphere because:
each element absorbs a unique set of wavelengths matching its energy level differences
each element emits light of a single colour
hotter elements absorb all visible light
dark lines show where the Sun emits no light at all
Each element's level structure is unique, so its absorption lines act as a fingerprint.
An electron with kinetic energy 12.5 eV collides with a ground-state hydrogen atom (E₁ = −13.6 eV, E₂ = −3.40 eV, E₃ = −1.51 eV, E₄ = −0.85 eV). What is the highest level the atom can be excited to?
A colliding electron can transfer part of its energy: 12.09 eV is needed for n = 3, but n = 4 requires 12.75 eV, which is more than 12.5 eV.
Calculate the wavelength of the photon emitted in hydrogen's n = 2 to n = 1 transition (E₁ = −13.6 eV, E₂ = −3.40 eV), and state the region of the spectrum. (hc = 1.24 × 10^-6 eV m)
ΔE = 10.2 eV; λ = 1.24 × 10^-6/10.2 = 1.22 × 10^-7 m (about 122 nm), which is ultraviolet.
Both the value and the region are needed.
Use de Broglie's matter-wave idea to explain why electrons in an atom occupy only certain orbits.

An electron in an orbit behaves as a wave, and a stable orbit is one where a whole number of wavelengths fits around the circumference (nλ = 2πr), forming a standing wave. Other orbits would cause destructive interference, so only certain orbits and energies are allowed.
Key terms: standing wave, whole number of wavelengths, quantised energy.
Hydrogen's energy levels are −13.6, −3.4, −1.51 and −0.85 eV. Atoms excited to the −0.85 eV level can emit how many different photon energies, and what is the wavelength of the 3 → 2 transition?
physics-7-4: physics-7-4-1
Young's double-slit experiment provided strong evidence that light:
is made of photons
has mass
behaves as a wave
travels instantly
The interference pattern of bright and dark bands comes from superposition of waves, which a simple particle model cannot explain.
physics-7-4-2
Which experiment provides the clearest evidence for the particle nature of light?
Young's double-slit experiment
Single-slit diffraction
Polarisation of light by a filter
The photoelectric effect
The threshold frequency and instant emission require light to arrive in discrete packets of energy hf.
physics-7-4-3
Which statement best describes the current understanding of the nature of light?
Light shows wave or particle behaviour depending on the experiment, and neither model alone explains all observations.
Light is purely a wave, and the photon model is only a mathematical convenience.
Light is purely a stream of particles, and interference is caused by photons colliding.
Light behaves as a wave in a vacuum and as a particle in matter.
This is wave-particle duality: interference needs the wave model, while the photoelectric effect needs the photon model.
physics-7-4-4
Describe what is meant by the wave-particle duality of light, referring to one piece of evidence for each model.

Light shows both wave and particle behaviour, and which appears depends on the experiment. Young's double-slit interference pattern is evidence for the wave model; the photoelectric effect, with its threshold frequency and instant emission, is evidence for the photon (particle) model.
One wave and one particle experiment, each correctly linked to its model.
physics-7-4-5
A double-slit experiment is performed with light so dim that only one photon is in the apparatus at a time. Over a long time the screen shows:
two bright bands opposite the slits
individual dots that gradually build up an interference pattern
a uniform glow with no pattern
no detection, because single photons cannot interfere
Each photon arrives as a localised particle, yet the probability of arrival follows the wave interference pattern.
physics-7-4-6
Newton's particle model and Huygens' wave model made different predictions about light entering water. Experiment showed that light:
speeds up in water, supporting the particle model
travels at the same speed, supporting neither model
slows down in water, supporting the wave model
speeds up in water, supporting the wave model
Newton's model needed light to speed up in a denser medium to explain refraction; measurements showed it slows down, as the wave model predicts.
physics-7-4-7
In a double-slit experiment, light of wavelength 600 nm passes through slits 0.30 mm apart onto a screen 2.0 m away. What is the fringe spacing?
40 mm
4.0 mm
physics-7-4-8
Explain how a double-slit experiment performed one photon at a time supports the idea of wave-particle duality.

Each photon is detected at a single point on the screen, showing particle behaviour. As many photons accumulate, they form the interference pattern, showing that the probability of where each photon lands is governed by wave interference.
Both aspects needed: localised detection and build-up of fringes.
physics-7-4-9
In a double-slit pattern, what is the path difference from the two slits to the second dark band from the centre?
2λ
λ
Dark bands occur at path differences of (n − ½)λ: 0.5λ for the first and 1.5λ for the second.
physics-7-4-10
Diffraction of a wave through a gap is most noticeable when:
the gap is much larger than the wavelength
the wavelength is similar to or larger than the gap width
the wave has a very high frequency
the wave has a very large amplitude
The amount of spreading depends on the ratio λ/w; it is significant when λ/w is around 1 or greater.
physics-7-4-11
Solar sails can propel a spacecraft using sunlight. This works because photons:
have rest mass that pushes the sail
heat the sail and create exhaust gases
carry momentum, which is transferred to the sail when they reflect
create a magnetic field around the sail
Photons have momentum p = h/λ; reflection reverses their momentum, exerting a force on the sail.
physics-7-4-12
A green laser (532 nm) shines on two slits 0.25 mm apart, and the pattern forms on a wall 1.5 m away. Calculate the fringe spacing.
Convert nm and mm to metres before substituting.
physics-7-4-13
A single slit produces a diffraction pattern on a screen. The slit is made narrower. The central bright band:
becomes narrower
stays the same width
disappears
becomes wider
Narrower slits increase λ/w, so the light spreads through larger angles.
physics-7-4-14
In the equation E = hf, which quantities describe a particle property and a wave property of light respectively?
E (photon energy) and f (frequency)
f and E
h and E
h and f
Photon energy is a particle (quantum) idea, frequency is a wave property, and h links the two models.
physics-7-4-15
In a double-slit experiment, the distance from the slits to the screen is doubled. The fringe spacing:
halves
doubles
quadruples
is unchanged
Δx = λL/d, so the fringe spacing is directly proportional to L.
physics-7-4-16
Explain why the results of Young's double-slit experiment could not be explained by Newton's particle model of light.

Newton's model predicts two bright bands behind the slits, with brightness simply adding where streams overlap. Young observed many alternating bright and dark bands, and the dark bands require destructive interference of waves, which particles cannot produce.
Focus on the dark bands as the key evidence for interference.
physics-7-4-17
Red laser light is replaced with blue laser light in a double-slit experiment, with everything else unchanged. The fringes:
move further apart
stay in the same positions
move closer together
change only in brightness
Blue light has a shorter wavelength, and Δx = λL/d.
physics-7-4-18
Which observation from Young's double-slit experiment cannot be explained by a simple particle model of light?
Light travels in straight lines to the slits
Two bright regions appear behind the slits
Light carries energy to the screen
Dark bands appear where light from both slits arrives
Dark bands come from destructive interference, where waves arriving half a wavelength out of phase cancel; particles alone would simply add.
physics-7-4-19
Using the wave model of light, which result would be predicted for the photoelectric effect?
Light of any frequency should eventually eject electrons if it is intense enough.
There should be a sharp threshold frequency.
Electrons should be emitted instantly even in dim light.
Maximum kinetic energy should depend only on frequency.
The wave model links energy to intensity, so it predicts no threshold and a time delay with dim light, which contradicts the observations.
physics-7-4-20
Using the photon model, explain why a more intense beam of light of the same colour delivers more energy each second.

Each photon of a given frequency carries the same energy, E = hf. A more intense beam contains more photons arriving each second, so the total energy delivered per second (the power) is greater, while the energy of each photon is unchanged.
Intensity is related to photon number, not photon energy.
physics-7-4-21
What is the momentum of a photon with energy 2.0 eV? (e = 1.60 × 10^-19 C, c = 3.00 × 10^8 m s^-1)
physics-7-4-22
A double-slit pattern has a fringe spacing of 3.0 mm with slits 0.40 mm apart and a screen 2.0 m away. What is the wavelength of the light?
150 nm
600 nm
267 nm
physics-7-4-23
Electrons fired one at a time through a double slit produce an interference pattern on a detector. This shows that:
electrons are actually photons
electrons split in half at the slits
the slits emit their own light
matter, as well as light, displays wave-particle duality
Each electron is detected at a point (particle) but the distribution forms interference fringes (wave), just like single photons.
physics-7-4-24
At a point P on a screen, the path difference from two slits is 1.2 μm. The light has a wavelength of 480 nm. Is P on a bright or dark band? Justify your answer.

Path difference/λ = 1.2 × 10^-6/4.8 × 10^-7 = 2.5, which is a half-integer number of wavelengths. The waves arrive out of phase and interfere destructively, so P is on a dark band (the third dark band).
Whole numbers of λ give bright bands; half-integers give dark bands.
physics-7-4-25
Explain how electron diffraction and the photoelectric effect together show that wave-particle duality applies to both light and matter.

The photoelectric effect shows that light, usually treated as a wave, also behaves as particles (photons). Electron diffraction shows that electrons, usually treated as particles, also behave as waves with λ = h/p. Together they show both light and matter have dual natures.
Need the 'reverse' behaviour shown for each.
physics-7-4-c1
Which observation supports a particle model of light and cannot be explained by a wave model?
Light produces a pattern of bright and dark fringes when it passes through two slits
Below the threshold frequency, no photoelectrons are emitted however intense the light
Light spreads out (diffracts) when it passes through a gap similar to its wavelength
Light can be polarised by a filter so that it vibrates in only one plane
In a wave model, enough intensity should eventually free electrons at any frequency. Photons of energy hf explain the threshold.
physics-8-1: physics-8-1-1
A student investigates how the length of a pendulum affects its period. What is the independent variable?
The length of the pendulum
The period of the pendulum
The mass of the pendulum bob
The amplitude of the swing
The independent variable is the one deliberately changed by the experimenter, here the pendulum length.
physics-8-1-2
In an investigation of how the length of a pendulum affects its period, what is the dependent variable?
The length of the string
The period of oscillation
The number of swings timed
The gravitational field strength
The dependent variable is the one measured in response to changes in the independent variable, here the period.
physics-8-1-3
A student investigates how the voltage across a resistor affects the current through it. Which is a controlled variable?
The current through the resistor
The voltage across the resistor
The temperature of the resistor
The ammeter reading
Resistance changes with temperature, so temperature must be kept constant; current and voltage are the dependent and independent variables.
physics-8-1-4
Why must controlled variables be kept constant during an experiment?
To increase the resolution of the measuring instruments
To eliminate all random errors from the results
To guarantee that the hypothesis is supported
So that any change in the dependent variable can be attributed to the independent variable
Keeping other variables constant ensures a fair test, so the observed effect is caused by the independent variable alone.
physics-8-1-5
Which is the best hypothesis for an investigation of how drop height affects the bounce height of a tennis ball?
If the drop height increases, then the bounce height will increase proportionally, because a constant fraction of the ball's energy is lost in each bounce
The tennis ball will bounce when it is dropped
Bounce height depends on many different factors
Drop height is the independent variable and bounce height is the dependent variable
A good hypothesis is testable, states the predicted relationship between the variables and gives a reason.
physics-8-1-6
In VCE Physics, what does the term 'validity' of an investigation refer to?
The closeness of agreement between repeated measurements
The extent to which the experiment actually investigates what it claims to investigate
The closeness of a measurement to the true value
The smallest change in a quantity that an instrument can detect
Validity is about whether the method and data genuinely address the aim, e.g. a fair test with controlled variables.
physics-8-1-7
Which statement best describes 'repeatability'?
The closeness of agreement between results obtained by different people using different equipment
The closeness of a mean value to the accepted value
The closeness of agreement between successive measurements made by the same person, with the same method and equipment, under the same conditions
The number of significant figures given by an instrument
Repeatability refers to repeated measurements under the same conditions; reproducibility involves changed conditions, people or equipment.
physics-8-1-8
A Year 12 class in Ballarat obtains a value for g that closely agrees with a value obtained by a class in Geelong using different equipment. This agreement demonstrates good:
repeatability
resolution
validity of the controlled variables
reproducibility
Agreement between results obtained by different experimenters with different equipment and locations is reproducibility.
physics-8-1-9
A student investigates how the mass of a stack of paper coffee filters affects their terminal velocity. Which action best improves the validity of the investigation?
Dropping every stack from the same height in the same draught-free room
Using only the heaviest stacks to make timing easier
Recording times to more decimal places than the stopwatch displays
Changing both the number of filters and their shape between trials
Controlling drop height and air movement means only mass varies, so changes in terminal velocity can be attributed to mass.
physics-8-1-10
Between trials, a student changes both the length of a pendulum and the mass of its bob. What is the main problem with this design?
The period cannot be measured if the mass changes
Two variables have been changed, so a change in period cannot be attributed to either one
Changing the mass always introduces a systematic error
The experiment will become more precise but less accurate
Only one independent variable should be changed at a time; otherwise the effects are confounded.
physics-8-1-11
Which is the most appropriate risk control when using a laser to investigate double-slit interference?
Wear ordinary sunglasses so the beam can be viewed directly
Aim the beam at shiny surfaces to make the pattern brighter
Use a low-power (Class 2) laser and never look directly into the beam or its reflections
Use the most powerful laser available to make the fringes clearer
Low-power lasers combined with avoiding direct and reflected beams minimise the risk of eye damage.
physics-8-1-12
Which of the following is a qualitative observation?
The current was 2.4 A
The temperature rose by 3.2 °C
The wire was 45.0 cm long
The wire became noticeably warm to the touch
Qualitative observations describe properties without numerical measurement; the others are quantitative.
physics-8-1-13
A student measures the period of a pendulum for lengths of 0.40 m, 0.42 m and 0.44 m only. Which change would best improve the design?
Use at least five lengths spread over a wider range, such as 0.20 m to 1.20 m
Repeat each of the three lengths fifty times
Use a heavier bob for each length
Measure the lengths to the nearest centimetre instead of the nearest millimetre
A wide range with enough data points is needed to reveal the true relationship between length and period.
physics-8-1-14
Why do students usually time 10 complete oscillations of a pendulum rather than a single oscillation?
It removes any systematic error caused by a faulty stopwatch
It reduces the percentage uncertainty in the period caused by reaction time
It improves the accuracy of the length measurement
It increases the period of the pendulum
The reaction-time uncertainty is about the same for any timing, so spreading it over 10 periods makes the percentage uncertainty much smaller.
physics-8-1-15
Which of the following is secondary data?
Times recorded by the student using a stopwatch
Voltages displayed on the student's multimeter
Values of g at different latitudes taken from a published scientific database
Distances measured by the student with a metre rule
Secondary data are collected by someone else; primary data are collected first-hand by the investigator.
physics-8-1-16
A student investigates whether the strength of a magnet depends on its temperature, using a magnetic field sensor. Which variable is most important to control?
The temperature of the magnet
The reading on the magnetic field sensor
The colour of the magnet
The distance between the magnet and the sensor
Field strength varies strongly with distance, so distance must be held constant; temperature is the independent variable and the sensor reading is the dependent variable.
physics-8-1-17
The aim of an experiment is 'to determine how the angle of an incline affects the acceleration of a trolley'. What is the dependent variable?
The acceleration of the trolley
The angle of the incline
The mass of the trolley
The length of the incline
The quantity measured in response to the changed angle is the trolley's acceleration.
physics-8-1-18
A student wants to test whether the resistance of a nichrome wire is proportional to its length. Which design is most appropriate?
Measure the resistance of five wires made of different metals
Measure the resistance of at least five different lengths of the same wire at constant temperature and plot R against L
Measure the resistance of one length of wire many times
Vary the current through one fixed length of wire
Varying length only, keeping material, thickness and temperature constant, and graphing R against L directly tests proportionality.
physics-8-1-19
A student drops a bar magnet through coils with different numbers of turns and records the peak induced EMF. Identify the independent variable, the dependent variable and two controlled variables.
Independent: number of turns in the coil. Dependent: peak induced EMF. Controlled (any two): strength of the magnet, drop height, coil diameter/area, orientation of the magnet, type of wire.
Award marks for correctly identifying each; controlled variables must be things that could plausibly affect the EMF.
physics-8-1-20
Write a suitable hypothesis for an investigation into how the angle of an incline affects the acceleration of a trolley rolling down it.
If the angle of the incline increases, then the acceleration of the trolley will increase, because the component of the gravitational force down the slope (mg sin θ) increases.
A good hypothesis is an 'if... then... because' statement linking the independent and dependent variables with a physics reason.
physics-8-1-21
Explain why a student should take repeated measurements in an investigation, and state one limitation of doing so.

Repeated measurements allow the effect of random errors to be reduced by averaging, help identify outliers and indicate the precision/repeatability of the data. However, repeating does not reduce systematic errors.
Mention of averaging random error plus the limitation about systematic error gains full marks.
physics-8-1-22
Explain the difference between repeatability and reproducibility.

Repeatability is the closeness of agreement of results when the same person repeats a measurement with the same method, equipment and conditions. Reproducibility is the closeness of agreement when the measurement is repeated by different people, with different equipment or in different locations.
The key distinction is same conditions (repeatability) versus changed conditions (reproducibility).
physics-8-1-23
A student estimates the speed of sound by clapping once in front of a wall 20 m away and timing the echo with a stopwatch. Suggest two improvements to the method.

Any two: increase the distance to the wall so the time is longer; clap in rhythm with the echoes and time many (e.g. 20) intervals, then divide; use microphones and a data logger instead of a hand-held stopwatch; repeat and average.
The round-trip time of about 0.12 s is similar to human reaction time, so the improvements should reduce the percentage uncertainty in time.
physics-8-1-24
Why should an investigation use at least five well-spread values of the independent variable?

A wide range with enough values allows the trend or relationship to be identified reliably, reveals any non-linearity, reduces the influence of any single uncertain point on the line of best fit and allows a meaningful gradient to be found.
Refer to both the number of points and the spread across the range.
physics-8-1-25
Define a controlled variable and explain what happens to the conclusion if an important controlled variable is not kept constant.

A controlled variable is a variable that could affect the dependent variable and so is kept constant throughout the experiment. If it is not controlled, changes in the dependent variable may be caused by it rather than the independent variable, so the conclusion is not valid.
Linking an uncontrolled variable to reduced validity is the key point.
physics-8-1-c1
Students measure the period of a pendulum by timing 10 oscillations and dividing by 10, rather than timing one. The main benefit is that:
It removes all systematic error
It makes the pendulum swing more regularly
It makes the result more accurate even if the stopwatch is wrong
The effect of reaction-time uncertainty on each period is reduced by a factor of 10
Human reaction time adds a similar absolute uncertainty to any timing; spread over 10 periods its effect per period is one-tenth.
physics-8-2: In VCE Physics, what does 'accuracy' describe?
How close a measurement is to the true value
How close repeated measurements are to each other
The smallest division on the measuring scale
The number of significant figures recorded
Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is closeness of repeated measurements to each other.
In VCE Physics, what does 'precision' describe?
How close a measurement is to the true value
How closely a set of repeated measurements agree with each other
The size of the systematic error
The range of the independent variable
Precise measurements have little spread, regardless of whether they are close to the true value.
A student obtains values for g of 9.52, 9.53, 9.51 and 9.52 m/s². The accepted value is 9.80 m/s². The results are best described as:
The values are tightly clustered (precise) but about 0.28 m/s² below the accepted value (not accurate).
A student obtains values for g of 9.2, 10.4, 9.6 and 10.0 m/s². The accepted value is 9.80 m/s². The results are best described as:
The mean is 39.2 ÷ 4 = 9.8 m/s², matching the accepted value, but the values are widely spread.
What is the resolution of a metre rule marked in millimetres?
Resolution is the smallest change the instrument can display, which is one scale division of 1 mm.
Using the convention of half the smallest scale division, what is the uncertainty in a single reading from an analogue ruler graduated in millimetres?
Half of the smallest division of 1 mm gives ±0.5 mm.
A digital voltmeter reads 3.47 V. Using the convention that the uncertainty of a digital meter equals its resolution, the reading should be recorded as:
The last displayed digit is in the hundredths place, so the resolution and uncertainty are ±0.01 V.
