A length is measured as 2.50 ± 0.05 m. What is the percentage uncertainty?
A rectangle is measured as 4.0 ± 0.1 cm long and 2.0 ± 0.1 cm wide. What is its area with absolute uncertainty?
Percentage uncertainties add when multiplying: 2.5% + 5% = 7.5%, and 7.5% of 8.0 cm² is 0.6 cm².
Two lengths, 12.0 ± 0.2 cm and 8.0 ± 0.1 cm, are added. What is the total length?
When quantities are added, their absolute uncertainties are added: 0.2 + 0.1 = 0.3 cm.
Water starts at 20.0 ± 0.5 °C and is heated to 35.0 ± 0.5 °C. What is the temperature change?
When subtracting, absolute uncertainties still add: 0.5 + 0.5 = 1.0 °C.
A speed is measured as 3.0 ± 0.1 m/s. What is the percentage uncertainty in v²?
The percentage uncertainty in v is 0.1 ÷ 3.0 = 3.3%; squaring doubles it to about 6.7%.
A 2.00 ± 0.02 kg cart moves at 4.0 ± 0.2 m/s. What is its kinetic energy with percentage uncertainty?
The time for 10 oscillations of a pendulum is 15.6 ± 0.2 s. What is the period?
Dividing by an exact number divides both the value and its absolute uncertainty by 10.
A voltmeter reads 12.0 V and an ammeter reads 0.35 A. The resistance should be reported as:
R = 12.0 ÷ 0.35 = 34.29 Ω, but the current has only 2 significant figures, so the answer is given to 2 significant figures.
Which instrument choice would most reduce the uncertainty when measuring the diameter of a thin copper wire?
A micrometer has a resolution of about 0.01 mm, giving a much smaller percentage uncertainty for a small diameter.
A runner covers 100.0 ± 0.5 m in 12.5 ± 0.1 s. What is the average speed with absolute uncertainty?
Percentage uncertainty = 0.5% + 0.8% = 1.3%, and 1.3% of 8.0 m/s is about 0.1 m/s.
Which statement best describes the 'true value' of a quantity?
The mean of the student's measurements
The value that would be obtained by an ideal measurement with no errors
The largest value recorded in a set of trials
The value displayed on the most expensive instrument
The true value is the ideal value, which can only be estimated because all real measurements contain some uncertainty.
Explain the difference between accuracy and precision, using an example.

Accuracy is how close a measurement is to the true value; precision is how closely repeated measurements agree with each other. For example, readings of g of 9.51, 9.52 and 9.53 m/s² are precise but not accurate, because they are clustered but well below 9.80 m/s².
Any valid example that separates the two ideas gains full marks.
A spring's extension is measured five times: 4.2, 4.5, 4.3, 4.4 and 4.6 cm. Find the mean extension and estimate its uncertainty using half the range.
Mean = 22.0 ÷ 5 = 4.4 cm. Half range = (4.6 − 4.2) ÷ 2 = 0.2 cm. Extension = 4.4 ± 0.2 cm.
Show both the mean and the half-range calculation.
A pendulum of length 0.800 ± 0.005 m has a period of 1.80 ± 0.02 s. Using g = 4π²L/T², find g and its absolute uncertainty.
g = 4π² × 0.800 ÷ 1.80² = 9.75 m/s². Percentage uncertainty = 0.625% + 2 × 1.11% ≈ 2.8%, so the uncertainty is about ±0.3 m/s². g = 9.7 ± 0.3 m/s².
Remember to double the percentage uncertainty in T because T is squared.
A resistor has 6.0 ± 0.1 V across it and 0.50 ± 0.02 A through it. Find its resistance with absolute uncertainty.
R = 6.0 ÷ 0.50 = 12 Ω. Percentage uncertainty = 1.7% + 4.0% = 5.7%, so ΔR ≈ 0.7 Ω. R = 12.0 ± 0.7 Ω.
A metal cube has sides of 2.00 ± 0.02 cm and a mass of 21.6 ± 0.1 g. Find its density with absolute uncertainty.
Volume = 2.00³ = 8.00 cm³ with 3 × 1% = 3% uncertainty. Mass uncertainty = 0.46%. Density = 21.6 ÷ 8.00 = 2.70 g/cm³ with about 3.5% uncertainty, so ρ = 2.70 ± 0.09 g/cm³.
The cube of the side triples its percentage uncertainty.
Explain why recording a calculated result with too many significant figures is misleading.
Extra significant figures imply a higher precision than the measurements can support. The result should be given to the same number of significant figures as the least precise data used.
Link significant figures to the precision or uncertainty of the original measurements.
A student's reaction time introduces an uncertainty of ±0.2 s in any stopwatch timing. Compare the percentage uncertainty in the period when timing one 1.5 s oscillation with timing 20 oscillations.
One oscillation: 0.2 ÷ 1.5 × 100 ≈ 13%. Twenty oscillations take 30 s: 0.2 ÷ 30 × 100 ≈ 0.67%. Timing 20 oscillations reduces the percentage uncertainty by a factor of 20.
The absolute uncertainty stays the same, so a longer measured time gives a smaller percentage uncertainty.
Four measurements of g are 9.62, 9.64, 9.63 and 9.62 m/s². The accepted value is 9.80 m/s². The results are:
They agree closely with each other (precise) but are consistently below the accepted value (inaccurate), which suggests a systematic error.
physics-8-3: physics-8-3-1
Which statement best describes random error?
Unpredictable variations that scatter readings either side of the true value
A consistent offset that shifts every reading in the same direction
An error caused by misreading a scale once
An error that can be removed by calibrating the instrument
Random errors vary unpredictably from reading to reading, so their effect can be reduced by averaging.
physics-8-3-2
Which statement best describes systematic error?
An error that scatters readings randomly above and below the true value
An error that shifts every reading in the same direction by the same amount or proportion
An error that is removed by taking more readings
An error that only affects the precision of results
Systematic errors are consistent biases, such as a zero error or a miscalibrated instrument.
physics-8-3-3
An electronic balance reads 0.3 g with nothing on the pan. This is an example of:
a random error
a mistake
a systematic (zero) error
a resolution limit
A zero offset adds the same amount to every reading, which is a systematic error.
physics-8-3-4
A student's reaction time varies slightly each time they start and stop a stopwatch. This mainly introduces:
systematic error
a zero error
a calibration error
random error
The reaction delay varies unpredictably from trial to trial, causing scatter, which is random error.
physics-8-3-5
Averaging many repeated measurements reduces the effect of:
random errors only
systematic errors only
both random and systematic errors equally
neither random nor systematic errors
Random errors tend to cancel when averaged, but a systematic bias is the same in every reading and remains.
physics-8-3-6
A student records a length of 25 cm when the scale actually read 2.5 cm. According to VCE Physics terminology, this is best described as:
a random error that is reduced by averaging
a mistake (personal error) that should be avoided or the reading repeated, not treated as an experimental error
a systematic error caused by the instrument
an uncertainty due to the instrument's resolution
Mistakes are not part of uncertainty analysis; the reading should be identified, excluded or repeated.
physics-8-3-7
A student always reads a ruler from the same angle above the pointer, so every reading is shifted the same way. This is:
a random error due to parallax
a resolution error
a systematic error due to parallax
an outlier
Reading consistently from the same off-normal angle biases every reading in the same direction.
physics-8-3-8
The first 2 mm of a metre rule has been worn away, and a student measures lengths starting from the worn end. What is the effect?
Every reading is 2 mm too small, a systematic error
Readings are randomly 2 mm too large or too small
There is no effect because the scale is still marked in millimetres
Every reading is 2 mm too large, a systematic error
The physical end now sits where the 2 mm mark used to be, so each length reads 2 mm more than the true value.
physics-8-3-9
A graph of extension against force for a spring is expected to pass through the origin but has a non-zero intercept. This most likely indicates:
a systematic error
a random error
that the spring obeys Hooke's law exactly
that more data points are needed to reduce precision
A consistent offset in every reading shifts the whole line, producing a non-zero intercept.
physics-8-3-10
One measurement in a set of repeated trials is far from the others. What is the most appropriate response?
Always include it so the data are not manipulated
Check for a mistake, repeat the measurement if possible, and exclude it from the mean with a note in the report if it is clearly anomalous
Delete it without comment
Change it to match the mean of the other values
Outliers should be investigated and, if justified, excluded transparently; data must never be altered.
physics-8-3-11
Which action reduces systematic error?
Taking more repeated readings
Using a larger range of the independent variable
Calibrating the instrument against a known standard
Recording more decimal places
Calibration identifies and corrects consistent offsets; repetition only reduces random error.
physics-8-3-12
In a free-fall experiment, air resistance on a light ball causes the measured g to be:
consistently higher than the true value, a systematic error
randomly higher or lower, a random error
unaffected because air resistance is negligible for all objects
consistently lower than the true value, a systematic error
Air resistance always opposes motion, reducing the measured acceleration in every trial.
physics-8-3-13
The reading on a voltmeter fluctuates slightly up and down because of electrical noise in the circuit. This is:
random error
systematic error
a zero error
a mistake
Fluctuations above and below the true value are unpredictable and are random errors.
physics-8-3-14
A stopwatch runs 2% fast, so every time it records is 2% too long. Which statement about the results is correct?
The results will be imprecise but accurate
The results may still be precise but they will be inaccurate
The results will be both accurate and precise
Averaging more trials will remove the error
A systematic error shifts all values equally, so it reduces accuracy while leaving the spread (precision) unchanged.
physics-8-3-15
Increasing the number of trials from 3 to 10 will most likely:
remove all systematic errors
make each individual reading more accurate
reduce the effect of random errors on the mean, but not change any systematic error
increase the resolution of the instrument
More trials improve the reliability of the mean against random scatter, but a systematic bias remains in every reading.
physics-8-3-16

A thermometer reads 1.5 °C too high at all temperatures. It is used to find the temperature change of water in a specific heat capacity experiment. What is the effect on the calculated temperature change?
The temperature change will be 1.5 °C too high
The temperature change will be 3.0 °C too high
The temperature change will be 1.5 °C too low
No effect, because the offset cancels when the initial temperature is subtracted from the final
Both readings are 1.5 °C too high, so their difference is unaffected.
physics-8-3-17
A light gate calculates speed as card length ÷ time. The card length is entered as 5.0 cm when it is actually 4.0 cm. What is the effect on the calculated speeds?
All speeds are 25% too high, a systematic error
All speeds are 20% too low, a systematic error
Speeds are randomly too high or too low
There is no effect because time is measured accurately
Speed is proportional to the entered length, and 5.0 ÷ 4.0 = 1.25, so every speed is 25% too high.
physics-8-3-18
Which pairing is correct?
Random errors mainly affect accuracy; systematic errors mainly affect precision
Random errors mainly affect precision; systematic errors mainly affect accuracy
Both mainly affect resolution
Neither affects accuracy
Scatter (random error) reduces precision, while a consistent bias (systematic error) moves results away from the true value.
physics-8-3-19
Distinguish between random and systematic errors, giving an example of each.

Random errors cause unpredictable scatter of readings either side of the true value, e.g. variation in reaction time when using a stopwatch. Systematic errors shift every reading in the same direction by a consistent amount, e.g. a balance with a zero error or a miscalibrated thermometer.
A clear definition and a valid example for each are needed.
physics-8-3-20
A student measures g with a pendulum as 9.42 ± 0.05 m/s². The accepted value is 9.80 m/s². Comment on the result.

The accepted value lies outside the range 9.37 to 9.47 m/s², so random error alone cannot explain the difference and a systematic error is likely. For example, measuring the length only to the top of the bob (making L too short) would make g consistently too low.
Compare the accepted value with the uncertainty range, then suggest a plausible systematic error in the right direction.
physics-8-3-21
Explain why repeating measurements and averaging does not reduce systematic error.

A systematic error affects every reading in the same direction by the same amount, so the mean is shifted by the same amount. Averaging only reduces errors that vary randomly above and below the true value.
Key idea: systematic errors do not cancel.
physics-8-3-22
A micrometer reads +0.03 mm when its jaws are fully closed. It then reads 1.27 mm when measuring a wire. What is the true diameter of the wire?
True diameter = 1.27 − 0.03 = 1.24 mm.
Correct a zero error by subtracting the zero reading from every measurement.
physics-8-3-23
Five timings of a trolley down a ramp are 2.31, 2.28, 2.35, 3.10 and 2.30 s. Identify the outlier and find the mean of the remaining values.
3.10 s is the outlier. Mean of the remaining values = (2.31 + 2.28 + 2.35 + 2.30) ÷ 4 = 9.24 ÷ 4 = 2.31 s.
The outlier should be checked, noted and excluded rather than deleted silently.
physics-8-3-24
Why is 'human error' not an acceptable explanation for discrepancies in a VCE Physics practical report?

It is too vague. Genuine mistakes (such as misreading a scale) should be avoided or the reading repeated, and are not part of the error analysis. The report should instead identify specific random or systematic errors and their effect on the results.
Show that you understand the difference between mistakes and experimental errors.
physics-8-3-25
A student predicts a trolley's acceleration down a ramp using a = g sin θ but ignores friction. Identify the type of error and how the measured acceleration compares with the prediction.

This is a systematic error: friction always opposes motion, so the measured acceleration will be consistently less than g sin θ. It could be reduced by friction-compensating the track (tilting it slightly until the trolley moves at constant velocity) or including friction in the model.
State the error type, the direction of the effect and a reasonable fix.
physics-8-3-c1
A balance reads 0.20 g with nothing on it, and this is not noticed. Which statement is correct?
It causes a random error that averaging can reduce
It causes a systematic error that repeating measurements cannot reduce
It only affects precision
It is a personal error, not a measurement error
A zero offset shifts every reading by the same amount. Averaging does not remove it; correcting the zero does.
physics-8-4: When graphing experimental data, which variable is conventionally plotted on the horizontal (x) axis?
The variable with the larger uncertainty
The independent variable goes on the x-axis and the dependent variable on the y-axis.
The period of a pendulum is given by T = 2π√(L/g). Which graph will give a straight line through the origin?
Squaring gives T² = (4π²/g)L, which is linear in L with a gradient of 4π²/g.
A graph of T² against L for a pendulum has a gradient of 4.0 s²/m. What is the value of g?
The intensity I of light from a point source is thought to follow I = k/r². Which graph should be plotted to test this?
If I = k/r², a graph of I against 1/r² is a straight line through the origin with gradient k.
For an object in uniform circular motion with fixed mass and radius, F = mv²/r. Which graph gives a straight line, and what is its gradient?
F is directly proportional to v², with constant of proportionality m/r.
A graph of current (y-axis) against voltage (x-axis) for a resistor has a gradient of 0.040 A/V. What is the resistance?
Which best describes a line of best fit for linear data?
A line joining each data point to the next
A line that must pass through the first and last points
A straight line with points scattered roughly evenly on either side, not necessarily passing through every point or the origin
A line that must always pass through the origin
A line of best fit represents the overall trend and balances the scatter of the points.
Theory predicts that a graph should pass through the origin, but the line of best fit has a clear non-zero intercept. This most likely indicates:
only random errors in the measurements
that the theory has been proven correct
a systematic error in the measurements
A constant offset in every measurement shifts the line, giving a non-zero intercept.
For the photoelectric effect, a graph of maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons against frequency of light is a straight line. What does the x-intercept represent?
Since E_{k} = hf − φ, E_{k} = 0 when f = f₀, the threshold frequency.
A trolley accelerates uniformly from rest. A graph of displacement s against t² has a gradient of 1.5 m/s². What is the acceleration?
With u = 0, s = ½at², so the gradient = a/2 and a = 2 × 1.5 = 3.0 m/s².
According to de Broglie, λ = h/p. Which graph gives a straight line with gradient equal to Planck's constant?
Since λ = h × (1/p), a graph of λ against 1/p is linear with gradient h.
What does the area under a force–extension graph for a spring represent?
The power delivered to the spring
The elastic potential energy stored in the spring
Work done = area under the F–x graph, which equals the elastic potential energy stored.
What is the purpose of error bars on a graph?
To show the uncertainty in each plotted value
To show the line of best fit
To show which points are outliers
To show the gradient of the line
Error bars show the range within which each true value is likely to lie.
Students draw the steepest and least steep lines that still pass through all the error bars on a graph. What is this used for?
Finding the mean of the data
Estimating the uncertainty in the gradient
Half the difference between the maximum and minimum gradients gives an estimate of the gradient's uncertainty.
A line of best fit passes through the points (0.10, 0.45) and (0.50, 2.05). What is its gradient?
For satellites orbiting the same planet, T² = (4π²/GM)r³. Which graph is linear?
T² is directly proportional to r³, with gradient 4π²/GM.
A graph of T² against r³ for moons of a planet has a gradient of 9.9 × 10⁻¹⁴ s²/m³. Given G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², what is the mass of the planet?
What does the area under an acceleration–time graph represent?
Area = acceleration × time, which equals the change in velocity.
The period of a mass on a spring is T = 2π√(m/k). Describe how to linearise this relationship to find k from a graph.
Square both sides: T² = (4π²/k)m. Plot T² (y-axis) against m (x-axis); the graph is a straight line through the origin with gradient 4π²/k, so k = 4π² ÷ gradient.
State the variables plotted, the gradient expression and how k is obtained.
A graph of T² against mass m for a mass–spring system has a gradient of 0.20 s²/kg. Calculate the spring constant k.
A student suspects that sound intensity I from a speaker on a sports oval is inversely proportional to the square of the distance r. Describe how a graph could test this.
Measure I at several distances, then plot I against 1/r². If the graph is a straight line through the origin, then I ∝ 1/r² is supported; the gradient gives the constant of proportionality.
The key is choosing axes that would give a straight line through the origin if the relationship holds.
From a graph, the steepest line through the error bars has a gradient of 5.2 and the least steep line has a gradient of 4.6. State the gradient with its uncertainty.
Use the mean of the extreme gradients and half their difference.
A graph of maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons against frequency has an x-intercept of 5.5 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Calculate the work function of the metal in eV (h = 4.14 × 10⁻¹⁵ eV s).
The x-intercept is the threshold frequency f₀ and the work function is φ = hf₀.
Why do physicists linearise data so that it produces a straight-line graph?

A straight line makes the relationship easy to recognise and test, deviations from the model are easy to see, and the gradient and intercept can be used to find physical constants (such as g or k) using all the data rather than one point.
Mention both identifying the relationship and extracting constants from the gradient or intercept.
A ball rolls from rest down a ramp. A graph of distance d against t² has a gradient of 0.60 m/s². Find the ball's acceleration.
d = ½at², so the gradient = a/2. a = 2 × 0.60 = 1.2 m/s².
Recognise that the gradient is half the acceleration.
For a pendulum, T = 2π√(L/g). Explain which graph gives a straight line, and find g if its gradient is 4.03 s²/m.
Plot T² against L; g = 4π²/gradient ≈ 9.80 m/s²
Squaring gives T² = (4π²/g)L, a line through the origin with gradient 4π²/g. g = 4π² ÷ 4.03 ≈ 9.80 m/s².
physics-challenge: Astronauts in a space station 400 km above Earth feel weightless because:
There is no gravity at 400 km, because Earth's gravitational field ends at the edge of the atmosphere
The station's high orbital speed creates an outward force that exactly cancels the pull of gravity
They and the station are in free fall together, though gravity there is still about 90% of its surface value
They are outside Earth's gravitational field, so only the Moon and the Sun pull on them, weakly
Gravity provides the centripetal force for the orbit. Since everything accelerates together, there is no normal force: apparent weightlessness.
In a velocity selector, crossed fields of E = 2.0 × 10⁴ V/m and B = 0.10 T let charged particles pass undeflected. Their speed is:
Undeflected means qE = qvB, so v = E/B = 2.0 × 10⁴ ÷ 0.10 = 2.0 × 10⁵ m/s, whatever the charge or mass.
A car drives around a flat (unbanked) curve of radius 40 m. The maximum sideways friction is 0.60 times the car's weight. Find the maximum safe speed.
Friction provides the centripetal force: 0.60mg = mv²/r, so v = √(0.60 × 9.8 × 40) ≈ 15.3 m/s. The mass cancels.
A spring of spring constant 200 N/m is compressed 0.10 m and launches a 0.050 kg ball horizontally. Find the launch speed, assuming no losses.
½kx² = ½mv²: 1.0 J = ½ × 0.050 × v², so v = √40 ≈ 6.3 m/s.
An electron (rest energy 8.2 × 10⁻¹⁴ J) travels at 0.60c, so γ = 1.25. Its kinetic energy is about:
KE = (γ − 1)mc² = 0.25 × 8.2 × 10⁻¹⁴ ≈ 2.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ J. The classical ½mv² gives 1.5 × 10⁻¹⁴ J, which is too small.
An ideal transformer steps 240 V RMS down to 12 V RMS and supplies 2.0 A to a lamp. The primary current and turns ratio (primary : secondary) are:
Power in = power out: 240 × I = 12 × 2.0, so I = 0.10 A. Voltage ratio = turns ratio = 240 : 12 = 20 : 1.
Electrons are accelerated from rest through 54 V. Find their de Broglie wavelength and say why they diffract from a nickel crystal (atomic spacing about 2 × 10⁻¹⁰ m).
About 1.7 × 10⁻¹⁰ m; it is similar to the atomic spacing, so diffraction is noticeable
Ten oscillations of a pendulum take 20.0 ± 0.2 s. The period with its uncertainty is:
Dividing by an exact number divides the value and the absolute uncertainty: 2.00 ± 0.02 s (1% either way).
A strong magnet is dropped down a vertical copper pipe and falls much more slowly than through a plastic pipe. Explain why, including the energy changes.

The falling magnet changes the flux through the copper, inducing eddy currents. By Lenz's law their fields oppose the motion, slowing the magnet. Gravitational potential energy becomes heat in the copper, not just kinetic energy.
Plastic is an insulator, so no current is induced. A full answer names induction, Lenz's law and the energy transfer.
Find the minimum energy needed to lift a 1000 kg probe from Earth's surface to a distance of 2R from Earth's centre (R = 6.37 × 10⁶ m). Why is mgh wrong here?
About 3.1 × 10¹⁰ J; g is not constant over this distance (it falls to g/4 at 2R)
ΔU = GMm(1/R − 1/2R) = GMm/(2R) = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 5.98 × 10²⁴ × 1000 ÷ (2 × 6.37 × 10⁶) ≈ 3.1 × 10¹⁰ J. mgh with g = 9.8 would give about 6.2 × 10¹⁰ J, double the answer.

X.title: Satellites in orbit
X.source: Original question in the style of the VCE Physics exam, Section B

pieces.text: A satellite moves in a circular orbit 600 km above Earth's surface. Use G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², mass of Earth = 5.98 × 10²⁴ kg and radius of Earth = 6.37 × 10⁶ m.

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Calculate the gravitational field strength at the satellite's orbit.

steps.working: Measure the orbital radius from Earth's centre: r = 6.37 × 10⁶ + 6.00 × 10⁵ = 6.97 × 10⁶ m.

pieces.mistake: Using 600 km as the radius. Distances in Newton's law of gravitation are measured from the centre of Earth.

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: Calculate the orbital speed of the satellite.

steps.working: Gravity provides the centripetal force: \(\dfrac{GMm}{r^2} = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}\), so \(v = \sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{r}}\).

pieces.mistake: Including the satellite's mass in the calculation. It cancels, so the orbital speed does not depend on the satellite's mass.

pieces.label: c
pieces.question: Calculate the period of the orbit, in minutes.
pieces.mistake: Leaving the answer in seconds. The question asks for minutes.

pieces.label: d
pieces.question: An astronaut inside the satellite feels weightless, even though the gravitational field strength there is not zero. Explain why.
pieces.answer: The astronaut and the satellite are both in free fall towards Earth with the same acceleration, so the floor does not push on the astronaut. With no normal force, the astronaut's apparent weight is zero.

steps.working: Gravity still acts on the astronaut and provides the centripetal force for the orbit.
The astronaut and satellite fall together with the same acceleration, so the floor exerts no normal force. With no normal force the apparent weight is zero, which is felt as weightlessness.

pieces.mistake: Saying there is no gravity in orbit. At 600 km gravity is still about 84% as strong as at the surface; the astronaut is in free fall, not free of gravity.

pieces.text: A geostationary satellite orbits Earth once every 24.0 hours.

pieces.label: e
pieces.question: Use Kepler's third law to calculate the orbital radius of the geostationary satellite.

steps.working: For a circular orbit, \(r^3 = \dfrac{GMT^2}{4\pi^2}\), with T = 24.0 × 3600 = 8.64 × 10⁴ s.

pieces.mistake: Leaving T in hours. Use seconds so that every quantity is in SI units.

pieces.text: The satellites send data to the ground using radio waves of frequency 1.50 GHz.

pieces.label: f
pieces.question: Calculate the wavelength of these radio waves. Use c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
pieces.mistake: Treating GHz as 10⁶ Hz. Giga means 10⁹.

X.title: Electrons: accelerated, turned and diffracted
X.source: Original question in the style of the VCE Physics exam, Section B

pieces.text: In an electron gun, electrons start from rest and are accelerated between two parallel plates 2.0 cm apart, with a potential difference of 2.00 kV between them. Use e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg, h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. Ignore relativistic effects.

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Calculate the magnitude of the electric field between the plates, and the magnitude of the force it exerts on an electron.
pieces.mistake: Using d = 2.0 instead of 0.020. Convert centimetres to metres before using E = V ÷ d.

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: Calculate the kinetic energy of an electron as it leaves the plates, in joules.

steps.working: The work done on the electron by the field is W = qV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 2.00 × 10³ = 3.20 × 10⁻¹⁶ J, and all of it becomes kinetic energy.

pieces.mistake: Mixing up kilovolts and electronvolts. Each electron gains 2.00 keV, which is 2.00 × 10³ × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.

pieces.label: c
pieces.question: Show that the speed of the electrons is about 2.65 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹.

steps.working: Set the kinetic energy equal to the work done: ½mv² = 3.20 × 10⁻¹⁶ J.

pieces.mistake: Leaving out the ½ in ½mv², which gives 1.88 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹, too small by a factor of √2.

pieces.text: The electrons then enter a uniform magnetic field of 5.00 mT, directed at right angles to their velocity.

pieces.label: d
pieces.question: Calculate the radius of the electrons' circular path in the magnetic field.

steps.working: The magnetic force provides the centripetal force: \(qvB = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}\), so \(r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}\).

pieces.mistake: Treating mT as 10⁻⁶ T. Milli means 10⁻³, so 5.00 mT = 5.00 × 10⁻³ T.

pieces.label: e
pieces.question: Explain why the magnetic field does not change the speed of the electrons.
pieces.answer: The magnetic force is always at right angles to the electron's velocity, so it does no work. The kinetic energy, and so the speed, stays constant; only the direction of motion changes.

steps.working: The force qvB acts at right angles to the velocity at every instant.
A force at right angles to the motion does no work, so the kinetic energy and the speed stay constant. The force only changes the direction, which gives circular motion.

pieces.mistake: Saying there is no force because the field is perpendicular to the motion. The force is largest when v is perpendicular to B; it changes the direction, not the speed.

pieces.text: Electrons with this speed are then aimed at a thin crystal, where they produce a diffraction pattern.

pieces.label: f.i
pieces.question: Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of the electrons.
pieces.mistake: Using λ = hc ÷ E, which applies to photons. For a particle with mass, use λ = h ÷ p.

pieces.label: f.ii
pieces.question: X-rays produce the same diffraction pattern from this crystal. Calculate the energy of one of these X-ray photons, in keV.

steps.working: The same pattern means the same wavelength, so E = hc ÷ λ = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.00 × 10⁸ ÷ 2.75 × 10⁻¹¹ = 7.23 × 10⁻¹⁵ J.

pieces.mistake: Giving the electrons' energy, 2.00 keV. A photon and an electron with the same wavelength have very different energies.

X.title: From generator to town
X.source: Original question in the style of the VCE Physics exam, Section B

pieces.text: A coil of 200 turns, each of area 0.050 m², sits in a uniform magnetic field of 0.40 T. It is rotated from a position where its plane is perpendicular to the field to a position where its plane is parallel to the field, in 0.025 s.

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Calculate the change in magnetic flux through one turn of the coil.

steps.working: The flux falls from BA to zero: ΔΦ = BA = 0.40 × 0.050 = 0.020 Wb.

pieces.mistake: Multiplying by the number of turns here. Flux is per turn; the number of turns enters Faraday's law.

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: Calculate the average EMF induced in the coil.

steps.working: Faraday's law: ε = N ΔΦ ÷ Δt.

pieces.mistake: Forgetting the factor N = 200, which gives 0.80 V.

pieces.label: c
pieces.question: State Lenz's law as it applies to the current induced in the coil.
pieces.answer: The induced current flows in a direction that creates a magnetic field opposing the change in flux.

steps.working: The induced current creates a magnetic field that opposes the change in magnetic flux through the coil.

pieces.mistake: Saying the induced current opposes the magnetic field. It opposes the change in flux.

pieces.text: A power station supplies 250 kW to a town at a transmission voltage of 5.00 kV RMS. The transmission lines have a total resistance of 4.0 Ω.

pieces.label: d
pieces.question: Calculate the current in the transmission lines.
pieces.mistake: Using V = IR with 5000 V and 4.0 Ω. The 5.00 kV is the transmission voltage, not the voltage drop across the lines.

pieces.label: e
pieces.question: Calculate the power lost in the transmission lines.
pieces.mistake: Using P = V²/R with the 5.00 kV supply voltage, which gives a huge, wrong value.

pieces.label: f
pieces.question: The voltage is stepped up to 50.0 kV before transmission. Calculate the new power loss, and explain why it is so much smaller.
pieces.answer: 100 W; the current is 10 times smaller, and power loss depends on current squared.

steps.working: Raising the voltage tenfold lowers the current tenfold; since P_{loss} = I²R, the loss falls by a factor of 100.

pieces.mistake: Saying the loss falls by a factor of 10. The loss depends on the square of the current.

pieces.label: g
pieces.question: Calculate the peak voltage corresponding to 5.00 kV RMS.
pieces.mistake: Dividing by √2. The peak is larger than the RMS value.

X.title: Green light: waves and photons
X.source: Original question in the style of the VCE Physics exam, Section B

pieces.text: Green light of wavelength 532 nm passes through two narrow slits 0.250 mm apart and forms an interference pattern on a screen 2.00 m away.

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Calculate the distance between adjacent bright fringes on the screen.
pieces.mistake: Leaving the slit separation in millimetres. Convert 0.250 mm to 0.250 × 10⁻³ m.

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: Explain why a dark fringe forms at some points on the screen.
pieces.answer: The path difference from the two slits is an odd number of half wavelengths, so the waves arrive out of phase and interfere destructively.

steps.working: At a dark fringe the path difference is (n + ½)λ.
The waves from the two slits arrive out of phase (crest meets trough) and cancel: destructive interference.

pieces.mistake: Saying the light is blocked by the barrier. Dark fringes come from interference, which supports the wave model.

pieces.label: c
pieces.question: Describe the effect on the fringe spacing of using red light instead.

steps.working: Red light has a longer wavelength, and Δx ∝ λ, so the spacing increases.

pieces.mistake: Saying the spacing decreases because red light has lower energy. Spacing depends on wavelength.

pieces.text: The same light shines on a metal surface with a work function of 2.10 eV. Use h = 4.14 × 10⁻¹⁵ eV s and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.

pieces.label: d
pieces.question: Calculate the energy of one photon of this light, in eV.
pieces.mistake: Using h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and then calling the answer eV. Match the units of h to the units you want.

pieces.label: e
pieces.question: Calculate the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted photoelectrons.
pieces.mistake: Adding the work function. It is the energy needed to release the electron, so it is subtracted.

pieces.label: f
pieces.question: The intensity of the light is doubled. Explain the effect on the number of photoelectrons and on their maximum kinetic energy.
pieces.answer: More photoelectrons are emitted, but their maximum kinetic energy is unchanged.

steps.working: Doubling the intensity doubles the number of photons per second, so more electrons are emitted each second.
Each electron still absorbs one photon of the same energy, so the maximum kinetic energy does not change.

pieces.mistake: Saying brighter light gives faster electrons, as the wave model predicts. The photoelectric effect shows energy depends on frequency, not intensity.

X.title: Challenge: electrons as particles and waves
X.source: Original challenge question in the style of the VCE Physics exam, Section B

pieces.text: In an electron gun, electrons are accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 2000 V. They then enter a region of uniform magnetic field of 2.0 mT, perpendicular to their velocity.

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Calculate the kinetic energy of each electron in joules.
pieces.mistake: Giving the answer in eV without converting to joules.

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: Calculate the speed of the electrons.
pieces.mistake: Forgetting the square root.

pieces.label: c
pieces.question: Justify the use of non-relativistic equations for these electrons.
pieces.answer: v ≈ 0.09c, so γ ≈ 1.004 and relativistic effects are below 1%.

steps.working: v/c ≈ 0.088, giving γ ≈ 1.004, a negligible correction.

pieces.mistake: Saying relativity only applies to spaceships.

pieces.label: d
pieces.question: Calculate the radius of the electrons' circular path in the magnetic field.
pieces.mistake: Using 2.0 T instead of 2.0 × 10⁻³ T.

pieces.label: e
pieces.question: Explain why the electrons' speed does not change in the magnetic field.
pieces.answer: The magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work.

steps.working: Force perpendicular to motion: no work is done, so the kinetic energy is constant.

pieces.mistake: Saying there is no force on the electrons.

pieces.label: f
pieces.question: Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of the electrons.
pieces.mistake: Using λ = hc/E, which is only for photons.

pieces.label: g
pieces.question: X-rays with the same wavelength pass through the same crystal. Compare the diffraction patterns and the energy of an X-ray photon with that of an electron.
pieces.answer: The patterns have the same spacing because the wavelengths are equal. Each X-ray photon has E = hc/λ ≈ 7.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ J (about 45 keV), much more than the electron's 2 keV.

steps.working: Same wavelength gives the same diffraction pattern.
Photon energy hc/λ ≈ 7.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ J, over 20 times the electron's KE.

pieces.mistake: Assuming equal wavelengths mean equal energies.

X.title: Challenge: from wind turbine to town
X.source: Original challenge question in the style of the VCE Physics exam, Section B

pieces.text: A simple generator has a 100-turn coil of area 0.020 m² rotating at 50 revolutions per second in a uniform 0.40 T magnetic field.

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Calculate the average emf induced as the coil turns from parallel to the field to perpendicular to it (a quarter turn).

steps.working: ΔΦ = BA = 0.40 × 0.020 = 8.0 × 10⁻³ Wb in a quarter period, Δt = 1 ÷ (4 × 50) = 0.0050 s.

pieces.mistake: Using a full period for Δt.

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: State the effect on the peak emf and the frequency of doubling the rotation speed.

steps.working: Peak emf doubles, since the flux changes twice as fast.

pieces.mistake: Saying only the frequency changes.

pieces.text: A wind farm produces 2.0 MW at 690 V RMS. A step-up transformer raises this to 66 kV for a transmission line of total resistance 8.0 Ω.

pieces.label: c
pieces.question: Find the turns ratio (primary : secondary) of the ideal step-up transformer.
pieces.mistake: Inverting the ratio for a step-up transformer.

pieces.label: d
pieces.question: Calculate the current in the line, the power lost in it and the voltage drop along it.
pieces.mistake: Using P = V²/R with 66 kV, which treats the whole line voltage as dropped across the line.

pieces.label: e
pieces.question: Show that sending the power at 690 V directly would not work.
pieces.answer: I ≈ 2900 A; I²R ≈ 67 MW, far more than the 2.0 MW produced, and IR ≈ 23 kV is more than the supply voltage.

steps.working: I²R ≈ 6.7 × 10⁷ W (or a 23 kV drop), which is impossible, so almost no power would reach the town.

pieces.mistake: Concluding only that losses are 'larger', without numbers.

pieces.label: f
pieces.question: Explain why a transformer cannot work with the DC output of a battery.
pieces.answer: Steady DC gives constant flux in the core, so no emf is induced in the secondary.

steps.working: A transformer needs a changing flux; DC gives a constant flux.

pieces.mistake: Saying DC is too weak.
